Like Elliot Anderson, signed from Nottingham Forest for £116m but so long ago that in transfer window time it no longer counts, Fernández is one of the new breed of Premier League central midfielders who seems to offer everything; albeit in modest qualities, and whose primary attribute appears to be the absence of exposed risk he represents.

This is the only real way of explaining the vastly inflated fee City have paid Chelsea in a race where they were the only realistic bidder. Angelo Stiller at Stuttgart – to pluck one name out of the ether – is a similar profile of midfielder of the same age who would probably have been available at half the price, and with exactly one fewer video in which he was filmed making racist and homophobic slurs. But unlike Stiller, Fernández is battle-hardened, Premier League-proven, a known known. Whatever flaws he possesses – from his slow recovery speed to occasional fits of petulance to his intolerance – have been priced in.

And if there is any coherent theme to the 2026 summer window, the Premier League’s surge-pricing era, this is probably it: the Barclays tax, the overwhelming premium applied to players who are adjusted to the league, who have been there, done that and taken the tactical yellow card. Manchester United have added Andrey Santos, Carlos Baleba and Youri Tielemans in an otherwise quiet summer. Tottenham have maxed out the credit card to bring in Sandro Tonali (£92.5m,) and Mateus Fernandes (£85m). In which context Arsenal’s purchase of Bruno Guimarães for £75m feels like a kind of weird bargain, the £4.50 pack of special offer supermarket butter.

Nevertheless, these are sums that in almost any other Premier League summer would have drawn audible gasps, that would at the very least have been attached to proven superstars, unicorn players, missing pieces of the jigsaw. With the greatest of respect, do any of the midfielders signed by Premier League clubs this summer strike you as that level of player? Anybody who might realistically hold a candle to your Vieiras and Keanes, your Lampard and Gerrards, your De Bruynes and Kantés? Perhaps the underpinning irony of this summer is that the most expensive generation of central midfielders in Premier League history is also – in relative terms – one of its most mediocre.

View image in fullscreen Enzo Maresca chose to play Marc Guéhi in central midfield rather than any of the midfielders he had available. Photograph: Conor Molloy/ProSports/Shutterstock

By way of proof, compile your own list of the best central midfielders operating in world football and count up how many of them are playing in this country. With a few exceptions, the best are elsewhere: Vitinha and João Neves at Paris Saint-Germain, Jude Bellingham at Real Madrid, Pedri and Rodri at Barcelona, Joshua Kimmich at Bayern Munich. Equally you may chuck in Frenkie de Jong, Fabián Ruiz, Fede Valverde, Aurélien Tchouaméni, Warren Zaïre-Emery.

In Premier League terms you have Declan Rice, Moisés Caicedo, Bruno Fernandes and maybe a couple of others. Enzo is handy, Mateus has promise, Baleba has played very well for very short periods of time. But for a league that is by far the world’s richest and most alluring, the absence of generational midfield talents – and particularly creative talents – is not simply an anomaly but a bug that may be progressing into a sickness.

Maresca’s deployment of Guéhi, while also a kind of unsubtle message to the City board, encapsulates this. “This is a country, a league, where you need strong midfielders,” he said, and by strong he meant physical, tenacious, good in duels, good with the shoulders and elbows. Great athletes. Capable of covering every blade of grass. The kind of thing Rodri, Bernardo Silva and Kevin De Bruyne, all in their 30s and pensioned off to slower leagues, can no longer do. A league in which running and duelling has become more important than passing, in which Dominik Szoboszlai has become Liverpool’s most important player more on his ability to get places than his ability to do anything once he gets there.

But while overt physicality is one element of the equation, it is by no means the only one. For football executives answerable to capricious owners and sensitive to public opinion, familiar players offer a kind of cherished security. Signing a known player for big money carries less reputational risk. When Arsenal blow £72m on Nicolas Pépé and it doesn’t work out, that’s Arsenal’s fault. When City blow £100m on Jack Grealish and it doesn’t work out, somehow that’s Grealish’s fault. So it will be with Anderson or Fernández or Morgan Rogers, none of whom are remotely proven, but who are at least responsible for their own failure, which in boardroom terms may as well be the same thing.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

This is how you end up with a league as a kind of feedback loop, an arms race in which the aim is not simply to sign the most suitable player for an appropriate sum of money but to ride the waves of the market, a place where inefficiency and overspending are treasured as signs of ambition. And in practice the market will reward you for this: Chelsea sign Alejandro Garnacho, he does nothing, and you potentially sell him on to Aston Villa at a small profit. What possible disincentive is there to keep doing this for as long as you can?

View image in fullscreen Sandro Tonali is a major part of Tottenham’s rebuild, signing from Newcastle in a club record £100m deal. Photograph: Tiego Grenho/Every Second Media/Shutterstock

At times it feels as if the Premier League has been reimagined as a kind of player trading vehicle, a transfer show with 380 football games inconveniently attached. But of course sport does often find a way. World Cup fatigue is yet to set in. Playing a high-energy pressing game in four or five competitions will quickly become an impossibility. According to New York Times data the Premier League still features more intensive sprinting than other “big five” leagues, but here the trend is down while elsewhere it is up. Perhaps this is the season where cohesion, craft, coaching and creativity make their long-awaited comeback?

I once interviewed a youth coach with a longstanding record of producing Premier League players, who lamented to me that academies had begun to neglect technical skill in favour of producing “800-metre runners”. And increasingly this feels like a kind of pivotal season for English football, a test of identities and values, a measure of what it ultimately wants to be. The fastest and the most furious, or the best and most beautiful? If Marc Guéhi ends up going for £150m when the window opens again, we’ll have our answer.

Sports.title: Azeez to Andrés: seven smart-looking Premier League deadline day deals
Sports.content:
Femi Azeez, Millwall to Brighton, £15m

A tricky, exciting, quick and versatile midfielder, Azeez has proven himself in the Championship with Millwall over the past two seasons and now deserves a chance to test himself in the top flight.

Brighton had been chasing him for a while and struck a deal on deadline day for a very reasonable reported initial £12.5m, rising to £15m. If he can make the step up and produce anything like his second-tier form, he’ll be a steal.

He is a high-volume producer at the sharp end of the pitch, constantly making things happen that threaten the opposition’s goal, but standing out most for his crossing. He ranked top of the Championship last season for open-play crosses (227) and expected assists from crosses (6.71 xA).

He also ranked fourth for dribble attempts (131), ninth for shots (95), sixth for chances created from open play (58). He created good-quality chances, too; only two players created more big chances than he did (18), and he ranked fourth for expected assists. His 9.12 xA alongside only seven assists suggests he may benefit from playing alongside better finishers.

View image in fullscreen Femi Azeez’s expected assists. Photograph: Opta

Ibrahim Mbaye, PSG to Aston Villa, £47m

A hugely exciting prospect. Despite being 18, Mbaye has significant and noteworthy experience under his belt. Last year he made six appearances, including in the final, for Senegal at the Africa Cup of Nations and this summer he made four appearances at the World Cup. He has also played in two Ligue 1 title-winning campaigns, including 2024-25, when he became the youngest player in PSG’s history to start a game, and won the Champions League in both of those seasons

He is a dribbling and ball-carrying menace, who always looks as if he’s about to do something special. Among players to play at least 900 minutes in Ligue 1 last season, he was 11th for carries (moving at least five metres with the ball) per 90, with 20.0, and 12th for progressive carries (moving at least five metres upfield with the ball) per 90, with 10.3. Most of the players above him in both lists are defenders, who naturally have more space to move into.

He was third for take-on-ending carries, or running with the ball for at least five metres before attempting to beat an opponent with a dribble, with 2.9 per 90. And he also has end product to boot. He scored at Afcon and the World Cup despite limited minutes and his 0.45 goals or assists per 90 for PSG last season is not to be sniffed at.

Kevin Danso, Spurs to Sunderland, loan with buy obligation

Danso had a pretty impossible task over his two years at Tottenham. He was the back-up to the first-choice centre-backs Cristian Romero and Micky van de Ven, playing intermittently on both sides of central defence in dysfunctional teams jumping between styles of play, and he very rarely played for any consistent run of games.

He was unfairly compared with the players he was replacing for much of his time there, but the truth is he was always reliable enough. He excelled, however, when Romero got injured during the run-in last season and he was called upon in Spurs’ time of need as they scraped clear of relegation.

He may not be the best on the ball – though he is hardly terrible – but he is an excellent deep defender. Among those to play at least 1,000 minutes in the Premier League last season, Danso ranked first for clearances (8.2 per 90) and headed clearances (6.3), and was fifth for aerial duels won (4.8 per 90).

He could thrive at Sunderland, who spent more of their out-of-possession game time in a low block than any other team in the Premier League last season (25%). Danso could be perfectly at home in this setup, paired alongside the player he beat into second place for clearances and headed clearances: Dan Ballard.

View image in fullscreen Sunderland’s low-block, time used. Photograph: Opta

Iliman Ndiaye, Everton to Man City, £65m

It was always said during Pep Guardiola’s time at Manchester City that attackers had their wings clipped in terms of individual freedom, limited to playing within the parameters of the manager’s meticulous gameplan.

But dribbling ability became increasingly important in the final years of his reign, with Jérémy Doku and Antoine Semenyo on the wings and Rayan Cherki in between. Doku (162) and Semenyo (144) ranked first and second for dribbles attempted in the Premier League last season, with Cherki ninth (111). They also ranked first (84), fourth (59) and eighth (51), respectively, for dribbles completed.

With the deadline-day addition of Ndiaye, City have gone in even harder on dribbling ability under Enzo Maresca. The Senegal international ranked second for dribbles attempted (136) and dribbles completed (73) in the Premier League last season.

View image in fullscreen Iliman Ndiaye’s dribbles. Photograph: Opta

Matias Fernandez-Pardo, Lille to Newcastle, £51m

Fernandez-Pardo’s versatility is a major attraction. He’s comfortable playing off the left and cutting in on to his right foot, or as a No 9. Although not the bulkiest, he has explosive pace and promises to be a threat in behind.

The Belgium international is arguably at his most threatening when running with the ball because he does so with such purpose. His 122 carries progressing the ball at least 10 metres upfield in Ligue 1 last term were bettered by only seven players, several of whom were defenders.

On top of that, he ranked top for carries into the penalty area (69) and seventh for carries ending with a shot or chance created (39).

View image in fullscreen Matias Fernandez-Pardo’s chance creating carries. Photograph: Opta

Malick Fofana, Lyon to Sunderland, £30m

Fofana appeared to be enjoying a swift rise in 2024-25, only for a serious ankle injury to massively disrupt his development in 2025-26. Sunderland will be hoping they can get him back to the levels shown the season before last, when he was a real livewire on Lyon’s left flank.

He contributed nine goal involvements (five goals, four assists) in 1,586 minutes in Ligue 1 in 2024-25, averaging one every 176 minutes. Only eight forwards (900+ mins) averaged more expected assists per 90 (0.25).

The most eye-catching aspects of his game, however, were his dynamism and pace. He could be difficult to stop once moving, and this made him a very useful outlet. Among Ligue 1 forwards (900+ mins), his 16.6 carries per 90 ranked him sixth, and he moved up to third for progressive carries per 90 (11.5).

Fofana is direct, exciting and has significant potential. He is a player Sunderland could make a profit on if he reaches the levels previously expected.

Chema Andrés, Stuttgart to Brighton, £20m

Andrés arrived to bolster Brighton’s midfield options after Carlos Baleba’s exit to Manchester United. Although a different type of midfielder to the Cameroonian, Chema is another with vast potential.

A product of Real Madrid’s academy, Chema joined Stuttgart last summer. During his sole campaign in the Bundesliga, he was in and out of the team but caught the eye at the base of their midfield.

Comparisons have been made to Rodri because of his physical attributes and nominal role as a holding midfielder. He doesn’t have anything like the same influence in possession but Chema is tidy on the ball.

It’s what he offers defensively that is most notable, however. He’s been broadly praised for his anticipation and reading of the game, ranking second among midfielders (900+ mins) since the start of last season for interceptions per 90 in the Bundesliga (2.3).

This is an article by Opta Analyst

Sports.title: Arsenal poised to land PSG’s Élisa De Almeida on WSL transfer deadline day
Sports.content:
Arsenal are expected to finalise the signing of the France defender Élisa De Almeida before the 11pm BST Women’s Super League transfer deadline. The club are understood to have agreed a fee of just over £500,000 with Paris Saint-Germain for the 28-year-old.

PSG, for whom De Almeida has played since 2021, are less willing to let their Nigeria midfielder Jennifer Echegini go. The 25-year-old is understood to be the subject of interest from Manchester City but PSG were fighting hard to keep her on Thursday morning.

The WSL champions’ desire to add to their squad is understood to have been fuelled partly by the knee injury sustained by Vivianne Miedema, which will keep her out for an unspecified time.

The WSL season gets under way on Friday when London City Lionesses host Manchester United. The new United head coach, Eva Olid, said on Thursday her team would not add more signings. United secured the Mexico midfielder Rebeca Bernal, who can also play at centre-back, on Wednesday, and Olid said at her first press conference since replacing Marc Skinner that Bernal would be available for Friday’s match.

Olid, the former Hearts manager, is promising to bring “attacking football” to United. She used the word “attacking” eight times during her 17-minute press conference and spoke of her enthusiasm for trying to develop young players. She said of her attacking style: “They appointed me for that reason. I have to go with that. We will be brave in attack, trying to play that attractive football. Our main focus [is] that attacking mentality. We want to play with the ball, a nice football, create a lot of chances.”

On waiting until January before adding more players, Olid said: “The players I need are different from the players the previous manager needed. [It has been a] short period to react. We have some plans in January about signing players that I really need for my style of play. It was not about signing players quick. It is about signing the right players.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Olid was also asked about United’s investment in the women’s game, with Chelsea spending nearly three times as much as United on their women’s team wage bill in the most recent set of published accounts. Olid spoke positively about her club’s backing, saying: “The message has always been about: ‘We want to invest in everything.’ As I said, not just on players. Because I think it is important we have the right staff, the right coaches … The message is that they want to win. They want to win. I think I am here to make that happen, but with a solid identity.”

Sports.title: Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 13: Tottenham Hotspur
Sports.content:
Guardian writers’ predicted position: 5th (NB: this is not necessarily Suzanne Wracks’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)

Last season’s position: 5th

Prospects

Last season Tottenham matched their best Women’s Super League season with a fifth-place finish. However, they ended with four points more than in 2021-22 and closed the gap on fourth from 10 points to four. That is all the more impressive given their 11th place the preceding season.

It’s fair to say then that Martin Ho has rejuvenated the side. That has come with increased support from the wider club. This summer their recruitment strategy has turned heads with top young talents such as the club-record signing Alice Sombath and the goalkeeper Selma Panengstuen added alongside experienced WSL performers such as Shekiera Martinez and Kirsty Hanson. The club secured their top five targets early in the window too, to give the team as full a pre-season together as possible.

They secured three friendly wins, against Granada and Birmingham, which sandwiched a 2-1 defeat against Real Madrid, and Bristol City. Their 5-0 defeat of Bristol City was particularly pleasing for Ho, who said: “As I’ve said to the players, we have a good enough squad with depth in it that we can really compete.” The manager is working his players hard, with many speaking about the intensity of training. Martinez said: “The intensity is really high, the training has been really tough, so I can’t wait until the league starts.” Players are enjoying the burn, though, because they have bought into Ho’s vision for the way the team should play and his and the club’s ambitions for the short, medium and long term. How well Tottenham will do when other teams are also investing heavily is hard to predict, but many regard Spurs as the dark horses who could frustrate the top teams and big-spending London City Lionesses.

Off-field picture

Backing for the women’s team has ramped up a gear from top to bottom after the departure of the former chair Daniel Levy. The arrival of Vinai Venkatesham as chief executive in April 2025 has probably played a part, given his vocal and active backing of the Arsenal women’s team while he was at Tottenham’s rivals. There has been some change this summer, with Andy Rogers departing as managing director of the women’s team after 24 years at the club in various roles. Financially, the club have increased their investment in the women’s team, with turnover up from £3.39m in 2023-24 to £4.41m in the year ending June 2025. Their next accounts will probably show further investment. In July the club were dealt a blow after a high-court decision to block plans for a new women’s and girls’ football academy in Whitewebbs Park.

The manager

Ho was patient in his approach to the squad he inherited last summer, keen to not write anyone off despite their flirtation with relegation. Toko Koga and Cathinka Tandberg were the only additions and Ho gave everyone a chance to show what they could do when playing the way he wanted. That earned him a lot of loyalty and respect and his careful and thoughtful approach to squad development alongside his tactical outlook have made him a key factor when players choose to join. That is reflected in the number of his former players who have signed up to work with him again, including Signe Gaupset in January and Hanson and Panengstuen this summer. Repeating or building on his debut season will be tricky with other teams also investing ambitiously, but Ho seems very capable of doing either.

Star signing

Sombath’s big fee will have made a lot of people very excited but the recruitment of Hanson is perhaps the shrewdest of the signings. The understated 28-year-old joined from Aston Villa having finished as the third-highest goalscorer in the WSL last season. Hanson, one goal behind Alessia Russo and nine behind the Golden Boot winner, Khadija Shaw, was the highest-scoring midfielder in the league. She is an exciting addition to Spurs’ spine, is hugely consistent and is in her prime.

View image in fullscreen The Scotland international Kirsty Hanson has joined Tottenham and signed a long-term contract. Photograph: Ali Painter/WSL/Getty Images

Stat attack

Tottenham had a very weird 2025-26 in front of goal. Excluding penalties, they scored 1.55 times more than expected. They were close to hitting par. Yet they were up by 8.12 goals against xG in open play but down by 6.57 on set pieces. Their per-game average for the latter (0.30) was worse than any men’s side in Europe’s big five leagues. Making more of their set plays could have a huge impact.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Set for a breakthrough

There are big expectations around Sombath. The 22-year-old centre-back has joined from the eight-time European champions Lyonnes, having been ushered into the senior set-up there by the now Chelsea manager, Sonia Bompastor. Sombath won a Champions League title and five league titles with the French club and has learned her trade under the tutelage of the influential centre-backs Wendie Renard and Griedge Mbock. She is able to play at right-back or centre-back and featured in each of France’s four games at the 2025 European Championship after getting her first cap in November 2024.

What they say

“I’m training now with her and I think she’s so underrated. It’s better when people call you underrated and all your teammates know how good you are. I think Drew is really good. So, she really surprised me. ‘Surprised me’ sounds bad, but it’s more just that now I’m training with her every day, I’m like: ‘Wow’” – Victoria Pelova on the new captain, Drew Spence

Where are they playing their home games?

Spurs will continue at Leyton Orient’s Brisbane Road, with select showpiece fixtures at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. The first of those will be on 25 October when they host Arsenal, and Manchester United will be welcomed to the main stadium in February. In the year ending June 2025, matchday revenue was down from £513,00 to £433,000. There will be a desire to get more people watching to help offset some of the increased investment. The football is delivering for fans who go or tune in so the club need to find a way to capitalise on that.

Sports.title: How the search for younger players is driving the Premier League’s internal transfer market
Sports.content:
The boy prophesied to be the next Frenkie de Jong made a mere 20 first-team appearances in the Eredivisie for Ajax before moving on to Newcastle United this summer. Sean Steur is 18. And once a credible Premier League club came calling, there was little the four-time European champions could do to hang on to a prodigy who would sooner play for the 1968-69 Inter-Cities Fairs Cup winners. Newcastle were willing to pay $27m (£20m) for him, or north of $1m per senior appearance.

De Jong, for what it’s worth, had been a regular in the Ajax first team for two years, before departing for Barcelona at age 22.

Rather than pass from Lille to one of France’s richest clubs, as a teenaged French-born standout would have done until recently, Ayyoub Bouaddi, Morocco’s 18-year-old World Cup sensation, bypassed this career step and hopped straight to Manchester City for $110m (£81.5m). Ibrahim Mbaye, who has played fewer than 1,000 Ligue 1 minutes for serial champions Paris Saint-Germain is off to Aston Villa, who paid $63m (£47m) for the 18-year-old winger.

The above signings notwithstanding, the Premier League’s transfer business has been remarkably insular this summer. Arsenal’s most expensive signing came from another Premier League team. So did Brighton’s. And Chelsea’s. And Crystal Palace’s. And Everton’s, Leeds’s, Manchester City’s, Nottingham Forest’s, Manchester United’s, and Tottenham’s. The latter two clubs, in fact, brought in all of their transfer or loan or free recruits from either current or freshly relegated Premier League teams.

And yet this incestuous transfer habit is also of a piece with the influx of teenagers.

If there’s a single conclusion one can draw from the last few transfer windows, it’s that the Premier League’s purchasing power is so much larger than everybody else’s that it is quietly but routinely vacuuming up the world’s best young players long before they hit their prime, just to see who pans out. The result: when those players mature, the market for them is largely contained to itself because so much of the top talent is already in England, where all the clubs that can afford them also are. You may as well shop locally when all the best products have been concentrated there for your convenience.

Besides, the league’s “profit and sustainability rules,” which have been replaced by the “squad cost ratio” regulations, encourage clubs to swap players at a high volume, only exacerbating this trend.

Crunching the numbers – with a solemn salute to the good people at Transfermarkt.com, who are doing the lord’s work in tracking all this stuff – it emerges that the Premier League has paid a transfer fee to sign teenagers to permanent transfers far more often than any of the other leagues in Europe’s traditional big five.

This may feel counterintuitive in the sense that England’s clubs are viewed as the apex predators in the market, picking off the best talent developed by others. But, increasingly, they are also bringing along the most promising young players themselves.

When the summer window closed on Tuesday, the Premier League’s 20 clubs had completed 16 permanent transfers for teenagers. This was actually down a tick from last season’s 22, or 2024-25’s tally of 27 – although there is, of course, another transfer window to come in the winter. That brought the five-year total of such recruits to 100, or an average of 20 per season.

By contrast, clubs in Spain’s La Liga have signed just 29 teenagers over that span, or 5.8 per season – highlighted this summer by Real Madrid winning the Yan Diomande sweepstakes. Ligue 1 clubs bought 47 teenagers over the past half decade, or 9.4 per season. There is a plausible explanation here, which might be that clubs from these two nations are committed to bringing through homegrown talent recruited at a younger age, rather than buying their future first-team talents. Yet Germany’s Bundesliga clubs, also renowned for incubating the stars of tomorrow, bought in more teenagers than either the French or the Spanish, at 62 over five years or 12.4 per season.

The only league to come close to the Premier League, in fact, was Italy’s Serie A, in a stereotype-inverting twist. Italian clubs bought 80 teenagers in five years, or 16 per season. But they mostly picked them up from a decidedly different segment of the market than Premier League clubs went shopping in.

In 2026-27, so far, the 16 teenagers signed in Serie A went for an average transfer fee of $8.2m (£6.1m), whereas the 16 that were England-bound fetched an average of $32m (£23.7m). This was also true in 2025-26, when the Italians spent $7.4m (£5.5m) on the typical teenager and the Premier League teams spent $21.8m (£16.1m). This was in part because Premier League teams were buying higher-profile players, but also because Italian teams – especially the middle class of clubs – have historically speculated on fairly cheap young players and collected them in bulk. They would, and often still do, pick them up by the handful in the equivalent of micro-transactions amounting to as little as $58,000 (£43,000).

In other words, Premier League clubs are buying equity in promising startups; their Serie A counterparts are betting on penny stocks. The former can simply afford to spend on a player who may well become a star in a few years for the same price as everybody else has available to lay out on their key recruits.

All of which goes some way towards explaining why the Premier League clubs no longer seem to go after the game’s true superstars playing abroad – why Vinícius Júnior never came to Arsenal this summer, aside from his apparent contract leverage ploy at Real Madrid. Rather, they seem to feel confident that all the talent they need is already available in their own back yards – with a proven track record in their league. They brought them there at a young age themselves, after all.

Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: US Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts, which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.

Sports.title: Deadline-day shambles leaves Everton and David Moyes fighting the odds again
Sports.content:
To be placed in the same bracket as owners whose lack of ambition, lack of resources and/or incompetence has contributed to the longest trophy drought in Everton’s history, particularly 20 months into a reign that has accompanied the move to a glittering new stadium and the clearing of onerous debt, should be cause for considerable discomfort and embarrassment at The Friedkin Group (TFG) on Wednesday. The slight on Everton’s owner is neither unkind nor unfair. At least Farhad Moshiri had a go before the taps were turned off.

TFG may have restored financial stability to Everton after the near-ruinous chaos of Moshiri’s final years and his attempts to sell to 777 Partners but its reputation as “winners” – as the club’s chief executive, Angus Kinnear, labelled his American employers – has been shredded in the space of four days. The description always appeared generous given its approach to the summer transfer window, part two of Everton’s strategic rebuild according to Kinnear. But from accepting Nottingham Forest’s £35m bid for Harrison Armstrong on Saturday morning to Folarin Balogun walking away from a £40m move from Monaco on Tuesday night, and more in between, TFG has positioned itself as just another Everton owner unable or unwilling to realise the club’s potential and to give an expectant fanbase grounds for optimism.

Evertonians hoped for an overdue departure when TFG acquired the club in December 2024 and proceeded to refinance damaging loans and the long-term repayment costs of Hill Dickinson Stadium. The shambles of deadline day, however, was all too familiar and has caused serious damage to its standing among supporters.

David Moyes kept his counsel throughout pre-season as Everton spent £16.5m on Hayden Hackney, rising to £25m for last season’s Championship player of the year, £18m on each of Merlin Röhl and Tyrique George, who he had on loan last season, £7m on Christian Nørgaard and swapped Dwight McNeil for Brennan Johnson. The most Everton paid up front for a player all summer would prove to be £18m.

When Moyes did eventually speak in public it was to stress, repeatedly, the need for Everton to sign more players, more quality and to keep their best talents. At the end of last season he had 22 outfield players at his disposal. At the start of deadline day he had 20 outfield players. By the end of transfer deadline day he had 18.

That total includes one striker, Thierno Barry, no back-up for either full-back and, strictly speaking given that Ainsley Maitland-Niles did not start out in the position, no natural right-back. Everton sold their most creative asset, Iliman Ndiaye, to Manchester City in a below-market price £65m deal despite the Senegal international having three years on his contract. They sold Beto, their only striking alternative to Barry, before securing a replacement and were left desperately scrambling around for one when Balogun’s medical went awry.

View image in fullscreen Everton have sold Iliman Ndiaye (left) and brought in Merlin Röhl (right) for £18m in the summer transfer window. Photograph: Robin Jones/AFC Bournemouth/Getty Images

Manchester United said no to a loan offer for Joshua Zirkzee that arrived a few hours before the deadline. Tammy Abraham said no to leaving Aston Villa. Finally Balogun, having arrived later than scheduled for his medical and seen Everton renegotiate the terms of his fee with Monaco, compounded the chaos by also saying no despite signing a deal sheet shortly before 11pm. Barry looked out of his depth for much of his debut season in the Premier League. Now he is the precious commodity that Everton cannot afford to lose.

Kinnear, perhaps in response to Moyes raising concerns over Everton’s business for the first time, gave several local interviews two weeks ago that painted a rosy picture of the club’s finances, transfer strategy and ambition. Subsequent events have cost him credibility on every count. The chief executive also got his manager’s back up by claiming TFG regarded not qualifying for Europe last season as “a failure” and that the squad is better placed to sustain a European challenge while striving to end Everton’s 31-year wait for a trophy.

Moyes’s team face-planted during last season’s run-in, failing to win any of their last seven games when Europe was in reach. He has been challenged to go further with fewer resources. An added annoyance for Moyes and supporters is that Everton have started this season brightly, only to be surrounded by problems entirely of the hierarchy’s making.

It was Kinnear who implemented a new “senior leadership team” at Everton and the move away from a director of football model. The team consists of the technical director, Nick Cox, director of scouting and recruitment, James Smith, director of football strategy and analytics, Chris Howarth and head of player trading, Nick Hammond. Moyes is also part of the leadership team, although he has appeared to be on a different page this summer. There has been sensible, cost-effective recruitment for Hackney, Röhl and Johnson but the end to the window invites criticism of the leadership team’s effectiveness and expertise. It resembles a case of too many chiefs and no clear direction, especially given some of the targets Everton went for in the final days.

View image in fullscreen Harrison Armstrong is Everton’s first academy prospect to establish himself in the first team since Anthony Gordon. Photograph: Michael Steele/Getty Images

The collapse of the Balogun deal has caused turmoil at Everton but a player getting cold feet over a move or a medical jeopardising a deal can happen. It is events under Everton’s control, and decisions they have taken, that are of greater concern. TFG’s decision to accept Forest’s offer for Armstrong, the first academy prospect to graduate through the ranks and establish himself since Anthony Gordon six years ago, was the first indication that Everton were struggling to meet the new squad cost ratios. So much for a new financial era at Hill Dickinson.

TFG merits some credit for listening to supporters over the proposed sale of Armstrong and pulling the plug. To then consider selling Ndiaye to Tottenham for £60m and spending £35m on Richarlison, however, was another alarming sign.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Everton have been looking for a right-back since Moyes returned to the club in January 2025, and needed one before then. Moyes wanted Guéla Doué from Strasbourg but the 23-year-old was deemed too expensive. Doué joined Bayer Leverkusen on deadline day for £25.7m. At least five alternatives were explored before Everton, their £9m deal for Fulham’s Kenny Tete having fallen through, signed Maitland-Niles as the £4.3m answer to one glaring problem.

A bigger weakness lay up front. No Premier League club of serious intent would enter a second season with their striking options limited to Beto and Barry. An upgrade was essential. Instead, Everton downgraded. So much for the leadership team’s vision and the owner’s ambition.

Everton are the lowest net spenders in the Premier League over the past five years and, more by accident than design, ended this summer making a net profit of £25m on transfers. TFG committed £78m on signings in a summer where, by the calculations of the football finance expert Kieran Maguire, the average spend per Premier League club was £181m. Everton’s outlay does not include the significant cost of re-signing Jack Grealish on loan.

TFG’s frugal spending and efficiency drive – redundancies were made behind the scenes at Everton this summer – has fuelled talk of Dan Friedkin and co looking to sell the club. However, the owners have allocated £40m to cover the compensation payable to Burnley should Everton fail in their appeal against the outcome of a profitability and sustainability breach case, and are investing almost £14m in infrastructure projects at Hill Dickinson, Goodison Park and Finch Farm training ground.

What is certain is the anger TFG would face if they attended Sunday’s home game against Manchester United. Dan Friedkin has yet to attend a match at Hill Dickinson, where some season ticket prices were increased by up to 10% this season.

The Everton fans’ forum and Everton fan advisory board issued statements on Wednesday criticising the club’s amateurish, unambitious approach to the transfer window. The 1878s, the group of volunteers responsible for the impressive tifos and banners at the stadium, has withdrawn its support for the foreseeable future. “We do not feel that our fanbase’s ambitions and the club’s ambitions align right now – what happened yesterday has proved that even more,” the group said.

It looks a long road back to acceptance for TFG, Kinnear and Everton’s senior leadership team.

Sports.title: Premier League money has lost all meaning amid chaotic spectacle of excess | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
There was a research study a few years back into a key period in the life of the TV show Location, Location, Location. You know the one. Half an hour of mid-morning drift. Hosted by two people whose common quality is they both look as if the minced essence of Wellington boots, the Volvo XC40 and the phrase “picky bits” has been reconstituted into human shapes, then sent out to judge people for buying houses.

The big reveal was always the bit where they came back a year later and saw how much the value had shifted. Because all conversations about houses are, in the end, an excuse to talk about money. Oh wow, it’s gone up by £20,000. You are good. Oh no, you’re now bankrupt and your flat looks like a hostage cell with fairy lights. Unlucky. You are bad.

What the study found was that prices basically always increased. Ripping out the stairs, living in a tent in the garden, arguing about what to do with the two-and-a-halfth bedroom – all of this was irrelevant. These were the boom times of the early 2000s, UK housing recast as a global money trap, an endlessly whirling laundromat, a bricks and mortar central bank bond.

These people could have bought their run-down three-bed, left it empty and done absolutely nothing for two years. The price would have still gone up. That drama about exactly which shade of Anaconda Breath Morgue And Cakebread Mega-Gloss to use in the underfloor wine cave? Just doesn’t matter. Buy the soil. Shut the door. Let money do its thing.

And yes, this is a way of talking about the 2026 summer transfer window, and the way in which everyone has basically now been Chelsea-ed. Think back four years to the start of the age of Clearlake, the first post-Roman spree. At that time it seemed impossible there could be a profitable outcome. Chelsea were out there buying the vintage copper-plate statement bidet. Chelsea were digging out a third sub-basement. Who will redeem this expense? Who will provide a similarly deranged response to such overinvestment?

Well, it turns out the market will do this for you. If you’d predicted then that Chelsea would miss out on the Champions League and go through five permanent managers, but still make a profit from selling Enzo Fernández, would anyone have believed it?

View image in fullscreen Todd Boehly has overseen big changes on and off the pitch during his time at Chelsea. Photograph: Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC/Getty Images

Or that Mykhailo Mudryk could run around briefly like a deranged hamster, get banned for failing a drugs test and still become a potential growth asset? This is pre-subprime crash energy. Yes, you can install a solar-powered mega-wetroom that fires sourdough breadsticks directly into your eyes. Whatever. Ownership is all. Money will take care of you.

There are still levels to this. The one Chelsea thing to shift in the window is that the curtain has now been drawn on those initial eight months, the period where Todd Boehly became the world’s worst director of football, a director of football who basically didn’t know what football was.

That period has now been safely capped off. Only two players remain. Rough out the numbers and Chelsea spent something like £200m in fees, wages, leaks and cuts, with only Malo Gusto and Wesley Fofana to show for it. No real damage. Money comes, money goes. We roll on.

This is the lesson of the latest summer transfer window. Right now it doesn’t really matter what you do in the Premier League. Just being in it is the thing. With one caveat, which is that nobody actually knows what’s happening here. We can marvel at a record window. We can see the biggest spenders are Manchester City on £457.5m, the lowest Crystal Palace on about £50m, the highest net Liverpool on £216.8m. We can pore over Aston Villa buying the bones of a new squad for £56.7m net gain.

View image in fullscreen Liverpool’s £123m signing Bradley Barcola checks out Anfield. Photograph: Liverpool FC/Getty Images

But we can’t know what it means, at least not financially. This is part of the design of money on this scale. As the then Federal Reserve chair Alan Greenspan put it in a famous speech on the mysteries of big money: “How do we know when irrational exuberance has unduly escalated asset values, which then become subject to unexpected and prolonged contractions?”

Nobody knew what this meant then. Nobody knows what it means now. “Irrational exuberance” is a good phrase, one Greenspan later said came to him in the bath. It was designed to convey the essential point: opacity, vagueness, invisible flows. If not for those actually riding the tide, because someone is always making money. Someone out there actively wants the Premier League’s financial chaos, and is benefiting from it gloriously.

Otherwise, reading the runes is just a matter of guesswork. Money moves between networked entities. Everyone inside wins. Everyone outside pays for it. But still, this feels new, if only in its extremity.

This was captured by the weirdness of Sky Sports’ transfer deadline programme on Tuesday. At one point a man appeared strumming a guitar, smiling as if he had just filleted a litter of kittens in his basement, and sang a Bradley Barcola Liverpool song to the tune of Don’t Dream It’s Over, like this is all just normal and fine.

Later there was a golden period at about 5.30pm where every deal just seemed wrong and impossible, a fever dream after an over-ripe seafood risotto. Aston Villa have paid £47m for an 18-year-old winger. Gabriel Jesus is going to Barcelona. Jack Grealish is having a medical at Everton, an event that seems to prove the non-linear nature of time, a medical that is always happening, never not happening, a constant time-space event.

View image in fullscreen Gabriel Jesus at his Barcelona unveiling. Photograph: Javier Borrego/AFP7/Shutterstock

Meanwhile two private jets are on the tarmac in Lyon as three clubs try to sign Malick Fofana. “We STILL don’t know what Malick Fofana is thinking,” the man with the microphone concluded, mournfully, and this seemed profoundly true and on point. We don’t. Does Malick Fofana even know this? If so, how can he? Nobody else has a clue what’s going on.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

It is worth trying to list the best deals. Harry Wilson on a free can only be good. Djed Spence to Inter is great. Forza, Djed. Barcola to Liverpool for £123m is lots of money, but he’s really young and knows how to score once he’s settled.

Newcastle seem to have had a good window, racking up a list of signings that scream inside knowledge and good data, and chime with Matthias Jaissle’s mercurial vibe. Manchester City’s signings have to be good. There’s so many of them, and they’re all excellent players. That midfield is surely just too big to fail.

Arsenal will also be fine, despite not signing a 1950s-style hotshot goal ace with dynamite in his boots and the brain of a hungry magpie. Yes, they’ve lost two, maybe three attackers. But these are Jesus and probably Gabriel Martinelli, meat in the room, plus Leandro Trossard, replaced by basically the same guy. Arsenal won the league with Kai Havertz, Martin Ødegaard, Bukayo Saka and Eberechi Eze short of their ceiling. If you can’t score enough to win with that lot then it’s really not the players.

Manchester United’s window looks quite good, but also scattergun. Carlos Baleba may be great, or may wander around like a lost child in Lidl before being loaned to Monaco. Tottenham have mined the club’s DNA, gone back to their spiritual roots, and signed players who will be really good for four games, then disappear and get tattoos.

Meanwhile Everton have swapped Dwight McNeil for Brennan Johnson. What does it mean? Can you even visualise this as an event? Beto and Iliman Ndiaye have gone, taking away a third of last season’s league goals. Welcome, Everton fans, to the fully immersive Thierno Barry multiverse.

Otherwise the main takeaway is the meaninglessness of big football money. Most notably the size of the most basic fees. Little wonder there is a sense of alienation from familiar notions of team building, blocks in place, footballers as recognisable avatars of graft and cultural chemistry. These are stocks, talent units, a flow of resources.

View image in fullscreen Caleb Yirenkyi challenges Arsenal’s Myles Lewis-Skelly on his Coventry debut, having joined for £23m this summer. Photograph: David Price/Arsenal FC/Getty Images

Remember the Peter Odemwingie deadline day fiasco, where Odemwingie sat fuming in his car while the world was sucked into this human drama? That whole thing was about the unbridgeable leap from £2m to £3m. Coventry have just signed Caleb Yirenkyi from Nordsjælland for £23m. Does “Caleb Yirenkyi” really exist? Are you sure?

Who pays in the end for this circulation of funds? You, for starters. There is no such thing as football money. It’s all TV rights, state propaganda funds and hard private investment from the kind of people who really don’t give without taking back in the end.

On one level books are being balanced, accounting rules satisfied, clubs swapping assets at fees driven in part by regulatory requirements. More obscurely Boehly once talked about a rush of cash being diverted football’s way as a sub-avalanche from quantitative easing in the US, because money just has to go somewhere. No, me neither.

All that seems certain is money is being pushed around the board. And that it feels wildly abstract. The window was thrilling, its possibilities endless, a shot of blood for the new season. Beyond this, big football and big finance are playing their own game, in a way that goes beyond the human scale and into a world of pure money. The message below the headlines is clear. This thing belongs to them. Your job, human consumer unit, is simply to look at it and have feelings.

Sports.title: Walsh caps Champions League progress for Chelsea despite Real Sociedad grind
Sports.content:
Chelsea ensured there will be three Women’s Super League teams in the league phase of the Champions League as Keira Walsh’s second-half strike against Real Sociedad extended their three-goal margin from the first leg of the third-round qualifier.

The 5-2 win against the Spanish side in Chelsea’s first game at Wimbledon’s Cherry Red Records stadium gave Sonia Bompastor’s side a commanding lead in the tie, after a rusty start had forced them to come from a goal down. It wasn’t a particularly pretty performance, though, and that continued into the second leg against La Real, who will now drop into the Europa League.

Bompastor, who returned to the dugout after serving a one-match ban in the reverse game, made four changes for the trip to San Sebastián, probably with one eye on the WSL opener on Saturday against Aston Villa. The scorer of Chelsea’s second last week, Veerle Buurman, was named on the bench, alongside Katie McCabe, Sjoeke Nüsken and Alyssa Thompson. Among those to come in was the 20-year-old midfielder Lexi Potter, who scored in her first league start for Chelsea, a 2-1 win against Brighton, in March.

There were only two changes for the home team. The change that mattered most, though, was the one that had taken place in the ­dugout. In between these two critical ­Champions League qualifying games, Arturo Ruiz, the Real Sociedad ­manager, exited and was unveiled as the new Brighton manager following the shock departure of Dario Vidosic. If Vidosic’s exit had been a surprise, Brighton poaching Ruiz was a bigger one. Gorka Álvarez, who left Real Sociedad in 2025 following three seasons managing the reserves and a year as an assistant to SD Eibar’s women’s team, was hurriedly brought in to lead them in their Liga F opener against Logroño on Saturday, a 2-0 loss, and the second leg against Chelsea.

It was a mountain of a task ­facing the 40-year-old and, in many respects, a bit of a free hit, with few expecting Real Sociedad to come close to overturning a three-goal ­deficit against European heavyweights.

However, setting the tone for his tenure and building confidence was important. La Real did well against the visitors, holding Bompastor’s side at bay until Walsh swept in from a corner in the 54th minute to kill any outlandish hopes there may have been of a comeback.

Until then, the London side ­struggled to create clear chances with La Real mirroring their well-organised display in the first half of the first leg.

Ellie Carpenter, playing further forward, ahead of Lucy Bronze on the right, was Chelsea’s best outlet but they couldn’t capitalise on her balls into the middle. Walsh’s side-footed effort in the first half was weak and easy for the goalkeeper Julia Arrula. Aggie Beever-Jones had a good chance to break the deadlock moments before Walsh’s goal but the forward’s strike was too central and Arrula made an easy save.

The perfectionist that Bompastor is, she will be unhappy with the nature of the two games, but the reality is that reaching the league phase, for a team desperately wanting European glory, was what mattered most. In the end the result was comfortable, even if the performance wasn’t, and Chelsea had the chance to give debuts off the bench to their new signings Nelly Las and Giulia Dragoni, and minutes to the talented 17-year-old Chloe Sarwie.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

They will have also benefited from valuable competitive minutes before they kickstart their WSL campaign by hosting Aston Villa at Stamford Bridge on Saturday.

Bompastor said: “Today we gave some really good opportunities to the young players to come and experience a Champions League game, so when you have the opportunity to do that, I think it’s always something really positive. I’m happy and really excited now to be in the Champions League this season. The goal was for us to qualify, which is what we have done.”

Sports.title: 'This could put people's lives at risk': The 'deeply worrying' dangers of Olympian boxer Anthony Fowler's Supreme Peptides selling unlicensed 'DIY Ozempic', a mystery London lab and how regulators are cracking down on 'repeat offender'
Sports.content:
'This could put people's lives at risk': The 'deeply worrying' dangers of Olympian boxer Anthony Fowler's Supreme Peptides selling unlicensed 'DIY Ozempic', a mystery London lab and how regulators are cracking down on 'repeat offender'

Unlock more of the best of our journalism with a DailyMail+ subscription - brilliant exclusives, in-depth insight and the writers you love every day

Former Olympic boxer turned influencer Anthony Fowler has joined the booming market in cheap 'DIY Ozempic' in a way which scientists have told us could be putting lives at risk, a Daily Mail Sport investigation has found.

Fowler, who we exposed last year for making potentially dangerous claims about his cannabis oil products, has now expanded into peptides, by spinning a new business out of his Supreme CBD firm. The company was willing to sell weight-loss products to a would-be buyer while not disclosing the contents of the product and simply instructing them to inject themselves over several weeks to lose weight and ‘see what results you get’.

After approaching Fowler, 35, who won Commonwealth Games gold in 2014 and boxed for Team GB at Rio 2016, as part of our undercover investigation into his activities, Daily Mail Sport was offered a 40mg dose of a weight loss peptide for £120 by his new Supreme Peptides business and told it had reduced Fowler’s brother’s weight by two stone. We were told the product was ‘similar’ to the licensed weight-loss drug Mounjaro but had ‘no side effects’.

Under UK law, any companies using medical claims to sell products – including those pushing obesity treatments – must have the appropriate authorisation from the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) before selling or supplying it. Daily Mail Sport has found no evidence that Supreme Peptides has any products registered with the MHRA.

The MHRA told us it did not comment on potential or ongoing investigations. It said: 'If a product is classified as a medicine and is not appropriately authorised, we take regulatory compliance action.'

One of the products pictured on Fowler’s Supreme Peptides website – Tesamorelin, used in the US by HIV patients and people looking to shed abdominal fat – is not an MHRA-authorised medicine and selling or supplying it in the UK is illegal. Fowler is offering it for sale at a price of £89.99 for 10mg.

Former Olympic boxer turned internet influencer Anthony Fowler has joined the booming market in cheap 'DIY Ozempic' in a way which scientists have told us could put lives at risk

Fowler, who we exposed last year for making potentially dangerous claims about his cannabis oil products, has now expanded into peptides - pictured with girlfriend Serena Stregapede

Fowler, 35, won Commonwealth Games gold in 2014 and boxed for Team GB at Rio 2016

Channa Jayasena, a professor of medicine at Imperial College London, told us that it was ‘deeply worrying’ to see people, desperate to lose weight but unable to access prescription-only drugs, being offered unlicensed products.

Jayasena, a professor of reproductive endocrinology, which deals with hormone and fertility issues, said: ‘This could put people's lives at risk. You have to make peptides using very strong chemicals and then purify them using more strong chemicals.

'These chemicals are highly toxic and they are purified under incredibly rigorous conditions and standards, that need to be kept. My concern is that these are black market synthesised peptides, which have potential impurity and no guarantee of what is inside them.’

A major investigation by the Daily Mail into ‘DIY Ozempic’ sellers last year found that peptides – the active ingredient in licensed weight-loss drugs – were being sold to people to make cheap home-use kits without the legally required medical checks or monitoring. Scientists told us that customers didn’t know what they were buying or whether the advised dosage was safe.

Potential harms include increased cancer risk and damage to organs. Huge demand for weight-loss injections – now believed to be used by around 2.5 million Britons – has fuelled a booming black market.

Liverpool-based Fowler, who continues to use retired professional footballers Paul Merson, Chris Kirkland, Matt Le Tissier, John Aldridge and Emile Heskey to promote his cannabis oil products, is openly claiming on his social media channels that his peptides should be taken for weight loss. In a post last month he claimed to have 'a lab I use in London’ which tested them. Aldridge and Heskey have been promoting his weight-loss claims.

Katie Price has also been posting about Supreme Peptides, saying this week: 'Only the best from @SUPREMEPEP_1' on a post talking about how 'brilliant' tesamorelin is.

One of Fowler’s Instagram posts depicts a chiselled man bearing a six pack beside a fat man scoffing food, and declares of the health safety authorities: ‘They don’t want you having whats good for you (sic).’

Since setting up his peptides business, which he registered at Companies House in June, Fowler has fallen foul of Instagram rules and the platform suspended his account last month, depriving him of a key way of getting orders and issuing payment instructions to customers. He told his followers that Instagram had ‘grassed' and ‘banned’ him and that he was ‘absolutely fuming’.

Former professional footballer Emile Heskey has been promoting Fowler's Supreme CBD products

Katie Price is a public backer of Fowler's Supreme Peptides brand on social media

One product pictured on Fowler’s Supreme Peptides website – Tesamorelin, used in the US by HIV patients and people looking to shed abdominal fat – is not an MHRA-authorised medicine

The ex-boxer set up an alternative account but Instagram has continued to prevent him from responding to customers’ direct messages. From his sun lounger on holiday, Fowler told his followers on August 27 that his DMs were working, only to state in a later post that he was being ‘harassed’ because they were blocked ‘yet again’.

Amid his Instagram difficulties, Fowler directed followers to the account of an ‘Anthony Lloyd’ whose WhatsApp profile picture is the Supreme Peptides brand, telling them this person would ‘look after you if you want to LOSE WE*IGHT or get in shape’.

Fowler avoids spelling ‘peptide’ and ‘weight’ properly in his posts – posting instead about ‘p*ptides’ and ‘we*ight’. Concerns have been raised that users on Instagram have been deliberately disguising words with asterisks, symbols and altered spellings in an apparent attempt to avoid automated moderation, which will hide posts from a user's feed.

When we approached Lloyd, posing as a buyer seeking a cheaper alternative to Mounjaro for his overweight wife, he immediately took our inquiry off-platform so that we could securely communicate via WhatsApp.

In an exchange there, Lloyd told us that it would be £120 ‘for 40mg’ of the weight loss peptide. He detailed the paraphernalia he was including at that price, including the ‘pen’ – a syringe – with which to inject the drug and an ice pack to keep it at a low temperature. It was 'lab tested' and 'already mixed ready to go,' he said.

At no stage did Lloyd ask the buyer’s wife’s Body Mass Index (which tells doctors whether such a drug may be prescribed) or about any underlying health conditions and he was vague about the quantities, telling us to inject 2mg once a week for three or four weeks and ‘see what kind of results you get’.

When our customer asked if this product was 'similar' to the medically licensed weight loss drug Mounjaro, Lloyd replied: ‘It’s similar mate but this has no side effects.’ Lloyd claimed that Fowler’s brother has ‘already lost two stone’.

We messaged Fowler when he temporarily regained access to his Instagram messages, posing as another customer, ‘Emma’, asking for ‘weight loss if you have a product that works?’ He passed her straight on to Lloyd, who offered the same dosage as our first buyer at the same price and told us he was Fowler’s supplier.

The second customer asked if the product was similar to Ozempic. Lloyd replied: ‘It slows down (your) appetite' and told her that the 40mg dosage should last her ‘two to three months’ if she took 2mg per week.

Fowler's Supreme Peptides website, which makes multiple claims that the products are sold for research only

The former boxer appears prominently on the website's homepage

'Emma' asked for an image of the bottle of the weight-loss drug she was buying, to establish what it contained, but could not get one out of Lloyd. It transpired that the product being sold for weight loss was not among the scores pictured on the Supreme Peptides website. Lloyd told her: ‘All other peptides are on the website but if you wanted that one you would have to contact me.’

She asked: ‘Mind if I ask why this one is different to the ones on the website?’ He seemingly avoided answering, telling her simply: 'This one is a weight-loss peptide.’

When ‘Emma’ again asked Lloyd about the specific chemical ingredients in the weight loss peptide she was being offered, he simply told her it was for ‘research purposes’ and referred her to the Supreme Peptides website, where there is no information.

Supreme Peptides products require a bank transfer for the weight-loss drug, which would entail revealing our identity, so we have not followed through on the £120 purchases.

Fowler appears to be trying to exploit an MHRA loophole, under which certain substances may be supplied for legitimate 'research' without being licensed as medicines, by claiming that he is supplying them for ‘research purposes’.

Professor Jayasena, who has examined Fowler’s Supreme Peptides claims for us, said: ’I find the mention that this is “for research use only” deeply worrying and completely incongruous with what I'm seeing – which is a clear solicitation of members of the public.

'The idea of members of the public who clearly don’t have any likely or plausible role in doing research, such as a university or a government or a private laboratory would have, asking for small quantities of peptides is completely far-fetched. It's inconsistent with conducting research. Researchers do not do mail order delivery with needles or answer emails on how to inject stuff.’

Lynda Scammell, head of borderline products at the MHRA, told Daily Mail Sport: ‘We disregard claims that products are for “research purposes” if it is clear that such claims are being used as an attempt to avoid medicines regulations. If there is evidence within the promotional material that the products are in fact unauthorised medicines intended for human use, we will take appropriate regulatory action.’

Since setting up his peptides business, which he registered at Companies House in June, Fowler has fallen foul of Instagram rules and the platform suspended his account last month

He told his followers that Instagram had ‘grassed' and ‘banned’ him and that he was ‘absolutely fuming’

Many peptides are sold with no medical claim, such as those sold for bodybuilding, so do not fall within MHRA scrutiny. But the huge growth in their use as a cut-price Ozempic alternative has seen the regulator raid a number of premises involved in manufacturing and distributing unlicensed weight-loss medicine this year.

Fowler also repeatedly tells his followers that his products are British-made and superior to substandard Chinese imitations.

Professor Jayasena added: ‘Any drug or high-quality chemical that's made for human consumption, particularly medicine, needs to be subjected to standards – incredibly rigorous standards – which control even the temperature logs of the fridges and the freezers in which the drug is kept.

'You have to show the stability of your compound. You have to show bugs growing in it. You have to show purity. It is a real hole in the head – and that's why only big pharmaceutical companies do this type of stuff – and it doesn't matter where it’s made.'

After our series of exchanges with Anthony Lloyd over a period of ten days, his Instagram account disappeared on August 28. It is unclear whether he removed it, or it was forcibly closed.

From his sunshine holiday location, Fowler has now been directing customers who want to buy peptides from him to the Instagram account of his brother, Peter Fowler. Last week, he set up a new TikTok account to promote his peptides.

Daily Mail Sport can reveal that Fowler's Supreme CBD firm has been put on an Advertising Standards Authority 'non-compliant' list of repeat offenders after the body’s continued censure of him for claiming his cannabis oil supplements can have medical benefits failed to deter him.

That listing is supposed to trigger an investigation by Liverpool Council Trading Standards. But throughout all of our reporting on Fowler, Liverpool City Council has been singularly unwilling to provide us with any sense of whether Supreme CBD has been or might be subjected to its scrutiny.

Former Liverpool and England goalkeeper Chris Kirkland has also promoted Fowler's products

Fowler also repeatedly tells his followers that his products are British-made and superior to substandard Chinese imitations. But he did not respond to any of our questions

The council said: ‘We don’t comment on investigations. Any issues that are raised are investigated as and when they arise.’

Daily Mail Sport approached Fowler and asked him if he knew that MHRA approval was needed to legally sell peptides being marketed as an obesity treatment.

We asked him the nature of the ‘research’ his customers were being told the peptides being sold to them was for. We asked him why he didn’t picture the £120 weight-loss peptides on his website, like all his other peptide products?

We asked him for the name and location of his London ‘testing lab’ and the name of his supplier. He has not responded to our questions.

Sports.title: Fans call for investigation into Premier League refs after Mike Dean reveals their 'minigames' of deliberately not blowing the whistle for 25 minutes or refusing to leave the centre circle - but senior officials cast doubt over claims
Sports.content:
Football fans are calling for former referee Mike Dean to be investigated over his admission that he used to play ‘minigames’ when officiating Premier League matches.

Dean, 58, retired from refereeing in 2023 after over 20 years of officiating at the highest level in English football.

Now that the dust has settled on his professional career in the game, Dean has admitted to playing a game where he would see how long he could go without blowing his whistle during Premier League matches.

The ex-official also revealed that he would try and stay in the centre circle for as long as he could during some games.

‘There used to be games we would have for a laugh,’ Dean said on Jamie Vardy’s Having a Party podcast.

‘It would kick-off, right; see how long we could go without blowing a whistle. I done that a few times in the Premier League, before VAR, obviously. Went 20, 25 minutes without blowing the whistle.’

Mike Dean has admitted to sometimes trying to see how long he could go without blowing his whistle when refereeing Premier League matches

Dean was a professional referee in English football for over 20 years before retiring in 2023

Dean continued: ‘I used to do another one in the Premier League, I used to stand in the centre circle and see how long I could stay in the centre circle before I had to leave. That was just me joking about. Got about 15 minutes once, in one game.’

His comments have raised eyebrows within the refereeing community, with senior figures questioning the plausibility of his claim given the lack of detail.

According to senior officials, Dean provided no indication of when these alleged ‘minigames’ took place. He also claimed they occurred before VAR was introduced for the 2019-20 season, meaning any such incidents would have taken place under previous leadership - and current bosses are insistent that 'integrity and impartiality' are at the heart of referees' decision-making.

Nevertheless, Dean's revelations have sparked outrage within the football community, with many fans taking to social media to voice their displeasure. One X user even claimed that Dean should be investigated.

They wrote: 'Why the f***‘s he admitting to this? “Oooh look at me I ruined the integrity of top level football matches while getting paid a f***ing fortune for a laugh”. And people wonder why we all think refs are ****.'

Dean admitted, somewhat dismissively, that sometimes there was an element of wanting to be the ‘centre of attention’ when he was on the field.

‘It’s about wanting to be more a part of the game than what I should have been,’ Dean said. 'If you play an advantage and it works off, you do celebrate it; if you get a decision right you kind of want to celebrate.

‘I’d celebrate with the lads in my ear pieces and stuff. If you play an advantage and somebody scores, I think it’s great. Love it.’

But despite his prior explanations to Vardy, whom he officiated several times while the striker played for Leicester, fans found his declaration ‘baffling’.

Well-known X account, @HLTCO, wrote: ‘Yeah, not like your job was to officiate games properly. Mike Dean has said stuff like this before, Clattenburg has openly talked about letting teams self-destruct too. They seem to think it makes them sound like lads. Baffling mentality.’

Dean revealed his 'minigames' when speaking on Jamie Vardy's podcast, and his quotes have caused outrage

Another person added: '“Professional” referee by the way. This is something you would expect from a Sunday league keeper who’s earning pittance to get abused.

‘What an absolute f***ing ****. Always behaved like he was more important than the game being played around him.’

A different account wrote: ‘How about, and I might be going out on a limb here, concentrating on officiating the matches properly rather than playing silly little games with yourself. Mike Dean thinking this makes him sound like a right lad is baffling to me.’

One football fan believed there should be further furore about what they deem ‘corruption’, despite the already high number of disapproving takes.

'I’m sorry but how is this guy not being taken to the cleaners for brazenly admitting this s*** in public???

‘The first part about seeing how long he could go without blowing whistle is actually corruption, bc that’s tacitly admitting to altering outcomes…’

Sports.title: England football legend Millie Bright reveals she is pregnant as she settles down with influencer barber Tom Mitchell
Sports.content:
England football legend Millie Bright reveals she is pregnant as she settles down with influencer barber Tom Mitchell

Have YOU got a story? Email tips@dailymail.co.uk

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

England football legend Millie Bright appears to have finally kicked her colourful love life into touch after finding the man of her dreams – and announcing she is set to become a mother.

The former England and Chelsea captain couldn't contain her joy as she revealed she is pregnant in an interview.

She told Women's Health: 'It's been very hard to keep it a secret, but it's finally out.

'It's the greatest gift you can be given – to bring a life into the world – so we're excited.'

The announcement comes just four months after it was revealed Millie, 33, was quietly settling down with influencer barber Tom Mitchell.

They revealed their relationship after first meeting to create content together, saying: 'Turns out we ended up creating something a lot more special.'

It came just months after the former Lioness announced she was quitting football as she declared herself 'not happy' before pulling out of the England squad for the Euros in Switzerland.

England football legend Millie Bright appears to have finally kicked her colourful love life into touch after finding the man of her dreams - and announcing she is set to become a mother

They have since gone on to show off their glamorous lifestyle together attending film premieres and dressing up for awards ceremonies as well as enjoying holidays in Portugal and America.

In the US they watched England defeat Panama at New York's MetLife stadium during the World Cup, and took an 'unforgettable' helicopter trip over the Manhattan skyline.

The couple are documenting their life of 'laughs, chaos, adventures' and behind-the-scenes 'random moments' on a joint Instagram page.

Now Tom, who runs his own salon in Sheffield, has said of their happy news: 'We're grateful. I was very excited when I found out. I jumped up out of bed and then I was an emotional wreck until about 3 or 4am in the morning.'

Now in her second trimester, Millie said the hardest part of pregnancy so far has been navigating the changes to her body.

She said: 'It's been difficult. I'm used to being very athletic and my body fitting into certain clothes, and that's been changing. Now I'm embracing it and I feel good about myself, confident and happy, because I'm getting to the stage where I look pregnant and feel pregnant, whereas before I just felt unfit.'

The former England and Chelsea captain couldn't contain her joy as she revealed she is pregnant in an interview with a glossy magazine

In 2020 she began dating Levi Crew, a performance coach, nutritionist and personal trainer from America

Millie gained a reputation as one of the most feared centre-backs in women's football during a 12-year career which saw her lift 20 major domestic trophies.

She played every game in England's triumphant Euro 2022 campaign and led the team to the finals of the women's World Cup one year later.

While her career went from strength to strength it appeared for a time that Millie may not be quite so lucky in love after the collapse of a string of high-profile romances.

In 2020 she began dating Levi Crew, a performance coach, nutritionist and personal trainer from America.

Millie ended up spending Christmas alone that year due to the Covid pandemic before the couple ended up sharing a home together in Surrey along with their two French bulldogs Zeus and Hera.

Millie had a tattoo of Levi's eye on her left forearm. The design also features half a tiger.

She said: 'It's my partner's eye and half a tiger, my core strength with me through thick and thin.'

The couple got engaged in December 2023 after Levi proposed during a tropical Christmas holiday.

At the time, Millie took to Instagram to share the happy news with her followers – showing off her stunning ring in the process.

But the couple split one year later and Millie began a relationship with married father-of-seven Dave Zetolofsky, 39

Mr Zetolofsky pictured with his wife Katie, who is also a director of the gym they own together

Posting photos from their break to Mauritius, Millie wrote: 'Little did I think this would be the most beautiful Christmas in my entire life…

'I said YES after the shock had settled and Levi reminded me yes or no.

'You was already my person but here's to the future bubba. I love you.'

But two years later the couple split after Millie began a relationship with married father-of-seven Dave Zetolofsky, 39.

She has told friends that her new romance with the former pro kickboxer and martial arts enthusiast had nothing to do with her withdrawal from the England squad at the time.

There was no suggestion the pair cheated on their partners.

However, their relationship devastated Dave's wife Katie, who gave birth in January that year.

Friends said Millie met Dave after she began training at the 21st Century Combat gym in Redhill, Surrey.

Sources say she joined his class this February and, after Millie ended things with Levi, Dave split from Katie 'out of the blue'.

Friends claim that after Dave left the family home, Millie paid for him to stay in hotels.

Shortly afterwards Dave was seen at Millie's home on a private road in Surrey, leaving devastated Katie with their five-month-old baby.

He is an expert in Muay Thai, a full contact martial art.

A source said: 'Millie and Dave's relationship is no secret. They've been seen out and about, and in the gym together.

'You can understand that Katie has found the whole thing pretty devastating.

'The fallout has been enormous but Millie has fallen hook, line and sinker for this guy.'

Millie was awarded an Order of the British Empire in the New Year's Honours List 2024 to recognise her contribution to the women's game, including winning the 2022 Euros and captaining England to the 2023 World Cup final. She has won 19 trophies with Chelsea.

Sports.title: Ismaila Sarr and Lamine Camara's furious agent accuses clubs of failing to 'respect African players' in astonishing attack after both stars fail to secure deadline day moves
Sports.content:
Ismaila Sarr and Lamine Camara's furious agent accuses clubs of failing to 'respect African players' in astonishing attack after both stars fail to secure deadline day moves

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

The agent of Crystal Palace's Ismaila Sarr and Monaco's Lamine Camara has astonishingly accused football clubs of failing to respect African players after his two clients missed out on deadline day transfers.

Diomansy Kamara, who previously played for Portsmouth, West Bromwich Albion and Fulham during his career, told clubs to stop treating African footballers as 'just a commodity' in a scathing attack on Instagram, hours after the window slammed shut.

Senegal international Sarr had hoped to secure a move away from Crystal Palace amid links to Liverpool and Galatasaray but ultimately finished the window at Selhurst Park, while Camara's £47million transfer to Chelsea collapsed at the 11th hour after Monaco pulled out of the deal.
