World.title: Gauteng PKTT arrests alleged mastermind behind Emfuleni electricity syndicate
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The Gauteng Political Killings Task Team (PKTT) has arrested the alleged mastermind behind a syndicate accused of facilitating illegal electricity connections and stealing infrastructure at Emfuleni Municipality.

The 25-year-old suspect was arrested on Thursday, shortly after being released on bail in an unrelated matter. She is the eighth person to be arrested in connection with the case.

The case against seven other employees attached to the municipality’s Revenue and Electricity departments has been postponed.

The syndicate is alleged to have cost the municipality R9.9 million in lost electricity revenue and the theft of critical infrastructure.

The woman is expected to make her first appearance in court on Monday, 7 September. She faces charges of theft, damage to and theft of critical infrastructure, and money laundering.

“Police investigations are continuing, with authorities working to identify and apprehend all those involved in the illegal electricity connections,” police said in a statement.

World.title: eThekwini Metro Police jobs 'not for sale' amid scam claims
World.content:
DURBAN - The eThekwini Municipality says Metro Police jobs are not for sale.

This follows allegations that a Metro Police official received more than R400,000 from people who were allegedly promised jobs.

According to an investigative report, 71 people were duped.

There have been allegations of a R20-million law enforcement recruitment scam. The matter was first flagged in 2019, prompting the Metro’s internal investigations unit to commission a probe.

A second report, completed in June 2026, could not verify the alleged multimillion-rand corruption. However, it found that a junior officer had allegedly received R420,000.

Metro Police Commissioner Sibonelo Mchunu says the junior officer was not part of the recruitment team.

“He was just a worker working at the park, monitoring the process and scamming people outside,” says Mchunu.

The officer was employed by Metro Police in 2024.

He has since been subjected to disciplinary and criminal processes.

The City is calling on members of the public to report any suspicious activity.

The DA, meanwhile, staged a protest outside the municipality, calling for lifestyle audits of Metro Police and senior municipal officials.

The City has promised to release the findings of the Metro Police investigation once all disciplinary processes have been completed.

World.title: History not a marketing gimmick: Stalwarts' families slam Glenlivet advert
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The families of South Africa’s struggle stalwarts featured in a controversial Glenlivet whisky advert have accused the brand of “commercially exploiting” the legacy of the 1956 Women’s March.

The advert, which triggered widespread outrage on social media, featured actress Dineo Langa observing portraits of five liberation figures, including Women’s March leaders Sophie Williams-De Bruyn and Lilian Ngoyi.

At the centre of the backlash was the way the advert connected Williams-De Bruyn’s age at the time of the historic march to Glenlivet’s 18-year maturation process.

Williams-De Bruyn was 18 when thousands of women marched to the Union Buildings in Pretoria on 9 August 1956 to protest against apartheid pass laws.

The advert’s attempt to draw a parallel between her age and the whisky’s maturation process struck a nerve, prompting criticism from political parties, members of the public and those connected to the women whose activism helped shape South Africa’s history.

Glenlivet and Langa subsequently apologised, while the advert was removed from social media platforms.

In a statement, the whisky brand said it was investigating how the campaign was conceptualised and approved.

But for the families of the struggle stalwarts, the controversy goes beyond what they describe as a poorly judged .

“Our mothers and grandmothers did not march so that their courage, suffering and sacrifices would one day be trivialised and turned into a convenient marketing gimmick for commercial gain.”

Williams-De Bruyn was equally unequivocal.

The struggle stalwart said seeing South Africa’s liberation history used to sell alcohol was “deeply painful”.

“I did not give Glenlivet permission to use my image or legacy,” she said.

Williams-De Bruyn said the history preserved by generations could not simply be removed from its context and transformed into a corporate asset at the discretion of a brand.

The families have acknowledged the apologies issued following the backlash but say they are still demanding answers.

Among their questions are how the campaign was conceived, what historical considerations were taken into account during its development and why the families were not consulted before the advert was released.

“Deleting the social media post does not erase the harm done,” they said, noting that the material continues to circulate online and is still being encountered by families, comrades and members of the public.

The families have also indicated that they will pursue accountability through the Advertising Regulatory Board.

World.title: US energy firms dominate Venezuela deals worth billions
World.content:
CARACAS - US energy firms on Wednesday signed a raft of multi-billion-dollar deals with Venezuela, days after the South American country agreed to grant the United States control of a huge chunk of its vast oil reserves.

US Energy Secretary Chris Wright travelled to Caracas to oversee the signing of deals worth "tens of billions of dollars of investment," seen as a quid pro quo for Washington winning majority control of 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil reserves.

Wright said the deals signed by Venezuela with US oil major Chevron, GE Vernova, a General Electric offshoot, and Italy's ENI were "critical in starting this ball rolling of peace, opportunity, and prosperity" in Venezuela.

President Donald Trump has talked up the agreement on Venezuela's oil reserves as the "biggest oil deal in world history."

It comes as US Republicans brace for possible losses in November midterm elections due to spiralling fuel costs brought on by his war against Iran, and a broader national affordability crisis in housing, food, utilities and other basic needs.

But the deals have raised major questions about Venezuela's sovereignty.

Critics in both the US and Venezuela accuse Trump of holding the country for ransom after ousting former president Nicolas Maduro in a raid and warning that Rodriguez could face a similar fate if she doesn't fall into line with Washington's demands.

The US was not "stealing Venezuelan oil," Wright insisted to AFP and other media as he prepared to leave later Wednesday.

"All we're doing is taking an idle, underground asset that isn't doing anything for Venezuelan people and bringing the money, the technology to develop it," he said.

Interim leader Delcy Rodriguez earlier denied she was surrendering her country's riches, saying that cutting the US in on Venezuela's oil wealth is necessary to secure investment in the oil sector.

More oil "translates into more jobs, higher wages, better public services, hospitals, schools and food," she said.

Rodriguez has estimated that Venezuela will make $209 billion in profit from the deals over 25 years.

- 'Large volumes' -

The new contracts signed Wednesday will see US company Chevron and Italy's ENI ramp up their operations in Venezuela while gaining greater stakes in the oil fields.

Chevron, the top private oil producer in Venezuela, has valued its deal to develop two additional oil fields in the Orinoco Belt at $7 billion and projects output will more than double in five years time.

ENI said it had gained exclusive rights to explore the giant Junin 5 oil field.

US energy company GE Vernova, an offshoot of General Electric, meanwhile, will help repair Venezuela's battered electricity grid.

Wright told CNBC that Venezuela's oil production would top 2 million barrels per day by the end of the decade, double the level in January when US forces seized Trump arch-foe Maduro.

That would still be far off Venezuela's peak of over 3 million barrels per day in the late 1990s.

The pivotal role in the deal played by a fraud-accused Venezuelan businessman, Alejandro Betancourt, has come under scrutiny.

Betancourt has been linked to a corruption scandal at state oil company PDVSA and runs North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), Venezuela's second-largest private oil company, in which the US government is taking a 35 percent stake under the deal.

Wright on Wednesday defended NABEP's "highly successful track record of producing large volumes of oil in Venezuela," adding: "That's a business partner you can believe in."

- 'Not ready' for elections -

The agreement is a major about-face for the "Chavismo" movement of late socialist firebrand Hugo Chavez, Maduro's mentor, who nationalised Venezuela's oil fields two decades ago on an anti-imperialist platform.

It has amplified fears that the Trump administration is entrenching former Maduro loyalists, like Rodriguez -- who have shown no readiness to hold democratic elections eight months after Maduro's overthrow.

Trump on Wednesday rebuffed calls from a number of Republican lawmakers for quick polls in Venezuela.

"I just don't think they're ready yet. You know, it's very new. We took them out of a dictatorship, and we're getting along great with the government," he said.

Rodriguez took a similar line, saying there would be "an electoral process" when "Venezuela is ready."

World.title: Farming experts tout 'conscious' food systems to fix agriculture woes
World.content:
PARO - Farmers around the world are struggling with the impact of climate change, financial pressures and depleted soil -- and industry experts say bringing consumers closer to the people who produce their food could provide a solution.

A group of farmers, scientists and development specialists are pushing for "conscious food systems", arguing that many of the problems in today's food production are the result of people being "alienated" from nature and each other.

Current food production systems are "not really fit for purpose," said Andrew Bovarnick, head of food systems at the United Nations Development Programme.

"It's causing huge environmental problems... we have more food in the world, but there are more than ever people who are malnourished and starving," he said.

Bovarnick spent years looking at technical solutions to food production challenges, but believes technology alone cannot solve the problem.

Instead, he and other members of the Global Conscious Food Systems Alliance, meeting in Bhutan this week, want more "mindful" food production focused on protecting the environment, farmers and consumers, rather than maximising profit or output.

World.title: George Lucas unveils art galaxy at his new LA museum
World.content:
LOS ANGELES - George Lucas, the legendary creator of the "Star Wars" saga, on Wednesday showcased his long-awaited Museum of Narrative Art, the culmination of nearly two decades of work and numerous obstacles.

"I'm used to doing the impossible. This one almost broke my will," Lucas said as he offered reporters a first glimpse inside, ahead of the museum's official opening on September 22.

Lucas has described the complex built with his wife and business partner, Mellody Hobson, as the "people's temple of art."

"Part of the problem is I'm a contrarian. I don't like to do things that people think can be done," he added. "I'm fascinated by doing things that people say can't be done."

The futuristic-looking museum was built on what used to be a parking lot next to the University of Southern California, the filmmaker's alma mater.

That personal connection, combined with Los Angeles's place at the heart of American cinema, made it the ideal home for the project, executive director Tracey Bates told AFP.

At the entrance, visitors are greeted by the yellow Naboo N-1 starfighter from "Star Wars: Episode I – The Phantom Menace" (1999), but with more than 9,300 square meters of exhibition space, the offerings go far beyond the beloved saga.

Its more than 30 galleries feature works by artists including Banksy, Frida Kahlo, Jacob Lawrence, Charles White and Robert Colescott; comics by Winsor McCay, Jack Kirby and Frank Frazetta; and illustrations by Norman Rockwell, Jessie Willcox Smith and N.C. Wyeth.

"Narrative art is stories that are illustrated," Bates said. "A story that you can see a picture in one frame, and it doesn't need further explanation."

World.title: Brussels Diamond League finals Day 1: Five events to watch
World.content:
BRUSSELS - Armand 'Mondo' Duplantis and Jamaica's world 100m champion Oblique Seville headline the opening day of the two-day Diamond League finals in Brussels on Friday.

AFP Sport looks at five stand-out events to watch:

Men's pole vault

Double Olympic and triple world champion Duplantis, with 15 world records to his name, continues to dominate the world of men's pole vaulting.

But the US-born Swede conceded after victory at last week's Diamond League meet in Zurich he would have to continue giving his A-game to fight off Greek rival Emmanouil Karalis.

Duplantis won in Switzerland with a best of 6.25 metres, while Karalis set a new personal best of 6.20m in what transpired to be a real contest.

"This is the highest level of competition that there's ever been," said Duplantis.

"Manolo's jumping is amazing right now, so I have to jump my A-game."

Karalis added: "Hopefully, in the future we are going to have amazing battles. Hopefully, I can get a win one day."

World.title: Patients robbed at gunpoint during brazen North West hijacking
World.content:
MAFIKENG - Five patients were robbed at gunpoint and forced out of a patient transport vehicle before an armed man drove off with it in a brazen hijacking in Moretele.

The incident happened shortly after 8.30pm on Tuesday in Tladistad village near Makapanstad.

The vehicle was transporting patients when the driver stopped after dropping off an elderly patient.

According to the North West Department of Health, an armed man then approached the vehicle, pointed a firearm at the driver and demanded his cellphone and wallet.

The driver was ordered to lie on the ground.

The five patients inside the vehicle were then robbed of their cellphones and ordered to get out before the suspect fled in the vehicle.

READ | Three suspected hijackers killed in shootout

The stolen vehicle was recovered less than 40 minutes later at Kalkpunt near Rabosula village.

The suspect remains at large, with police continuing their search for the armed hijacker.

North West MEC for Health Sello Lehari condemned the attack and called for the swift arrest of the suspect.

“A patient transport is not a luxury vehicle,” Lehari said.

He said the vehicles were public health resources intended to safely transport patients, particularly elderly and vulnerable people, to and from healthcare facilities.

“There is absolutely no justification for hijacking a vehicle that is serving our communities,” Lehari said.

World.title: Embu MCA's six vehicles, land frozen over Sh111.5m graft
World.content: The Standard Group Plc is a multi-media organization with investments in media platforms spanning newspaper print operations, television, radio broadcasting, digital and online services. The Standard Group is recognized as a leading multi-media house in Kenya with a key influence in matters of national and international interest.

World.title: IG Kanja orders probe into abduction of Standard Group Associate Editor
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Standard Group PLC Associate Editor Alex Kiprotich. [Stafford Ondego, Standard]

The Inspector General of Police Douglas Kanja has ordered immediate and transparent investigations into the alleged abduction of Standard Group Associate Editor Alex Kiprotich in Gilgil.

The National Police Service (NPS) said it had taken note of reports that Kiprotich was allegedly kidnapped on Tuesday and had moved swiftly to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident.

NPS spokesperson Muchiri Nyaga said the police service treats kidnapping and abduction with the utmost seriousness, describing the offences as a threat to the lives, liberty and security of Kenyans.

“The Inspector General of Police has accordingly ordered immediate investigations to determine what transpired, including the identity of the heavily armed individuals reportedly seen ordering occupants out of their vehicle,” Nyaga said in a statement.

The NPS said its Anti-Abduction Unit, established to investigate abductions and disappearances, had taken up the matter and would work to ensure that those responsible are brought to justice.

“We unequivocally condemn any act of kidnapping, abduction, or intimidation intended to interfere with press freedom or any other constitutional right,” Nyaga said.

The police service assured the public that the investigation into the Gilgil incident would be conducted transparently, stressing that no one was above the law.

The development comes amid growing condemnation of Kiprotich’s alleged abduction, with the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) also calling for an immediate investigation.

CPJ Africa Director Angela Quintal described the incident as a “shameful indictment” of the Kenya Kwanza administration, raising concerns over the safety of journalists and press freedom in the country.

“The attempt to forcibly disappear Alex Kiprotich, three days after President William Ruto railed against The Standard Group, reflects the growing dangers that journalists face in Kenya, despite the president’s earlier promise to allow the press to work freely,” Quintal said.

The New York-based press freedom organisation further expressed concern over what it described as an escalation in cases of abductions and enforced disappearances in Kenya.

World.title: Trumpets of reforms blow louder as Kenya marks 16 years under 2010 Constitution
World.content:
The Constitution, Kenyan flag and the National anthem. [PCS]

On Thursday, August 27, a group of people largely composed of the youth gathered under some trees at Jeevanjee Gardens in Nairobi, carrying Kenyans flag, and banners and placards inscribed with "implement the constitution. Kenyans first" words.

These were in protests against what they believed is deliberate failure of those in authority to fully implement the 2010 Constitution.

World.title: Ruto allies hit back at Gachagua over IEBC tender concerns
World.content:
The Kenya Integrated Elections Management System (KIEMS) kit. [File, Standard]

President William Ruto’s allies led by National Assembly Speaker Moses Wetang’ula have launched a scathing attack on former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua and the Opposition over their criticism of the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC), citing blackmail by the Opposition.

The leaders warned that attempts by politicians to dictate how the electoral agency procures technology and other election materials could undermine public confidence in the 2027 General Election.

World.title: IEBC rejects Gachagua's claims, defends 2027 polls preparations
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

IEBC dismissed Gachagua's claims of political interference, graft and voter suppression in 2027 polls.

The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) has dismissed allegations of political interference, corruption and voter suppression surrounding preparations for the 2027 General Election, terming the claims false, unsubstantiated and aimed at undermining public confidence in the electoral body.

In a statement issued on Thursday, IEBC Chairperson Erastus Edung Ethekon said the allegations followed statements made by Democracy for Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua during a press briefing on Wednesday.

The commission specifically rejected claims that politicians had purchased a house for its chairperson to influence him, saying the allegation had changed from an alleged Sh80 million property to one worth Sh200 million.

"The allegations that a house has been purchased for the Chairperson of IEBC by some politicians for purposes of influencing him are unfortunate, unfair and unsubstantiated to date," Ethekon stated.

The commission also challenged Gachagua to provide evidence, including the location of the property, sale and transfer documents, payment receipts and details of the parties involved, and submit them to the Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission for investigation.

The electoral body also dismissed claims of improper staff changes, saying deployment and redeployment of employees was part of its normal administrative functions and was guided by its human resource policies and public service regulations.

"The Commission complies with its Human Resource policies, guidelines and other relevant instruments under the larger public service when engaging employees," the statement read in part.

It further denied allegations of malpractice against the chairperson and vice-chairperson, describing them as fabricated claims intended to damage the reputation of the commissioners and the commission.

Magarini by-election

On the Magarini by-election, IEBC said the poll was conducted in a free, fair and credible manner and was not challenged through an election petition. The commission added that it had successfully conducted several by-elections and was prepared to oversee the 2027 General Election.

At the same time, IEBC also defended its procurement process for election technology and ballot papers, saying all tenders were being conducted in accordance with Chapter 12 of the Constitution and the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, 2015.

"Two key tenders, one for the Integrated Elections Management System, hardware and accessories, and another for ballot papers and other election materials, have temporarily been halted following a request for review filed before the Public Procurement Administrative Review Board," IEBC stated.

According to IEBC, documents for the technology tender were uploaded on its website and the Public Procurement Information Portal on August 11, 2026.

The commission said the technical specifications were generic and performance-based and open to all qualified suppliers. It stressed that the procurement process was still at its initial stages and that no company had been awarded the tender.

Voter register protected

The commission also dismissed claims that voter registration data could be manipulated or shared with external parties, insisting that the Register of Voters remained under its exclusive custody.

"Voter registration involves several stages, including in-person registration, verification of identity, collection of biometric and biographical data, transmission to a central database and automated biometric deduplication," IEBC added.

Flagged records are subjected to data cleaning, validation and adjudication before valid records are incorporated into the register.

The register will subsequently undergo a 30-day biometric verification exercise, followed by an independent audit before it is finalised and certified for use in an election.

IEBC said allegations of bribery, predetermined tender awards and voter suppression were false and potentially harmful to public confidence in the electoral process.

World.title: Ruto hands Sh2.6bn to Mau Forest evictees
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto also announced the lifting pf the caveat that had been placed on land bordering the Mau Forest. [PCS]

President William Ruto has announced the payment of Sh2.6 billion to 13,000 families evicted from the Mau Forest in Narok six years ago, marking what he described as the closure of a long chapter.

Each beneficiary received Sh200,000 through M-Pesa to help them resettle and rebuild their lives away from the water tower.

Speaking at Sogoo in Narok South Constituency on Wednesday, during the final day of his two-day tour of Narok County, Ruto said the Government had taken steps to address the longstanding Mau Forest resettlement problem.

He noted that in 2023, the Government gave Sh300,000 each to 2,000 families living in tents in the Mau Forest to enable them to leave the water tower and purchase land elsewhere.

“We are today officially closing the long and painful chapter of people who were removed from the Mau Forest, which the County Government of Narok will now manage,” Ruto said.

The President criticised politicians who, he said, had continued to politicise the Mau Forest issue without providing lasting solutions.

“Many politicians have talked of the Mau question, but I talked of the Mau answer. This is why we are here today closing this chapter,” he said.

Ruto also announced that the Government had purchased 5,800 acres of land to settle families who have been living as squatters on property previously owned by the family of former Provincial Commissioner Isaiah Cheluget.

“We are processing title deeds of the people living on the land after buying the Cheluget farm,” he said.

Construction of Johanna Ng'eno University

The President also announced the allocation of Sh1.2 billion for the construction of Johanna Ng’eno University in Emurua Dikirr Constituency.

Speaking during the laying of the foundation stone, Ruto said the institution would fulfil a pledge to residents while expanding access to higher education for students from across the country.

“You told me, as residents of Emurua Dikirr, that you want a university. Today, I have brought KSh1.2 billion to construct the university that will be named after our brother Johana Ng'eno,” he said.

He said the university would create employment opportunities and attract new investments to the region.

At the same time, Ruto maintained that his administration had fulfilled at least 80 per cent of the pledges contained in its 2022 campaign manifesto.

“Kenyans will elect leaders based on their development record. Sloganeering will not make Kenyans vote for them. They have a long way to go,” he said.

The President further launched the construction of the 18-kilometre Mogondo-Cheramgoi-Mogor-Soit road in Emurua Dikirr, saying the project would improve connectivity and unlock economic opportunities in the region.

“This new road will strengthen connectivity and unlock greater economic opportunities in the region,” Ruto said.

World.title: Gachagua to Duale: You don't own pastoralists
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

DCP leader Rigathi Gachagua and delegates from Isiolo and Marsabit at Wamunyoro, Nyeri County on August 25, 2026. [Ali Abdi, Standard]

Democracy for Citizen Party (DCP) Leader Rigathi Gachagua has accused Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale of allegedly doing nothing for pastoralist communities in the country.

Mr Gachagua said Duale, while being the only CS from northern Kenya and claiming to be the spokesperson of the group, had instead been a liability to pastoralists.

“You, the Borana who are here, along with the Turkana and Somali, are all complaining like other Kenyans. You suffer from runaway insecurity and widespread underdevelopment. We must join hands to vote out this rogue government (in next year's general election),” the former Deputy President told a delegation of grassroots leaders and residents from Isiolo and Marsabit who paid him a courtesy call at his Wamunyoro rural home in Nyeri.

“Duale thinks that the pastoralists are his property, his children or servants. What has he done for the people of Isiolo and Marsabit? (He has) only rhetoric, shouting pastoralists everywhere, every day,” he said.

Gachagua questioned how Duale would be able to marshal ‘millions’ of votes for President Ruto in the 2027 General Elections while he (Duale) could only raise 7,000 votes for the UDA presidential candidate in the 2022 polls in his Garissa Township Constituency backyard.

Despite his little contribution to the Kenya Kwanza administration's victory, Gachagua said Duale was appointed as the only CS from northern Kenya but had ended up doing nothing for the region and pastoralist communities.

“He only gave him (Ruto) 7,000 votes in Garissa Township. It's Central Kenya that propelled this government,” Gachagua told the gathering.

“Duale was appointed CS and he has nothing to show apart from empty words, going round shouting (the name of) pastoralists, and you (the pastoralists) are suffering. If you love them, then why are their livestock stolen every day?” He asked the CS.

“These pastoralists are killed every day and their cows and goats stolen. What have you done for them and you are in the government?” Gachagua posed.

The Opposition leader claimed that the government was ill-prepared for the heavily forecasted El Niño rainfall, pointing out that those living in flood-prone areas like the Tana Delta and Garissa are exposed to danger.

“Now, going into El Niño, what plan has been put in place to save people from death as a result of floods and how livestock will survive?” he asked the State.

During the event, Gachagua revealed that Yusuf Huka Jillo from Isiolo would represent Upper Eastern at the DCP secretariat and serve as a member of the National Executive Committee (NEC) in an acting capacity.

Gachagua said the mountain was now complete, with Isiolo and Marsabit forming Mt Kenya North.

The locals alleged that the Health CS was interfering in Isiolo County politics, with elder Hussein Jama claiming that Duale and the Office of the DCI were shielding a section of leaders accused of corruption and criminal activities.

Speakers claimed that there was massive corruption at the local lands registry office, while Mr Jillo faulted the State for the slow pace of registration of community land in Isiolo.

Jama said Isiolo International Airport, which was constructed during the administration of President Kibaki to help in the export of miraa and horticultural goods from the Mt Kenya region and livestock products, mainly meat and hides, lies idle because the expansion of the runway from 1.5 metres to 3 metres had not been done.

In response, Gachagua said the airport was meant to create employment and wealth, but the Kenya Kwanza administration had instead left it in ruin deliberately, claiming the move was aimed at sabotaging the economy of Mt Kenya and pastoralists’ economies.

“What was the good about destroying the Imenti forest to construct an airstrip for an individual while there is an international airport meant partly to serve the entire region just a few kilometres from Meru town?” Asked the DCP leader.

World.title: Relief for schools as government releases Sh18.5b capitation
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Education CS Julius Ogamba. [File, Standard]

The government has released Sh18.5 billion in capitation to support operations in public basic education institutions during the third term of 2026, as schools reopened across the country on Monday.

Education Cabinet Secretary Julius Ogamba said the funds have already been released and will support learners in pre-primary, primary, junior and senior schools.

The allocation is intended to facilitate smooth school operations and ensure learning activities continue without disruption.

The Sh18.5 billion has been distributed across three major capitation programmes, with Free Day Secondary Education (FDSE) allocated Sh10.963 billion, accounting for the biggest portion of the Term Three capitation.

The money will support operations in public day and secondary schools and comes as institutions prepare learners for a busy academic term.

Free Day Junior School Education has received Sh6.1 billion, to support learners in the second tier of basic education and help institutions meet operational requirements as the Competency-Based Education system continues to expand.

Meanwhile, Free Primary Education has been allocated Sh1.4 billion to support learning in public primary schools.

The funds come as a relief to school heads who had raised concerns on the insufficient funds disbursed to schools this year.

However, Ogamba said the disbursement demonstrates the Government's commitment to ensuring that learners have access to free and compulsory basic education as provided for under Article 53(1)(b) of the Constitution.

“The Government affirms its commitment to fulfil its duty to learners and educational institutions,” said the CS.

Ogamba also warned school heads and principals against misuse of the funds, directing them to ensure the money is spent prudently and for the benefit of learners.

School administrators have further been cautioned against imposing unauthorised levies on parents and learners.

Ogamba said the Ministry would take firm action against institutions found to have misappropriated public resources or imposed illegal charges.

“We will deal firmly with any verified cases of misappropriation of resources and the imposition of unauthorised levies,” he said.

The warning comes as schools reopen for the third term, a period that is expected to be particularly demanding for institutions and learners because of the academic activities and assessments scheduled for the school calendar.

The Ministry has maintained that capitation is meant to ease the financial burden on families and enable schools to provide essential services without passing prohibited costs to parents.

Ogamba reiterated that school administrators must remain accountable for the public funds entrusted to them, warning that verified cases of misuse will attract action from the Ministry.

The Government has also reaffirmed that every child is entitled to free and compulsory basic education, placing the responsibility on education officials and school managers to ensure capitation achieves its intended purpose.

World.title: Egypt, Jordan FMs discuss Sinai bus crash, facilitation for Jordanian victims
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty held a phone call on Wednesday September 2,2026 with Jordanian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign and Expatriates Affairs Minister Ayman Safadi to convey the sincere condolences of the Egyptian government and people to Jordan over a passenger bus crash that occurred earlier in the day on the Dahab-Nuweiba road in South Sinai, leaving several people dead and injured.

He affirmed that the relevant Egyptian authorities were providing all necessary assistance to care for the injured and complete arrangements for transferring the bodies of the Jordanian victims to Jordan.

For his part, Safadi conveyed his sincere condolences to Egypt, its government and people, and to the families of the Egyptian victims.

He also expressed his gratitude and appreciation to the Egyptian government for its solidarity and cooperation during the difficult circumstances, as well as for the assistance provided in following up on the condition of the injured and transferring the victims’ bodies.

World.title: Egypt’s Hana Goda snatches women’s singles table tennis gold at Mediterranean Games
World.content:
Egypt’s table tennis star Hana Goda clinched the gold medal in the women’s singles event at the Taranto 2026 Mediterranean Games, adding a new milestone to her decorated athletic career.

Goda secured the gold medal after beating France’s Xiaoxin Yang 4-1 to claim the top spot on the podium.

She also won a silver medal in the mixed doubles competition, competing alongside teammate Omar Assar of the men’s national team.With this achievement, Goda continues to make history for Egyptian table tennis, reinforcing her status among the sport’s leading stars and continuing her journey of winning medals to raise Egypt’s flag high on international podiums.

World.title: Investment minister witnesses signing of MoU between Mansour, China’s Tianneng to explore battery manufacturing
World.content:
Minister of Investment and Foreign Trade Mohamed Farid witnessed on Wednesday, September 2, 2026, the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between Mansour Group and China’s Tianneng Battery Group Co Ltd to explore cooperation and investment opportunities in battery manufacturing and energy storage solutions in Egypt.

The MoU covers a study of opportunities to produce lead-acid batteries for automobiles, as well as lithium batteries for new energy vehicles, supporting Egypt’s drive to deepen local manufacturing, increase value-added production and strengthen export capacity.

The minister said lithium batteries and components for new energy vehicles were among the promising sectors under the State’s strategy to deepen local manufacturing, adding that proposed cooperation with Tianneng would enable Egypt to benefit from the company’s expertise and advanced technologies while supporting the localization of industries supplying new energy vehicles.

Egypt has strong competitive advantages for such projects, including its strategic geographic location, infrastructure, transportation and logistics networks, as well as the General Authority for the Suez Canal Economic Zone (SCZONE), Farid said.

All factors would help meet domestic market needs and expand exports, he added.

The minister further said the government was ready to provide support during the project study phase, including offering suitable industrial sites and expediting procedures for land allocation and preparation once a final site was selected.

Tianneng’s Vice President and head of the International Business Eric Xu outlined the group’s nearly 40 years of experience in battery manufacturing.

Its activities include automotive batteries, motors and mobility equipment, battery recycling and energy storage solutions, Eric said.

The group had multiple battery technologies, including lead-acid, lithium, sodium-ion and solid-state batteries. Tianneng is one of the world’s leading battery manufacturers and ranks first in China in lead-acid battery production.

Tianneng was keen on cooperating with Mansour Group and exploring investment opportunities in Egypt, citing the country’s market potential and regional location, according to Eric.

The company was currently evaluating possible sites for the project, identifying products to be manufactured locally and preparing a feasibility study, he said.

The signing ceremony was attended by Chairman of the SCZONE Mostafa Sheikhoun took part in the signing ceremony.

The meeting concluded with an agreement to continue coordination between Mansour Group, Tianneng and relevant government agencies to complete studies on the project and determine its location and target product portfolio, paving the way for implementation and helping localize battery manufacturing and boost Chinese investment in Egypt.

World.title: PM directs continuous monitoring of medicine, medical supply stocks at various hospitals
World.content:
Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly stressed the need for continuous monitoring of the availability of medicines and medical supplies at hospitals nationwide, including those affiliated with the Ministry of Health and Population and university hospitals affiliated with the Ministry of Higher Education and Scientific Research, to ensure regular supplies meet patients’ needs.

Madbouly made the remarks during a meeting on Wednesday September 2,2026 at the government headquarters in the New Capital to follow up on the availability of medicines and medical supplies at various hospitals.

The meeting was attended by Minister of Health and Population Khaled Abdel Ghaffar, Minister of Finance Ahmed Kouchouk, Minister of Higher Education and Scientific Research and Acting Minister of Culture Abdel Aziz Konsowa, Egyptian Drug Authority Chairman Ali el Ghamrawy, Egyptian Authority for Unified Procurement, Medical Supply and the Management of Medical Technology Chairman Hisham Stait, and officials from the relevant ministries and authorities.

Madbouly stressed the importance of continuously monitoring medicine and medical supply stocks to ensure hospitals maintain adequate strategic reserves, particularly amid supply-chain disruptions resulting from political developments and events in the region.

He said the state has allocated around LE90 billion in the current fiscal year’s budget to secure various medicines and medical supplies and build up adequate stocks at hospitals.Madbouly noted that the Unified Procurement Authority has an integrated system for the storage, distribution and supply of medical needs, contributing to the sustained availability of medicines and supplies.Abdel Ghaffar reviewed the availability of medicines and medical supplies at hospitals affiliated with the ministry, affirming that stocks are currently at reassuring levels and that there is no chronic shortage of medicines or medical supplies.He explained that temporary shortages of certain medicines may occasionally occur, but the required quantities are provided immediately through coordination with the Unified Procurement Authority. He described such shortages as a normal occurrence in a country with a population exceeding 120 million.

Stait stressed the importance of optimizing the use of assets and stocks, improving spending efficiency, and strengthening the resilience and sustainability of supply chains.He said the medical supply system, whose implementation has expanded significantly, has become a national tool for measuring performance and improving the efficiency of healthcare resource management by supporting the availability of medicines and medical supplies, reducing waste, improving spending efficiency, and enabling data-driven decision-making based on unified, measurable data.

Stait said 38,000 healthcare workers currently use the system to monitor procurement, supply, inventory and delivery procedures.

The system also covers 11,000 medical facilities, allowing the monitoring of needs, inventory, consumption and the movement of items across the healthcare sector, in addition to 2,000 suppliers integrated into the procurement and supply cycle.He explained that the system has helped standardize warehouses across the government healthcare sector and classify them according to their actual operational status, providing an accurate picture of warehouse activity and inventory movement.Stait stressed that electronic inventory-taking is a key pillar of the system.

A mobile application has been launched to enable healthcare teams to conduct field inventories electronically through rapid scanning using mobile phones.He said the approach reduces technology infrastructure costs while offering several strategic benefits, including generating and printing inventory records directly through the system, reconciling physical inventories with stock data recorded in the system, and updating inventory balances in real time with a high degree of accuracy and reliability.The system also ensures that inspection and inventory procedures comply with the requirements of the Central Auditing Organization and the Ministry of Finance, while standardizing inventory procedures and documenting them in a unified digital record, Stait said.

He noted that the initiative was accompanied by an extensive training program comprising online and in-person workshops and field visits to ensure that employees and warehouse managers are able to conduct electronic inventories efficiently.Stait said implementation of the system represents an important step forward for the Unified Procurement Authority, enabling financial planning and inventory management based on accurate, real-time data. This will support the optimal use of public resources and help direct medical supplies to entities with actual needs.He added that the system will improve the efficiency of supply and procurement chains, facilitate procurement and financial flows, and strengthen relations with suppliers, thereby enhancing the efficiency of the procurement and supply cycle as a whole.

He affirmed that the project falls within a broader vision to transform Egypt’s healthcare sector into an integrated digital system based on data, governance and transparency.

Stait noted that building an integrated health information database strengthens national pharmaceutical and health security, supports the application of governance and quality standards, and contributes to building a modern and sustainable healthcare system aligned with international standards.He emphasized that the healthcare-sector inventory management and governance project is not merely aimed at determining what is available in warehouses. Rather, it seeks to establish an integrated system covering the entire lifecycle of healthcare inventory, from planning, procurement, supply and receipt to storage, distribution, consumption, inventory-taking and reconciliation.During the meeting, Konsowa reviewed the availability of medicines and medical supplies at university hospitals.

He noted that the Unified Procurement Authority had increased strategic stocks of various medicines in recent days, helping improve the availability of pharmaceutical supplies and ensure continuity of medical services at university hospitals.

Konsowa also outlined several challenges facing patients receiving treatment at the expense of the state at university hospitals or through health insurance. He stressed the importance of addressing these challenges to ensure that such patients receive the necessary treatment and have access to the medicines and medical supplies they require.Madbouly directed the ministers to focus on activating the system and continuously monitoring its implementation to strengthen governance, ensure that its objectives are achieved, and improve the management and availability of medicines and medical supplies.

World.title: With Japan tightening rules for foreign residents, some wonder if it’s time to say ‘sayonara’
World.content:
Tokyo — Zen gardens, futuristic cityscapes and a vibrant food scene, combined with a favorable exchange rate against the yen, have turned Zen gardens, futuristic cityscapes and a vibrant food scene, combined with a favorable exchange rate against the yen, have turned Japan into a tourist magnet that has been drawing in record numbers of visitors in recent years.

The number of people settling down for longer-term stays, including work and study, also hit an all-time high last year, likely due to the reliable safety and convenient infrastructure the world’s fourth-largest economy has to offer.

But recently, a series of tightened immigration policies imposed by the government has made those who’ve come to call Japan their second home wonder: Is it time to say “sayonara”?

Japan has a long history of strict immigration policies and a homogeneous population. However, gripped by a spiraling demographic crisis, the country gradually opened up to foreign workers as well as seeking more international tourists.

But such efforts did not wholly succeed.

Overtourism and reports — some true, others misconceived — of foreign residents flouting local rules have recently fueled the rise of “Japan-first” politics and reshaped the trajectory of what was becoming a more open, diverse and welcoming society.

Last month, the Japanese government, led by conservative Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, said that a range of visa fees would rise in October — the latest in a series of stricter measures for foreigners.

Under the new rules, those looking to settle permanently in Japan will have to fork out 20 times more — 200,000 yen ($1,257) — to become a permanent resident.

Prices for other work and student visas will also rise.

The purpose of the spike in fees is to forge “an orderly society in which foreigners and Japanese citizens coexist,” said Justice Minister Hiroshi Hiraguchi.

That left some foreign residents in Japan worrying whether it’s the start of a trend of tougher policies for newcomers.

The people in the crosshairs

The most drastic shifts impact those who plan to stay in Japan for the longest – those applying for permanent residency, a status that grants rights to work, unlimited entries, and infinite stay.

Effective from October, applicants are required to have an income level higher than that of average Japanese households. And from next April, aspiring permanent residents need to have a projected pension fund equivalent to 30 years of payouts. They also have to speak intermediate-level Japanese.

“Considering that permanent resident is the most stable status of residence, this revision makes necessary updates to the application of independent livelihood and national interest requirements to ensure applicants do not become a public burden,” said Hiraguchi during a press conference last month.

Tourists walk along the street in Tokyo. Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP/Getty Images

Earlier this year, the government also tightened rules for foreign business owners, raising the capital requirement of a business manager visa popular among entrepreneurs from five million yen ($31,000) to 30 million ($126,000).

An impossible balance

The number of foreign residents recached 4.1 million last year, a record high representing about 3.4% of the Japanese population. More than 930,000 Chinese nationals live in Japan, making it the largest group, while about 70,000 Americans also reside there.

The recent changes followed reports that some foreign residents had been driving up home prices or evading payments for their public health insurance. Japan has a national healthcare system which requires every resident to pay a monthly or yearly fee in order to access discounted medical services.

Others have been accused of exploiting the relatively affordable policies to acquire residency by creating shell companies, prompting calls to plug loopholes.

A surge in tourists has also annoyed some locals, who’ve accused them of causing a nuisance and increasing the cost of living– problems political pundits say were sometimes wrongly attributed to foreign residents.

The anger fueled the rise of Sanseito, a minor right-wing party that rallied against immigrants in recent elections, putting pressure on the ruling Liberal Democratic Party government.

Attendees hold signs that read ‘Monitoring Hate Speech’ and ‘Sanseito, Discrimination Party, Don’t be fooled’ as Sohei Kamiya, leader of the Sanseito party, second right, delivers a campaign speech in Tokyo earlier this year. Toru Hanai/Bloomberg/Getty Images

But the government’s new policies have sparked concerns among foreigners who have built a life in the country.

Some business owners have complained that the new capital requirement, which surged sixfold, significantly reduced their cash flow, rendering their business unsustainable.

Many Indian and Nepali restaurants were reportedly forced to close after their owners — most of whom came from their native countries to seek business opportunities in Japan — said their visa renewals had been rejected.

One of those affected by the new regulations is a transgender teacher from the US, who asked CNN for anonymity, fearing it could jeopardize her immigration status.

Although she and her American spouse have been living in Japan for nearly 10 years and she speaks fluent Japanese, she told CNN that her plans-in-progress to become a permanent resident are now more challenging.

“Our long-term goal is always to gain permanent residency, and that in particular is outrageously expensive under the currently proposed guidelines,” she said. “Obviously, it’s something that we could save up for, but it’s a wholly unpredicted expense.”

Her gender identity also adds levels of difficulty. Currently, her passport identifies her as a man and she is married to a woman. She can’t change it because Japan doesn’t recognize same-sex marriage. That would eliminate the possibility of using a spousal visa in Japan, which would have provided a backup option to staying in the country should her current work visa fall through.

Tokyo-based immigration lawyer Kazuki Yuda, from Touch Immigration Law Firm, said inquiries had spiked recently as people rushed to file their applications before the new changes came in.

He said the new rules were too strict and he expected the number of people qualifying for permanent residency to drastically drop.

Takaichi’s government is walking a fine line between the need to calm public anger, on which its political foes ride, while addressing the urgent need to replenish the country’s workforce, at a time when its neighbors, from South Korea to Singapore, are loosening rules to attract young talent.

Japan’s fertility rate — the average number of children a woman is expected to have during her lifetime — plunged to the lowest in a decade last year at 1.14, although there appeared to be a slight uptick in the first half of this year, according to official statistics.

A fertility rate of at least 2.1 is required to maintain a stable population without immigration. As a result, Japan finds itself in a precarious position, caught between a lack of locals to fill roles in the workforce and a distrust of immigrants who can provide labor.

For some, Japan was already losing its appeal as a destination for work, as the yen fell to 40-year lows against the dollar. Now worries about visa costs and the uncertainties are causing some to think twice.

“As a fresh graduate, fees like this would have been impossible for me. Even now, I’m barely scraping by,” a foreign student wrote on X.

“Looking at the Japanese market 10 years from now, I genuinely feel from the bottom of my heart that things are heading for serious trouble,” she wrote.

World.title: Germany blames Russia for drone attack on Leipzig airport
World.content:
Germany has accused Russia of being responsible for the drone attack targeting Leipzig airport last month, and announced a slew of new measures against Moscow.

“We are not at war, but we are a daily target of hybrid attacks,” Germany’s interior minister Alexander Dobrindt told reporters on Tuesday, as he raised the country’s threat level assessment from “general” to “high”.

Germany’s foreign minister Johann Wadephul also ordered the closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn, and the Russian House, a cultural center, in Berlin. Germany is also tightening controls Russians entering the country.

Ursula von der Leyen, president of the EU’s executive arm, said European foreign ministers would announce a “clear response” to Russia including “additional sanctions” later this week.

The US previously assessed that an explosive-laden drone discovered at the airport in east Germany belonged to a Russian intelligence service, a US defense official in Europe told CNN.

The incident caused major disruptions and sparked security concerns across Europe. According to German authorities at the time, the drone was discovered inside a secure area of the Leipzig/Halle Airport overnight on August 4 near the airport’s south runway, where cargo flights operate.

A bomb disposal robot was deployed and the detonator attached to the drone was removed. Images of the scene showed the robot close to a Ukrainian cargo plane. The US defense official told CNN the drone was carrying military-grade explosives.

Later on August 5, a second flying object hit a cargo plane near the airport, causing minor damage. The aircraft later landed safely in Hannover.

Russia said the suggestion it was responsible for the ​drone attack was absurd. Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday night accused Germany of planting evidence in order to blame Moscow, without offering any evidence for such allegations, according to Reuters.

Moscow’s ambassador to Germany, Sergey Nechayev, earlier accused Berlin of an “unprecedented escalation of Russian-German relations.” He described the accusations as “unsubstantiated, absurd, and irrational,” and warned of retaliatory measures.

NATO chief Mark Rutte welcomed the measures announced by Germany, said the alliance’s commitment to Ukraine remained “unwavering,” and reiterated that “NATO will continue to strengthen our ability to deter and defend all Allies against any threat – including malign actions like those seen in Leipzig.”

German media also recently reported that a third drone was found in a field near the airport about a week after incidents, prompting speculation that multiple drones were meant to be used in the attack. The German Federal Prosecutor’s Office, which is handling the case, declined to comment when contacted by CNN, citing an ongoing investigation.

Leipzig/Halle, one of the busiest cargo airports in Europe, has been the base for Ukraine’s Antonov Airlines cargo airline since Russia destroyed its home base in the town of Hostomel, northwest of Kyiv, in the early days of their full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The explosives-laden drone was found near one of the Ukrainian aircraft at the airport.

Dobrindt said at the time that the incident represented a serious escalation. “Drone sightings, drone threats including in a hybrid context, are something we know from the past. That a drone armed with explosives is at an airport is a new threat scenario,” he said.

Police officers pictured searching a field at the Leipzig/Halle Airport for evidence. Hendrik Schmidt/picture alliance/Getty Images

Hybrid warfare

Western intelligence services have repeatedly pointed fingers at Russia over a series of seemingly unrelated security incidents across Europe. These have included arson, high-profile hacks, GPS jamming as well as sabotage actions against key infrastructure, including undersea communication cables, logistics centers and railways.

The US has warned that Russia might escalate further. Recent US intelligence assessments indicate Russian President Vladimir Putin could try to test NATO’s resolve by launching a limited attack on an allied country within the next few years, according to three sources familiar with those reports.

CNN contacted the Kremlin for comment on the US intel assessment on Putin.

Power grid targeted

In a separate incident on Tuesday, German authorities said part of the country’s electricity grid was sabotaged. Police discovered “several improvised explosive devices,” including some which resembled rockets, at a substation near one of Germany’s largest power plants, a police spokeswoman told CNN.

The devices were attached to a powerline leading to the substation in Turnow-Preilack, near the border with Poland, rather than inside the facility itself, the spokeswoman added. Authorities don’t yet know who is behind the attack, but they cannot rule out a foreign power or left-wing activists, Brandenburg’s interior minister Jan Redmann told reporters Tuesday.

The perpetrators used rockets to fire a “conducting material” into the high-voltage lines, causing two short circuits, Redmann said. Authorities are searching the area and have already found at least 10 rockets, though the number is still rising, he added.

50 Hertz, which operates the electricity grid in northern and eastern Germany, confirmed there had been a brief power outage but that all lines are now operating again.

World.title: It’s always Shark Week in Putin’s world. That doesn’t bode well for Trump’s Ukraine peace hopes
World.content:
Russian President Vladimir Putin traveled to Kyrgyzstan this week for the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit, a regional confab that also brought together Xi Jinping of China, Narendra Modi of India and Masoud Pezeshkian of Iran.

The leaders convened in the capital Bishkek during a week of high geopolitical anxiety, with a fresh round of tit-for-tat strikes by Iran and the US, Russian drones and missiles pummeling Ukraine and Germany accusing Russia of being responsible for a drone attack targeting Leipzig airport last month.

But Putin appeared firmly in his comfort zone. At a press conference late Tuesday, he seemed to go out of his way to make one point explicit: nations exist in a state of Darwinian competition, and Russia will prevail in a survival-of-the-fittest contest.

Asked by Kremlin pool reporter Pavel Zarubin about some unusual remarks he made a few days earlier about killer whales eating polar bears – more on Putin’s views on marine biology in a moment – the Russian president described his statement as a “spontaneous” analogy for Russia’s ongoing confrontation with the West.

“I would say that the orca is, without doubt, a formidable predator, yet it is also a highly intelligent creature, a cunning one,” he said. “The collective West, for its part, was assigned a specific definition in the Soviet era, which remains current to this day – the sharks of imperialism.”

Sharks and orcas may not quite be the same class of animal, but Putin continued with his analogy.

“The thrust of my remarks was that if anyone attempts to drag us down the food chain and devour us, to consume us, they would be well advised to expect their teeth to be broken,” he said. “And Russia stands ready to do precisely that, despite the insatiable appetites and ever-sharpening teeth of these sharks.”

Russian President Vladimir Putin talks sharks during a press conference following the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit. Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Sputnik/Reuters

The messaging here was clear, both to a domestic audience and to Putin’s international counterparts. When it comes to the war in Ukraine, Putin intends to double down, regardless of where the lines are on the battlefield and whatever economic pain Kyiv manages to inflict on ordinary Russians through a campaign of deep strikes.

Putin knows that Ukraine is on the back foot when it comes to defending its skies, and Russian forces have been blanketing Ukrainian cities with drones and missiles.

While Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned Tuesday that Russian airspace “will effectively be closing” due to the presence of Ukrainian drones, Putin dismissed the escalatory rhetoric, saying he had not heard the remark.

Such comments, Putin said, “amount to nothing less than a call for state-sponsored terrorism. And I would point out that they are asking us to resume negotiations and requesting face-to-face meetings. One does not negotiate with terrorists.”

People pass by the site of a Russian drone strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Saturday. Alina Smutko/Reuters

Putin was equally dismissive of a claim by Germany that Russia was responsible for a recent drone attack at Leipzig airport, suggesting Berlin had planted evidence in a deliberate provocation.

“There is only one explanation offered: the need to counter an ‘aggressive Russia,’” Putin said. “But where is the proof? Well, now some ‘proof’ has been planted.”

Putin’s remarks in Bishkek may have been bellicose, but he was a bit more conciliatory when it came to the Trump administration.

Asked about the recent visit by CIA Director John Ratcliffe to Moscow, Putin suggested Ratcliffe’s contacts with Russian intelligence officials were constructive, without letting slip any new details.

“Contacts are always there, even during the most difficult times of the Cold War, and they are even more so now,” he said. “We favor negotiations, any negotiations, being filled first and foremost with concrete content. And if someone makes or can make a concrete contribution to this process, we’re all for it.”

Putin also made clear whom he favors as interlocutors when it comes to striking any bargains with US President Donald Trump: the unconventional diplomatic duo of special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law.

“These are people close to President Trump. In my opinion, they are sincere people and strive to bring concrete substance to our work. And the president trusts them, which is very important, and without this it is generally impossible to conduct any negotiations,” the Russian leader said. “Both Mr. Kushner and Witkoff are always welcome guests to us, and we are happy to work with them.”

Witkoff and Kushner have made several trips to Moscow since Trump began his second term. But Putin’s preference may spark unease in Kyiv: Witkoff and Kushner have not visited Ukraine since taking on their roles as Trump’s point men for peace, and some observers worry they may support a deal weighted in Russia’s favor.

Russian President Vladimir Putin, center right, accompanied by Kremlin economic envoy Kirill Dmitriev and Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov, meet with US special envoy Steve Witkoff, center left, and Jared Kushner at the Kremlin in December. Kristina Kormilitsyna/AFP/Getty Images

Ukraine has a difficult winter ahead and there are fears Russia may launch a new wave of mobilization following parliamentary elections later this month. Putin said such speculation was “total BS.” But Putin’s comments about the animal kingdom may give a sense of where his head is these days.

The orcas vs. polar bears story first surfaced during a meeting at Moscow Pedagogical State University on Saturday, when a participant mentioned a visit to the Arctic. That comment seemed to fire the imagination of the Russian president, who asked if the student had seen polar bears.

“And killer whales live right next to them; they eat these bears like small fry – they attack in a pack and tear them apart,” Putin said, adding some political context: “That is the food chain, and children need to be told about this too, so they understand the world we live in and why we are conducting the Special Military Operation.”

Several observers noted that orcas do not, in fact, hunt polar bears – and speculated whether Putin has been watching AI slop videos. But leaving aside the dubious zoology, Putin’s almost Trumpian non-sequitur suggested that, on the existential question of continuing war with Ukraine, his stance is as hard as ever. It’s always Shark Week in Putin’s world.

World.title: 60 targets struck, 18M barrels of oil protected: The US military’s record day in the Strait of Hormuz
World.content:
The US military escorted 40 commercial vessels carrying 18 million barrels of oil through the Strait of Hormuz, marking a wartime high as Iran and the US exchanged a new round of strikes on Tuesday, two US officials familiar with the operations told CNN.

Prior to the launch of the war just over six months ago, roughly 20 million barrels a day were passing through the strait.

The US used a range of air, sea and space assets to not only continue hitting Iran’s capability to attack commercial vessels in the strait but simultaneously fended off waves of drone attacks as it conducted the risky escort operations for the ships carrying millions of barrels of oil, the officials said.

US forces also neutralized anti-ship cruise missiles during the escort operation, the first official added.

It comes as the US has focused its strategy in the war to prioritize striking targets around the strait, conducting escort operations for commercial vessels through the key waterway and maintaining its naval blockade on Iranian ports as part of a “full court press” by the Trump administration to ramp up economic pressure on the regime’s leadership, according to the officials.

Even though Tuesday’s operation was a success, officials are under no illusion that a swift solution to the conflict is close, and energy companies are still wary about the huge risks involved in sending their ships through the strait, even with military escorts. And energy prices remain high, causing turbulence in the global bond market.

President Donald Trump’s other stated priorities, including operations focused on eliminating elements of Iran’s nuclear program, have been effectively “backburnered,” for the time being, according to the first official, who reiterated that US Central Command has been directed to focus all of its efforts toward the strait and preventing oil exports from leaving or entering Iranian ports.

Trump himself has recently suggested he is content to leave Iran’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium, which was not completely destroyed in last year’s US strikes on three key nuclear facilities, buried and to monitor it from satellite imagery — despite previously insisting that securing the material was a top priority in the current conflict.

On Tuesday, the US conducted the multi-faceted operation in line with the current strategy, hitting nearly 60 military targets around the strait — including air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets, mine-laying capabilities, and communications sites — while simultaneously escorting the ships, both officials told CNN.

The US military expects to continue conducting offensive strikes near the strait, in part, because Iran has demonstrated it has the capacity to reconstitute its capabilities in a way that requires persistent maintenance, the second official said. Conducting those strikes amounts to “mowing the grass” or a game of “whack-a-mole,” in service of degrading Iran’s ability to threaten commercial ships.

People inspect damage and debris at a building that Iranian media said was hit by a US strike while a wedding celebration was taking place there, in Kuhestak, southern Iran, near the Strait of Hormuz, on Wednesday, Sept. 2. Morteza Akhoondi/Tasnim News Agency/AP

Chipping away at Iran’s leverage

But they are also a critical part of the broader military strategy for systematically chipping away at Iran’s ability to leverage the strait.

The US blockade, meanwhile, has prevented Iran from exporting any oil since July, the second US official said.

Trump said Wednesday that the most recent round of US strikes went beyond targeting Iran’s radar systems, in an effort to eliminate the nation’s ability to track ships through the Strait of Hormuz.

“They were trying to see the ships,” he said from the Oval Office. “They can’t see it because they have no radar, because we blew it up, and we blew up much more than their radar last night.”

Trump did not specify what else was targeted in its attack. But he insisted again that the US maintains control over the strait and has demonstrated that it can both strike Iranian assets along the shoreline while defending ships against any incoming attacks.

Still, it remains to be seen whether the multi-pronged military operations will ultimately force Iran to capitulate — and even if it does — how long it might take for that to happen.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent alluded to an uptick in oil flowing through the strait earlier this week, amid a recent flare-up of tensions between the US and Iran, telling CNBC that those exports hit a wartime record on Monday of more than 17 million barrels per day. “That is not Iranian control of the strait,” Bessent said.

US officials have told CNN they believe the strait is a depreciating asset for Iran, pointing to the recent progress as evidence of that assessment. But Iran, meanwhile, still likely sees its ability to negatively influence the flow of traffic through credible threats to commercial shipping as a leverage point, and shippers broadly remain skeptical that the US can implement a sustainable system.

Trump officials have repeatedly insisted that more oil is transiting the strait than is publicly known due to ships’ increasingly routine practice of turning off their transponders to remain undetected as they move through the waterway. Most if not all of the 40 commercial vessels that moved through the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday turned off their transponders in an effort to avoid detection, according to the first official familiar with the operation.

In August, Energy Secretary Chris Wright claimed that oil exports from the Middle East had risen to pre-war levels for a period.

People spend time at a beach as commercial vessels are anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran, on Wednesday, Sept. 2. Razieh Poudat/ISNA/AP

Skepticism of ‘total control’ claims

Yet despite weeks of concerted efforts to take over the strait, the administration continues to face heavy skepticism from industry officials and analysts who say the US hasn’t yet demonstrated it can reliably back up its claims of “total control” of the shipping route.

“Safe to say the administration has not covered itself with credibility,” said one person familiar with the industry dynamics, adding that even if the daily spikes in shipping volume are legitimate, “I don’t know anyone who thinks the average is that much.”

In the meantime, commercial shippers that do opt to transit the strait are largely making those decisions on a case-by-case basis, two people familiar with the dynamics said. The price of chartering an oil tanker through the strait has also skyrocketed, with some estimates putting the cost at more than $500,000 per day, offering an added financial incentive for charter companies willing to risk the voyage.

But the industry writ large is still looking for more reassurance. The cost of insuring ships, which soared at the beginning of the war, is still high, adding to the difficult calculations being made by maritime companies. And even if not successful, the continued reports of Iranian attacks on ships going through the strait remains a deterrent.

Oil also represents just one form of energy-related cargo that moves through the waterway. Tankers carrying other energy sources, namely liquefied natural gas, appear to be demonstrating even more caution due to the potentially catastrophic consequences should vessels carrying that type of cargo be hit by an Iranian drone, mine or missile, according to the first official familiar with ongoing US military operations around Iran.

Some US officials acknowledge that it will likely take time and persistence for the US military to not only continue working through its unfinished target list of Iranian military assets near the strait — capabilities that have been at least partially reconstituted during the recent pause in fighting — but also to convince the shipping industry that it is safe to travel.

The latter involves conducting consistent escort operations like what took place on Tuesday where US forces shepherd commercial vessels through a passage that has been cleared of mines. By next month, the US military hopes to widen that lane through the strait to allow vessels to maneuver more freely — with the goal of steadily increasing the amount of oil flowing through the waterway.

CNN has identified the specific inbound and outbound commercial vessels that made the trip through the strait on Tuesday — ships flagged from various foreign countries ranging from Saudi Arabia to France.

Earlier during the conflict, the US military attempted to launch a similar escort operation — dubbed Project Freedom — which was quickly shut down after the announcement caught key Gulf allies, namely Saudi Arabia, off-guard, prompting threats to block American access to basing and overflight for operations against Iran.

Months later, the war has appeared to enter a new phase, and with the Houthi rebels now launching attacks against Saudi Arabia, there is more support from regional partners for escort operations through the strait, the first official familiar with the operation said.

World.title: Liberia: Ex-President Weah Declares Democracy Under Threat, Defends Jewel Howard Taylor, Vows to Rally Opposition Unity
World.content:
MONROVIA — George Manneh Weah’s return to Liberia was always likely to carry political significance. But his first major intervention after months abroad has revealed something more consequential than the former president’s homecoming: he appears ready to re-enter the country’s political conversation at a moment when one of his closest political allies, former Vice President Jewel Howard Taylor, is facing serious criminal charges and detention.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

For Weah, the Howard Taylor case is no longer simply a legal matter involving a former member of his administration. It has become a test of how far he is willing to go for a political partner he has repeatedly treated as family, and whom he now publicly calls his “sister.”

Standing before reporters and supporters at his Rehab residence in Monrovia following his return from abroad, Weah delivered an unusually forceful denunciation of the government’s handling of Taylor’s case.

He described the charges as “bogus and unacceptable,” accused authorities of tampering with the rule of law and warned that Liberia cannot afford a justice system that appears selective. “What’s happening to the former Vice President is wrong. The rule of law is being tampered with,” Weah said.

The language was unmistakably political. But it also exposed the difficult position in which the former president now finds himself. Taylor is not merely a former vice president. She was Weah’s constitutional partner throughout his presidency from 2018 to 2024, serving beside him through the triumphs, controversies and political battles that defined his administration.

Now she is facing allegations connected to Liberia’s investigation into a major cocaine seizure, including drug trafficking and money laundering charges that she has denied.

Weah’s decision to publicly challenge those proceedings places him in a potentially delicate confrontation with the administration of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai.

His remarks suggest that his answer may extend beyond visiting Taylor in detention or issuing public statements of solidarity. “I intend to visit her,” Weah said, making clear that he wants to personally empathize with his former vice president. But the former president also linked Taylor’s situation to what he sees as a broader threat to Liberia’s democratic order.

By placing the Taylor prosecution inside a larger argument about the rule of law, Weah is attempting to transform what could otherwise remain an individual criminal case into a national political debate about justice, democracy and the conduct of government.

His argument is that Liberia cannot afford a justice system in which political identity determines who is prosecuted and who is protected. “We need to be honest with the law,” he said. “We have to be fair.”

If Weah’s position is interpreted as opposition to the prosecution simply because Taylor served in his administration, his democratic argument could lose force. But if he succeeds in separating his demand for due process from the question of Taylor’s guilt or innocence, he could establish a broader political argument capable of resonating beyond the Coalition for Democratic Change.

Weah and Taylor entered Liberia’s highest political office together after the 2017 elections, forming one of the country’s most consequential political partnerships in recent history. Whatever disagreements may have emerged during or after their administration, Taylor remained closely associated with the Weah presidency.

Now, with Taylor facing prosecution, Weah’s public defense can be viewed as a measure of political loyalty. The former president’s return comes at a particularly sensitive moment because his political influence remains significant within the opposition community.

The reception he received at Roberts International Airport was, in itself, a political statement. Supporters turned out in large numbers to welcome him home, giving Weah an opportunity to demonstrate that his political base has not disappeared despite his absence from Liberia. He interpreted the reception as evidence of the continuing strength of the opposition. “The strength of our opposition political parties,” he said, referring to the supporters who came to receive him.

Beyond defending Taylor, the former president used his return to call for a broader opposition gathering.
