He wants opposition actors to sit around a table, listen to one another and develop a common approach to what he describes as threats to Liberia’s democracy. “The voice of the people, the opposition, we need to listen to each other and find a way to move forward,” he said.

Liberia’s opposition has often been stronger in numbers than in cohesion. Political parties and personalities have historically competed for influence, sometimes making it difficult to construct a sustained opposition coalition outside election cycles.

Weah now appears to be arguing that the moment requires something different. He wants the opposition to organize around democratic principles rather than simply around the next presidential election.

Weah remains the most prominent figure associated with the CDC, but his effort to rally a wider opposition community will require him to work with politicians whose ambitions may not necessarily align with his own.

Some may see him as the natural leader of the opposition. Others may regard his political dominance as precisely the problem that a broader coalition would need to overcome. That makes Weah’s call for unity both necessary and complicated. “We all need to stand up to protect democracy,” he said.

His message is particularly significant because he framed his own conduct following the 2023 presidential election as evidence of his commitment to democratic continuity. Weah recalled that he accepted the election result after losing to Boakai by a relatively narrow margin.

His point was clear that he believes his acceptance of defeat demonstrated that Liberia’s democratic institutions can function even when political competition is intense.

That argument could become a central part of his political narrative as he seeks to reassert himself. If Weah wants to present himself as a defender of democratic institutions, his supporters and political opponents alike will expect his proposed opposition movement to operate according to those same principles.

And perhaps most importantly, it means convincing opposition leaders that his call for unity is about strengthening the opposition rather than simply restoring his own political influence.

The former president’s proposed meeting will have to confront the practical questions that have often weakened opposition politics: Who speaks for the opposition? What issues unite the various parties? How will disagreements be resolved? Will the coalition support a single candidate in 2029? And, perhaps most importantly, can political leaders subordinate individual ambitions to a common objective?

For now, Weah appears to be building the argument that Liberia needs an organized political counterweight to the Unity Party-led government. His criticism of the administration over Taylor’s prosecution gives that effort an immediate rallying point. But the former president is also taking a significant political risk.

The harder he pushes the Taylor issue, the more the government may frame his intervention as an attempt to shield a former administration official from accountability.

The more he broadens the matter into a democracy debate, however, the more he places himself in a position where he must explain precisely what reforms or safeguards he wants.

His strongest position would be to insist that Taylor receive a fair and transparent judicial process while allowing the courts to determine the merits of the allegations. That would enable him to defend his former vice president without appearing to place her beyond the reach of the law.

His weakest position would be one in which political loyalty is allowed to substitute for evidence. Weah’s own words appear designed to avoid that trap. He did not simply say Taylor should be released because she served as his vice president.

The former president also raised questions about developments within the government’s own system, suggesting that reports of officials being removed while remaining connected to prosecutions raise concerns about the credibility of the process.

His comments indicate that he intends to scrutinize not only Taylor’s case but the broader machinery through which the government is pursuing its investigations. That could place Weah on a collision course with the administration in the months ahead. And if that happens, Taylor’s case could become the first major issue around which Liberia’s opposition begins to regroup.

World.title: Liberia: Pres. Boakai Sacks Justice Minister, Solicitor General Amid $336M Cocaine Bust Probe
World.content:
Monrovia — President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has removed Justice Minister and Attorney General Cllr. N. Oswald Tweh and Solicitor General Cllr. Augustine Fayiah from their posts, abruptly reshuffling the leadership of the Ministry of Justice at a critical stage in Liberia’s investigation and prosecution of suspects linked to the country’s largest-ever cocaine seizures.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

The Executive Mansion announced Wednesday that Cllr. Betty M. Lamin-Blamo has been appointed as the new Minister of Justice, while Cllr. Abrahim Boimah Sillah, Sr. will serve as Solicitor General.

The shake-up comes as the Ministry of Justice, under Tweh and Fayiah, has been at the center of the government’s legal response to two major cocaine seizures with a combined estimated street value of more than US$336 million.

The timing of the changes is likely to draw scrutiny, given that the investigation and prosecution remain active and several suspects are facing serious criminal charges.

Among those charged is former Vice President Jewel Howard Taylor, who has been accused by the government of drug trafficking and money laundering in connection with the broader narcotics investigation. She has denied the allegations.

The government has also charged other suspects in connection with the drug cases, while investigators continue efforts to establish the full network behind the massive consignments.

Tweh and Fayiah had been publicly associated with the government’s legal handling of the cases, including the announcement of charges and the prosecution of suspects before the courts.

The Executive Mansion, however, did not link their removal to the cocaine investigation.

Instead, Presidential Press Secretary Atty. Kula B.N. Fofana said the changes form part of President Boakai’s “ongoing efforts to strengthen key institutions of Government and enhance the effective delivery of public services.”

The President said the two outgoing officials will be reassigned to other levels of government, although the Executive Mansion did not immediately specify their new assignments.

Major Legal Shake-Up

The removal of the two top Justice Ministry officials means the administration is changing both its political and prosecutorial leadership at a moment when the government faces the challenge of sustaining several high-profile narcotics prosecutions.

Cllr. Lamin-Blamo now takes charge of the ministry responsible for representing the government in criminal proceedings and overseeing the broader administration of justice. Cllr. Sillah will assume the Solicitor General’s role, including responsibilities tied to the government’s litigation and prosecution functions.

Analysts say the changes could have significant implications for the handling of the cocaine cases, particularly as prosecutors move forward with ongoing proceedings and investigations.

The first major seizure involved 237.6 kilograms of cocaine, valued at more than US$19 million, intercepted in Liberia.

A second and larger seizure involved approximately 3,971 kilograms of cocaine, with an estimated value of US$317.68 million, bringing the combined estimated value of the two consignments to more than US$336 million.

The seizures have triggered intense public and political scrutiny, including calls for an independent investigation into the identities of those behind the shipments and possible political or institutional connections.

The government’s handling of the investigation has also generated controversy following the arrest and prosecution of Howard Taylor, with opposition political actors and her defense team questioning aspects of the case.

New Leadership Takes Over

The Executive Mansion provided no detailed explanation for the timing of the Justice Ministry changes beyond the need to strengthen government institutions.

In addition to the Justice Ministry appointments, President Boakai made changes at the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, the Public Procurement and Concessions Commission, the Ministry of Local Government and the National Transit Authority.

At Gender, Children and Social Protection, Angel M. Morris was appointed Deputy Minister for Public Affairs, while Harrison K. Sorsor was named Assistant Minister for Research, Policy and Planning.

Alex Chersia Grant was appointed Commissioner of the Public Procurement and Concessions Commission, while Christopher Ben Bailey was appointed Superintendent of Grand Gedeh County.

Benedict Yeke Harleysion, Sr. was also reappointed Chairman of the National Transit Authority Board.

The Executive Mansion said nominees requiring legislative approval will be subject to Senate confirmation.

But for the Justice Ministry, the immediate question is whether the leadership change will alter the government’s approach to Liberia’s unprecedented cocaine investigation—and whether the new legal team will continue the prosecutions already underway without interruption.

World.title: Liberia: Senator Snowe, Mercy Ahun, and Roy Onyango Chosen to Provide Strategic Leadership for Africa’s Immunization Advisory Council
World.content:
MONROVIA — Bomi County Senator Edwin Melvin Snowe Jr. has been appointed First Vice Chair of the Continental Immunization Advisory Council (CIAC), placing the Liberian lawmaker in a key leadership position within a continental body responsible for providing strategic guidance on immunization and related public health priorities across Africa.

The appointment, formally communicated by the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), brings Senator Snowe into the leadership of the CIAC alongside two other officials selected to guide the council’s work.

Under the new leadership arrangement, Dr. Mercy Ahun has been appointed Chair of the Continental Immunization Advisory Council, while Senator Snowe will serve as First Vice Chair. Mr. Roy Douglas Onyango Otieno has been appointed Second Vice Chair.

The appointments, according to the CIAC Secretariat, reflect Africa CDC’s confidence in the three leaders’ experience, leadership capabilities and commitment to advancing immunization, primary healthcare and health security across the continent.

For Senator Snowe, the appointment represents an expanded role in regional and continental public health discussions at a time when African countries continue to strengthen vaccination systems, improve access to essential healthcare services and respond to emerging health security threats.

In formally notifying the three appointees, the CIAC Secretariat congratulated them and requested confirmation of their acceptance of the appointments.

The Secretariat said the newly constituted leadership team will have a central responsibility in guiding the strategic direction of the council and helping ensure that its deliberations produce practical and evidence-informed recommendations for African Union Member States.

As First Vice Chair, Senator Snowe is expected to work closely with the Chair and Second Vice Chair in shaping the council’s agenda and supporting the effective coordination of its activities.

The leadership team will also be responsible for shaping plenary agendas, facilitating balanced and evidence-informed deliberations, building consensus among council members and helping ensure that recommendations produced by the CIAC remain independent, actionable and responsive to the priorities of African Union Member States.

The appointment therefore places Snowe at the center of continental conversations concerning immunization policy, primary healthcare and health security.

The CIAC is part of Africa CDC’s broader efforts to strengthen continental health systems and support African countries in addressing public health challenges through evidence-based policies, technical guidance and coordinated action.

The council’s work is particularly significant as African governments continue to confront challenges involving vaccine access, immunization coverage, healthcare delivery and preparedness for public health emergencies.

The appointment of Senator Snowe also adds a Liberian voice to the leadership of a continental platform dealing with issues that have direct implications for the country’s healthcare system and public health priorities.

Liberia, like other African countries, has continued to rely on partnerships and coordinated interventions to strengthen routine immunization, improve healthcare delivery and protect vulnerable populations against vaccine-preventable diseases.

Through his new continental role, Snowe will be expected to contribute to discussions aimed at translating Africa’s immunization commitments into practical outcomes for governments and communities.

The CIAC leadership is also expected to help strengthen collaboration among experts and representatives involved in immunization policy while ensuring that recommendations are grounded in scientific evidence and remain relevant to the needs of individual African countries.

The Africa CDC Secretariat has scheduled the council’s next meeting for Tuesday, October 6, 2026.

Ahead of that meeting, the Secretariat is seeking to convene a one-hour virtual leadership briefing involving Dr. Ahun, Senator Snowe and Mr. Otieno.

The briefing is intended to prepare the newly appointed leadership team for the upcoming council meeting and allow the three officials to discuss their responsibilities, strategic priorities and expectations ahead of the October gathering.

The Secretariat has asked the three leaders to confirm their availability for the briefing and agree on a convenient time before October 6.

Africa CDC, in congratulating the three appointees, expressed confidence that their leadership will help strengthen the council’s ability to translate continental immunization commitments into measurable results for African Union Member States and communities.

The Bomi County Senator has served in Liberia’s national political space for several years, and his new appointment gives him an opportunity to contribute to continental policy discussions extending beyond the traditional boundaries of national politics.

His role on the CIAC is expected to require engagement with health experts, policymakers and representatives from across Africa as the council works to promote stronger immunization systems and more effective primary healthcare interventions.

The appointment of Snowe alongside Dr. Ahun and Mr. Otieno also signals Africa CDC’s intention to establish a leadership team capable of guiding the council through complex discussions surrounding immunization and health security.

The three leaders are expected to work collectively to facilitate consensus among council members while ensuring that the council’s recommendations are independent, practical and responsive to the priorities of African countries.

With the next CIAC meeting scheduled for October, attention will now turn to the new leadership team as it prepares to assume its responsibilities and help shape the council’s agenda for the period ahead.

World.title: Liberia: In US$19m Cocaine Case: 10 Indicted Over 200kg Haul, US$100k Bribe Plot
World.content:
MONROVIA — A Montserrado County Grand Jury has indicted 10 defendants in connection with the alleged trafficking of a 200-kilogram cocaine shipment through Roberts International Airport (RIA), including an alleged attempt to bribe law enforcement officers with US$100,000 to recover the seized drugs.

The indictment, filed in the August Term of Criminal Court “C,” accuses George Wah Harris, alias Leroy Harris; Paul Jamaal King; Philip Yeoh Jr.; Mohammed O. Gbowrah; Moses Jallah; Michael U.S. Brown, alias Rahim/Raheem Bah; Polo Bah; Oscar J. Brown; Usman Ali; and a private bar entity/person yet to be identified of multiple offenses.

The charges include unlicensed possession of controlled drugs or substances, unlicensed importation, unlicensed sale, trading in transit and transportation of controlled substances, illicit trafficking, criminal conspiracy, criminal facilitation and money laundering.

At the center of the prosecution’s case is a June 5, 2026 shipment that investigators allege contained approximately 200 kilograms of cocaine concealed inside six boxes falsely declared as Maggi cubes and lappas.

According to the indictment, Paul King, identified as Global Logistics Services’ Operations Manager, allegedly contacted Arthur B. Abdullai, Country Manager of Express Cargo Handling, and arranged for the six boxes to be shipped aboard Brussels Airlines to Heathrow Airport in London, with Usman Ali listed as the consignee at an address in Birmingham, England.

Prosecutors allege that King instructed Emmanuel Kpah to deliver the cargo and US$2,150 in shipping expenses to his Old Road residence.

The indictment says the boxes were subsequently collected from King’s residence and transported to RIA for shipment.

But the alleged plan began to unravel when GLS personnel detected a discrepancy between the actual weight of the cargo and the weight recorded on the air waybill.

The cargo was nevertheless sent through the airport scanning process, where an officer reportedly raised an alarm after the contents appeared blurred and dark on the scanner.

A subsequent physical inspection allegedly revealed a white powdery substance inside one of the boxes.

According to prosecutors, the substance was later identified as cocaine.

US$100,000 OFFER TO LDEA OFFICERS

The indictment alleges that after the cocaine was discovered, George Harris, identified as one of the proprietors of Private Bar Entertainment Center in Paynesville, made a dramatic attempt to have the shipment released.

Prosecutors claim Harris contacted LDEA Special Agents Clarence Clarke and Moses Jallah, who were assigned at RIA, and allegedly offered US$100,000 to have the six boxes returned.

The indictment further alleges that Harris subsequently gave US$5,000 to Jallah at the office of Private Bar as a bribe or inducement to facilitate the recovery or swapping of the drugs.

Investigators further allege that Harris told Jallah he owned 25 percent of the drugs and was determined to get the cocaine back after it had been seized at the airport.

The indictment says Harris also offered the use of a warehouse in Sayon Town, Bushrod Island, for storage of the cocaine, although prosecutors allege the facility was unsuitable.

King Allegedly Offered US$400 TO US$600

The prosecution’s allegations also extend to King, who investigators say was informed of the cocaine discovery after GLS personnel raised concerns about the shipment.

According to the indictment, after receiving images of the white powder from Philip Yeoh, King allegedly provided telephone numbers to Yeoh and instructed him to contact individuals who could help retrieve the cargo.

Prosecutors further allege that King asked Yeoh to negotiate with RIA security personnel and initially offered US$400, later increasing the offer to US$600, for the release of the shipment.

The indictment portrays those alleged efforts as part of a broader attempt to prevent law enforcement from taking possession of the cocaine.

Former RIA Employee Allegedly Involved

Michael U.S. Brown, alias Rahim/Raheem Bah, a former Roberts International Airport employee, is also accused of playing a role in the alleged operation.

Prosecutors allege that Brown contacted King in connection with an earlier shipment on May 20, 2026, involving four black-and-yellow-lidded boxes that were allegedly declared as Maggi cubes and lappas.

The indictment alleges that the May shipment followed a similar pattern to the June consignment and that US$1,400 was paid to facilitate its shipment to Europe.

Brown is further accused of arranging the June 5 shipment and later attempting to intervene after the cocaine was discovered at RIA.

According to the indictment, Brown allegedly contacted an RIA security officer and proposed giving him money to facilitate the release of the six boxes.

Prosecutors also allege that Brown and Harris headed toward RIA after learning that the cocaine had been intercepted, with Brown allegedly assuring King that he was going to the airport to retrieve the drugs.

A Second Shipment Under Investigation

The indictment raises questions about whether the June seizure was an isolated incident.

Prosecutors allege that the May 20 shipment of four boxes followed a pattern similar to the June 5 consignment, including the declaration of the contents as Maggi cubes and lappas and the alleged payment of US$1,400 to facilitate shipment.

The May shipment is therefore being cited by prosecutors as part of the broader alleged narcotics-trafficking conspiracy.

Serious Felony Charges

The Grand Jury alleges that the defendants acted knowingly and intentionally to facilitate the possession, movement, transportation and attempted exportation of cocaine.

The prosecution is relying on provisions of Liberia’s Controlled Drugs and Substances Act of 2023, including Section 14.89 on unlicensed possession, Section 14.83 on unlicensed importation, Section 14.85 on unlicensed sale, trading in transit and transportation, and Section 14.93 on illicit trafficking.

The indictment also invokes provisions of Liberia’s Penal Law dealing with criminal conspiracy, criminal facilitation and money laundering.

The indictment seeks the arrest of the named defendants and their appearance before the Criminal Assizes to answer to the charges.

The case is now before Criminal Court “C,” where the prosecution will have to prove its allegations beyond a reasonable doubt.

All defendants are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty by a court of competent jurisdiction.

World.title: BREAKING:Tweh Out as Justice Minister Amid Drug Scandal Fallout, Reassigned to Undisclosed Government Post
World.content:
Monrovia — September 2, 2026

President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, Sr. has removed Cllr. N. Oswald Tweh as Minister of Justice and Attorney General, replacing him with Cllr. Betty M. Lamin-Blamo, according to a release issued Wednesday by the Executive Mansion’s Office of the Presidential Press Secretary. Outgoing Solicitor General Augustine Fayiah is also being moved, alongside Tweh, to other levels of government, the statement said. Cllr. Abrahim Boimah Sillah, Sr. has been named the new Solicitor General.

The Mansion’s announcement gave no reason for the shake-up, describing it only as part of a broader round of appointments touching the Ministries of Justice, Gender, Children and Social Protection, and Local Government, along with the PPCC and the National Transit Authority. But the reassignment lands at the end of a turbulent stretch for Tweh, whose tenure atop the Justice Ministry became entangled in Liberia’s sprawling narcotics-trafficking investigations.

Background: A Minister Under Pressure

Tweh spent much of 2026 as the government’s public face in the fight against drug trafficking, overseeing a period that produced some of Liberia’s largest-ever narcotics seizures — including roughly 237 kilograms of cocaine intercepted at Roberts International Airport and a nearly four-ton cocaine find in Duazon, Margibi County, which authorities called the largest in the country’s history. He repeatedly pledged that no one — regardless of wealth or political connection — would be shielded from prosecution if credible evidence existed.

But as the investigations widened to touch senior political figures, including a case alleging former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor’s connection to a $317 million drug case, scrutiny increasingly turned on Tweh himself.

In late August, reports emerged that Tweh had “voluntarily” appeared before the Senate Committee on Defense, Security, Intelligence and Veterans Affairs over questions about a vehicle he received from Police Inspector General Gregory Coleman — a vehicle critics alleged was traceable to drug-cartel money tied to the same trafficking networks under investigation.

The Justice Ministry pushed back, framing the vehicle as an official assignment rather than a personal gift from Coleman.

Journalist Aaron Kollie had characterized Tweh’s Senate remarks as effectively a confession that Coleman gave him the car, a characterization the Ministry disputed.

Days later, as recently as Wednesday, allegations resurfaced directly linking Tweh to individuals connected with the $317 million case, with some accusing him of accepting gifts from suspected traffickers.

His special assistant, Atty. Siafa Bahn Kemokai, publicly defended Tweh’s character and integrity, arguing that unproven claims of wrongdoing should not be conflated with ordinary political disagreement.

Separately, civil society and press figures — including CENTAL’s Anderson Miamen and Senator Amara Konneh — had pressed for an independent panel to probe the broader drug crisis, a call Tweh resisted, arguing that ongoing prosecutions, backed by cooperation with the U.S. DEA, Homeland Security and FBI, should not be interrupted.

Whether Wednesday’s reassignment is connected to the vehicle controversy, the trafficking-linked allegations, or is part of a routine cabinet reshuffle has not been confirmed by the Executive Mansion.

The appointments, the Mansion said, are part of the President’s “ongoing efforts to strengthen key institutions of Government,” and nominees requiring Senate confirmation will go through that process.

World.title: Liberia: Rep. Fahnbulleh Hails Pres. Boakai’s Support After Talks on Bong’s District Seven Development Priorities
World.content:
MONROVIA — Bong County District Seven Representative Foday Fahnbulleh has expressed excitement following a meeting Tuesday with President Joseph Nyuma Boakai at the Executive Mansion.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

Rep. Fahnbulleh said the meeting provided him an opportunity to engage the President directly on issues he considers critical to the welfare of residents, particularly the participation of local contractors in development activities, the impact of concession operations on host communities and the need to protect the interests of citizens living in areas where major economic activities are taking place.

The lawmaker described the discussion as frank and productive, stressing that he went into the meeting with the concerns of his constituents at the center of his engagement with the President.

According to Rep. Fahnbulleh, one of the major issues he placed before President Boakai was the situation confronting local contractors in Fuamah and Sanoyea, where he said Liberian businesses should have greater opportunities to participate in development activities.

He argued that the presence of concessionaires and major development projects should result in opportunities for local businesses rather than leaving communities and Liberian entrepreneurs on the sidelines.

For Rep. Fahnbulleh, the question of local participation is directly connected to whether communities hosting major economic activities are actually benefiting from the resources and investments taking place within their areas.

He told the President that development must go beyond infrastructure and investment figures and translate into practical economic benefits for ordinary Liberians, including employment, business opportunities and improved livelihoods.

The Bong lawmaker also raised concerns about the relationship between concession operations and host communities, emphasizing the need for citizens’ rights to be protected while ensuring that communities receive meaningful benefits from activities carried out on their land and within their areas.

Rep. Fahnbulleh said he was encouraged by President Boakai’s response to the concerns, particularly the President’s acknowledgment of the issues raised and his stated willingness to support efforts aimed at protecting the rights and interests of affected communities.

The response, according to the representative, gave him renewed confidence that the concerns of Fuamah and Sanoyea could receive greater attention through continued engagement with the Executive Branch.

The meeting also provided an opportunity for Rep. Fahnbulleh to discuss an initiative he considers particularly important to the future of Bong County’s young population — the recently passed Bong Mines Vocational Training Institute Act.

The legislation, which was passed by the House of Representatives, seeks to establish a vocational training institution designed to provide young people with practical and marketable skills that can improve their chances of securing employment and becoming economically independent.

Rep. Fahnbulleh said he was particularly pleased with President Boakai’s expressed support for the initiative, describing the President’s position as an encouraging development for the county and its young people.

He said the President commended Bong County lawmakers for demonstrating leadership by supporting legislation intended to address the needs of citizens and complement the administration’s broader development agenda.

The representative said the President’s support was significant because the vocational training initiative could provide a direct response to the challenges of youth unemployment and the shortage of skilled workers.

Rep. Fahnbulleh believes the proposed institution could eventually help create a pool of trained Liberians capable of taking advantage of employment opportunities generated by mining, construction, agriculture, infrastructure and other economic activities.

He said the initiative could also create an avenue through which young people could acquire skills for self-employment, rather than depending exclusively on limited formal-sector jobs.

The lawmaker’s excitement following the meeting appeared to be tied not only to the President’s support for the vocational training legislation but also to what he described as a willingness by the Executive to work with Bong County lawmakers in addressing the concerns of their constituents.

Rep. Fahnbulleh said lawmakers have a responsibility to maintain direct communication with the Executive while remaining committed to representing the interests of their people.

He stressed that elected representatives must continue to raise citizens’ concerns, demand accountability and work with the government whenever such collaboration can produce concrete benefits for their constituents.

The District Seven representative said his engagement with President Boakai demonstrated the importance of constructive dialogue between the Legislature and Executive, particularly when national development policies intersect with local concerns.

He said he welcomed the President’s commitment to working with lawmakers and viewed the meeting as an opportunity to strengthen collaboration around development initiatives affecting Bong County.

Fahnbulleh also emphasized that his advocacy for local contractors is part of a broader effort to ensure that Liberians benefit directly from economic activities taking place in their communities.

He said local businesses should not merely observe development projects from the sidelines but should be positioned to participate in contracts, supply chains and other opportunities created by government and concession investments.

The lawmaker further maintained that host communities should have a meaningful stake in development taking place within their jurisdictions.

His position reflects a broader concern among communities across Liberia over the distribution of benefits associated with concession agreements and large-scale investments, particularly where local residents expect employment, contracts, infrastructure and other economic opportunities in return for hosting such operations.

Fahnbulleh said the concerns he presented to President Boakai were therefore aimed at ensuring that development reaches the grassroots and that communities such as those in Fuamah and Sanoyea are not excluded from the economic opportunities generated within their own areas.

He expressed optimism that the President’s acknowledgment of the concerns and support for the vocational training initiative could lead to further engagement and concrete action.

The lawmaker said he remains committed to working with the administration while continuing to serve as an advocate for the people of District Seven and the wider Bong County.

For Fahnbulleh, the meeting represented more than a routine engagement between a lawmaker and the President. He said it offered an opportunity to place local concerns directly before the national leadership and secure commitments around issues affecting communities, businesses and young people.

He welcomed what he described as the President’s readiness to partner with Bong County lawmakers, saying such cooperation could help advance development priorities while ensuring that the voices of local communities remain part of national decision-making.

Rep. Fahnbulleh said he left the engagement encouraged by the President’s response and determined to continue pushing for initiatives that create opportunities for young people, strengthen local businesses, protect citizens’ rights and ensure that development produces tangible benefits for the people of Bong County.

He said his commitment remains to keep the concerns of Fuamah, Sanoyea and the wider county at the center of his legislative advocacy while working with the Executive to turn those concerns into meaningful development outcomes.

World.title: Liberia Wraps Up Rwanda Study Mission on Proposed Peace and Reconciliation Museum
World.content:
KIGALI, RWANDA — Liberia has concluded the Rwanda phase of a high-level study mission designed to gather practical lessons for the establishment of the proposed Liberia Peace, Reconciliation and Memorial Museum.

The initiative is intended to preserve Liberia’s history, promote national healing and ensure that lessons from the country’s civil conflict are passed on to future generations.

The delegation, headed by Minister of State without Portfolio, Hon. Hadja Mamaka Bility, engaged with Rwandan institutions involved in reconciliation, historical preservation, archives, education and post-conflict recovery.

Supported by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), the mission forms part of efforts to translate President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s vision for reconciliation and historical preservation into a lasting national institution.

Minister Bility said Liberia’s objective is to move reconciliation beyond speeches and discussions by establishing institutions capable of preserving the country’s experiences and helping future generations understand its past.

“This study tour is part of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s vision for national reconciliation, with the support of UNDP. We want to move Liberia beyond simply talking about reconciliation to building strong institutions that can preserve our experiences, tell our story, and pass the lessons of our past on to future generations,” Minister Bility said.

The initiative comes amid President Boakai’s broader reconciliation efforts, including his July 2025 public apology on behalf of the Liberian State to victims and families affected by the country’s civil conflict.

During the Rwanda phase, the Liberian delegation studied the country’s approaches to unity, reconciliation, citizenship education, community resilience and the preservation of historical memory.

The team visited and examined the Gacaca archives and their digitization, Rwanda’s National Archives, the Campaign Against Genocide Museum, the University of Rwanda’s Centre for Conflict Management, the Rwanda Peace Academy and the Mutobo Demobilisation and Reintegration Centre.

The engagements provided lessons on how Liberia could collect, authenticate, digitize and preserve photographs, films, documents, testimonies and other historical materials currently scattered across government institutions, private collections and archives within and outside the country.

The mission also underscored the need for a credible memorial institution to go beyond the construction of a museum building, with education, research, documentation, reconciliation and community engagement forming key components of its mandate.

UNDP Liberia Resident Representative, Amb. Aliou Mamadou Dia, said the initiative forms part of a broader effort to strengthen peacebuilding, reconciliation and national unity.

“UNDP is working with the Government of Liberia to support the establishment of a Peace and Reconciliation Museum as part of the President’s broader reconciliation agenda.

“This study mission gives us an opportunity to learn from the experiences of other countries, document lessons that can be adapted to Liberia, and engage partners who can support the Government in moving this vision forward,” Amb. Dia said.

Amb. Dia stressed that lasting peace requires Liberia to confront difficult issues from its past, pursue genuine reconciliation and strengthen accountability, while building an institution that preserves history, promotes healing and educates future generations.

As the Rwanda phase concluded, the leadership of Rwanda Cooperation emphasized experience-sharing and the prospects for continued technical partnership with Liberia.

The discussions identified potential areas of cooperation, including museum development and management, training for Liberian heritage professionals, preservation and digitization of historical records and testimonies, peace education and technical exchanges, including potential collaboration with Aegis Trust Rwanda.

The Liberian delegation will now proceed to South Africa to continue studying African experiences in national healing, peacebuilding, reconciliation and memorialization.

A central lesson emerging from the Rwanda experience is that Liberia cannot simply replicate another country’s model. Instead, it must develop an institution rooted in its own history and informed by the voices, photographs, documents and experiences of Liberians.

Such an institution, the mission emphasized, would help acknowledge the country’s past, educate new generations and contribute to preventing Liberia from returning to conflict.

World.title: Liberia: Security Tightens at RIA as Weah Returns Today
World.content:
Airport Restricts Access, Regulates Traffic as CDC Mobilizes Supporters for Former President

Monrovia — Security has been heightened at Roberts International Airport (RIA) ahead of the arrival of former President George Manneh Weah on Wednesday, with the Liberia Airport Authority (LAA) introducing special measures to manage the anticipated movement of passengers, supporters and dignitaries.

The LAA Aviation Security Department (ASD) said all well-wishers intending to welcome Weah must gather at the RIA Public School, while only designated supporters appointed by the former president’s organizing committee will be permitted beyond the designated point.

The measures are part of arrangements to ensure what airport authorities described as a smooth, secure and orderly arrival of the former president, who is expected to touch down at RIA later today.

In a public safety announcement issued for September 2, the Aviation Security Department advised passengers traveling through the airport to arrive earlier than their usual scheduled time to avoid delays.

The announcement also warned that vehicular and pedestrian traffic around the airport would be regulated by the Joint Security, with members of the public instructed to follow directions from security officers deployed to the area.

Despite the special arrangements, the LAA said normal airport operations would continue.

The heightened security follows a September 1 communication from LAA Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer Ernest R. Hughes to CDC National Chairman Janga Augustus Kowo, formally notifying the party of Weah’s scheduled arrival through RIA.

Hughes said stakeholders had been provided with Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) to ensure the efficient coordination of operational, security, protocol, safety and facilitation arrangements associated with the former president’s arrival.

He urged all relevant agencies and service providers to take the necessary measures within their respective mandates to ensure a seamless and secure reception in line with established airport procedures and applicable regulations.

CDC Mobilizes for Weah

Meanwhile, the Coalition for Democratic Change (CDC) is mobilizing partisans and supporters to turn out in large numbers to welcome Weah, who remains the party’s political leader.

A special steering committee established to coordinate activities surrounding his arrival has also submitted a list of 20 persons to the Liberia Airport Authority for access to the airport to participate in his official reception.

The committee, chaired by former House Speaker Dr. Bhofal Chambers, said the designated individuals would help coordinate the reception, subject to all airport security and operational protocols.

The former president’s return comes after a series of engagements outside Liberia, including stops in Ghana and Nigeria.

In Ghana, Weah participated in a charity football match, while in Nigeria he served as keynote speaker at an annual event of the Nigerian Bar Association.

Return Amid Drug Case Fallout

Weah’s return also comes against the backdrop of a major drug trafficking and money laundering case involving his former Vice President, Jewel Howard Taylor.

Taylor, who served as vice president during Weah’s 2018–2024 administration, is facing prosecution in connection with the government’s investigation into the seizure of a cocaine consignment valued at approximately US$317 million.

Weah has publicly rejected the allegations against his former vice president, describing the charges as bogus and pledging his support for Taylor.

Her prosecution has generated intense political debate, with the CDC and other political actors raising questions about the government’s handling of the narcotics investigation.

With supporters expected to converge around the airport area, authorities are urging the public to comply with security instructions as they seek to balance the anticipated welcome with normal airport operations.

The LAA has appealed for the cooperation and understanding of passengers, well-wishers and other stakeholders, saying the measures are intended to ensure safety, security and an orderly reception.

World.title: Mbala modern market nearly complete
World.content:
Construction of the new 278 table capacity modern market in Mbala district in Northern Province has reached an advanced stage, with works standing at 80 percent completion.

The project, valued at K6.5 million, is being financed under the Constituency Development Funds (CDF) and is expected to ease the shortage of trading space at the existing location market.

Mbala District Commissioner Jestus Sikazwe confirmed the progress, noting that once completed, the facility will provide a more organised and spacious environment for traders and customers alike.

“This development will cushion the shortage of space at the location market and give traders a dignified place to conduct business. The modern market will improve hygiene, order, and management standards, which are critical for the growth of Mbala’s trading sector,” Mr Sikazwe said.

Mr Sikazwe said the development of the Mbulu market will not only improve business operations but also enhance hygiene and management standards in the district’s trading sector.

He added that the modern market is part of the government’s broader efforts to expand infrastructure and support local economic activities through CDF funded projects.

“Government remains committed to ensuring that CDF projects deliver tangible benefits to communities, and Mbulu Market is a clear example of that commitment,” Mr Sikazwe emphasised.

He added that the government remains committed to ensuring that CDF projects deliver tangible benefits to communities, saying Mbulu market is a clear example of that commitment.

Meanwhile, Local traders have welcomed the development, saying it will transform their working conditions.

Getrude Mujimba expressed gratitude to the government for the project.

“We used to trade under the sun, and during the rainy season it was even worse. We are so grateful to the government for constructing this market,” Ms Mujimba said.

Another trader, Grace Nachilima, echoed similar sentiments.

“This market will give us proper shelter and space to conduct our business. It is a great relief for us,” Ms Nachilima said.

World.title: Economist optimist about 2027-2031 MTRS
World.content:
Lusaka based Economist Kelvin Chisanga says the launch of public consultations on the 2027-2031 Medium-Term Revenue Strategy (MTRS) is an important intervention to tap into different aspects of the country’s resource envelope.

Highlighting the importance of the Medium-Term Revenue Strategy, Mr Chisanga indicated its vitality in the case of how Zambia has been able to shape up in respect to the national budget implementation process.

He acknowledged the key fundamental aspect in the MTRS as a deliberate policy measure which is looking at how best to grow the country in meeting up the revenue capacity in line with trying to put up a proper framework for growth.

Mr Chisanga was speaking in an interview with to the media ahead of the launch of public consultations on the 2027-2031 Medium-Term Revenue Strategy tomorrow, carrying the theme’ mobilising domestic resources for sustainable growth and national development.

He explained that Zambia should be able to look forward to financing some of its projects in the domestic market, from the market participation point.

“The aspect of contracting more from the domestic market and interplaying more with tax structure is more sustainable to develop this country,” Mr Chisanga added.

He further observed that with external markets, the country is paying high interest rates and also suffering from different economic effects such as forex market erosion, among others.

Meanwhile, Mr Chisanga charged that the budget for Medium-Term Revenue capacity and the national budget should be in tandem with issues of tax relief incentives and policy reforms.

He said the meeting is therefore timely, saying it presents a platform for stakeholders to share ideas and see how Zambia’s economy can grow, based on implementation.

And reacting to President Hakainde Hichilema’s announcement yesterday that Zambia will move from economic stability to growth, Mr Chisanga said the growing Zambia agenda demands economic transformation that needs to be cultivated.

He noted that this requires the need to make full use of the country’s potential by interplaying with specific sectors, important to the formulation of the economy.

“The next stage as we have led the stabilisation foundation, is to look at best interventions to the specific industry, the requirements and elements,” he said.

World.title: ZPL forces cancellation of Mopani Challenge Cup
World.content:
The 2026 IRH-Mopani Challenge Cup has been cancelled after the Zambian Premier League – ZPL issued a directive to reschedule the two-legged charity competition.

The competition was to feature Nkana FC and Mufulira Wanderers FC on Saturday, 5 September and Saturday, 12 September 2026.

In a letter dated 31 August 2026, ZPL Chief Executive Officer Joseph Chimpampwe said the change was necessitated by the use of Levy Mwanawasa Stadium in Ndola for CAF Interclub Competition fixtures on the original dates.

The ZPL made it clear the adjustment was mandatory.

“Please note that this is an instruction and not a request. The affected clubs are therefore required to make the necessary logistical and operational arrangements to ensure that the matches are played on the revised dates,” Chimpampwe stated in the letter addressed to CEOs of Nkana and Mufulira Wanderers.

Following the directive, Mopani Copper Mines PLC said it would not be possible to reorganize the extensive arrangements already put in place at such short notice.

The company announced the cancellation on Thursday, 3 September 2026, just days before the first leg.

Mopani Public Relations Manager Nebert Mulenga explained the decision.

“After careful consideration of the implications of the Zambian Premier League directive, the Company has decided that it would not be feasible to reorganise the entire competition programme on revised dates at such short notice,” Mulenga said.

Mopani said logistics including venue setup, security, transport, fan mobilization and sponsorship activations had already been finalized for the two Saturdays.

The company expressed regret over the cancellation and the inconvenience caused to Nkana, Mufulira Wanderers, supporters, sponsors and other stakeholders.

The IRH-Mopani Challenge Cup was designed to use football as a vehicle for community development and social impact.

Despite pulling out this year, Mopani reaffirmed its commitment to supporting both clubs and “promoting sport as a means of contributing to community development.”

World.title: UPND Losing Candidates Flood Courts With Election Petitions Across Provinces
World.content:
More than 20 losing United Party for National Development (UPND) parliamentary candidates have filed petitions challenging the outcome of last month’s general election in their respective constituencies, as the constitutional window for lodging such challenges drew to a close.

In Muchinga Province, UPND has petitioned two parliamentary seats in the Chinsali High Court. In Chinsali Central, National Restoration Party for Unity and Prosperity candidate Chanda Mwansa polled 11,254 votes against UPND’s Christopher Chiponde, who received 4,430 votes. In neighbouring Shiwangandu, NRPUP’s Stephen Kampyongo secured 11,536 votes against UPND’s Robert Kapeya, who polled 9,941. Both seats were formally petitioned on 28 August.

Former Chama North MP Davison Mung’andu has also filed a petition to nullify the Chama North parliamentary election, citing electoral irregularities, after NRPUP candidate Benson Njobvu won the seat with 4,660 votes against his 4,382.

On the Copperbelt, UPND candidates have challenged results in three constituencies. In Chingola Central, UPND’s Joseph Kazhila is contesting the NRPUP candidate’s victory, which came with 21,948 votes against Kazhila’s 10,782, alleging that NRPUP supporters and agents engaged in corrupt practices, including offering food to voters and distributing money through a candidate’s husband at a polling station. In Kabushi, UPND’s Emeldah Mpumpuni has challenged NRPUP’s Tillas Sichinga, alleging bribery, violence, obstruction of voters and campaigning on polling day, including claims that agents distributed between K50 and K100 to voters using pens containing concealed money.

In Western Province, UPND’s Sibeso Sefulo has petitioned against independent Mwandi MP Iris Kaingu, who won the seat by a margin of just 485 votes, polling 6,595 against Sefulo’s 6,110, alleging bribery, corruption and undue influence of voters by Kaingu’s agents. The petition further alleges the Electoral Commission of Zambia failed to properly adhere to procedure during the counting and announcement of results.

In Lusaka Province, former minister Sylvia Masebo has petitioned her loss in Chongwe East, where she polled 6,798 votes against independent winner Anita Kamanga’s 16,058.

Luapula Province has also produced a petition, with losing UPND candidate for Mwense Constituency Susan Mulala challenging the election of David Mabumba as Member of Parliament, after Mabumba polled 13,852 votes against her 5,262.

Central Province has generated two further cases. In Milanzi, UPND candidate Tylad Lungu, who polled 4,424 votes against independent winner Lumankio Zulu’s 5,004, has alleged the election was marred by widespread illegal practices and other misconduct. In Chitambo, UPND’s Remember Mutale, who polled 7,662 votes against NRPUP’s Nelson Kabanda’s 7,819, is seeking an order for scrutiny and recount of ballots, alleging corrupt practices by the respondent.

Eastern Province has also featured. In Nyimba South, UPND candidate Olipa Phiri has challenged NRPUP’s Mackson Kapantha’s victory, alleging vote-buying, bribery, violence, corruption and irregular invalidation or swapping of votes. A further UPND petition has been filed by Sunday Chanda, who is challenging Sampa Muswema’s election in Kanchibiya on the NRPUP ticket, alleging violence, intimidation, corruption and widespread non-compliance with the Electoral Process Act.

Kabwata MP Andrew Tayengwa and Copperbelt figure Lee Mukupa have also joined the list of UPND candidates petitioning results in their respective constituencies, according to court filings reported this week, though further specific detail on their individual grounds was not immediately available.

Reacting to the wave of litigation, UPND Deputy Spokesperson Elvis Nkandu said the party had not instructed losing candidates to petition, stressing that the surge in filings should not be read as a sign Zambia is moving toward a one-party state. UPND Elections Chairperson Likando Mufalali said there was no guarantee that petitions would automatically result in nullifications, adding that each case would be determined on its own merit.

Political analyst Dr Neo Simutanyi has cautioned that Zambians should not be shocked if some UPND petitioners succeed in court, while the GEARS Initiative has predicted that most petitions are unlikely to succeed. The Zambian Civil Liberties Union (ZCLU), through executive director Isaac Mwanza, has urged all parties to allow the courts to independently examine the evidence before pre-empting any outcome, noting that the electorate had already expressed its will through the ballot.

Petitions are proceeding through the Lusaka, Chinsali and Livingstone High Courts, alongside the separate presidential petition still before the Constitutional Court and the treason case against former opposition figures Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu, adding to an unusually crowded post-election legal calendar.

World.title: Muf Wanderers hire new CEO Mvula
World.content:
MTN Super Division side Mighty Mufulira Wanderers have confirmed the appointment of promising sports administrator Mangulenje Mvula as their new Chief Executive Officer, effective immediately.

Mvula arrives at Shinde Stadium a day after resigning as Trident Football Club CEO.

“Mufulira Wanderers Football Club is pleased to announce the appointment of Mr. Mvula Mangulenje as our new Chief Executive Officer, effective immediately,” Wanderers announced on Thursday morning.

“Mr. Mvula brings extensive experience in football leadership, having served as CEO of Trident FC and Jumulo FC,” the statement added.

Mvula inherits the Wanderers CEO’s seat from club loyalist Mumba Mwila.

Mvula is a FIFA-certified football administrator and current Manager of the Zambia U20 Boys National Team.

Meanwhile, when Mvula walked into Trident Football Club offices in 2022, the Kalumbila side was a National League team with ambition but no guarantees.

Four years later, he leaves a club that has tasted Super League football twice, reached an ABSA Cup semi-final, and established itself as one of Northwestern Province’s flagship sporting brands.

On Wednesday, Trident FC announced Mvula’s departure following his formal resignation, closing a chapter that redefined the club’s trajectory.

Mvula arrived at a time when Trident was pushing to be more than just a mining-town team. His brief was clear: professionalize the administration and get results on the pitch.

He delivered both.

The headline achievement came in the 2022/2023 season when Trident won the National League and secured promotion to the Zambia Super League for the first time. It was a breakthrough that put Kalumbila on the national football map.

Even after relegation battles, the club bounced back. In 2024, Trident reached the semi-finals of the ABSA Cup, proving they could compete with the country’s elite in knockout football.

Then in 2026, the club secured qualification to the Super League again, underlining that 2022/23 was not a fluke.

“During his tenure, Mr. Mvula Mangulenje made a valuable contribution to the Club’s administration, development and overall growth,” the club said in its official statement.

Those inside the club say Mvula’s impact went beyond trophies. He oversaw structural changes: tighter financial controls, improved player welfare, better scouting networks, and stronger community engagement in Kalumbila and surrounding districts.

For a club owned by a mining company, that meant aligning football ambitions with corporate governance — something Mangulenje, a career administrator, was brought in to do.

The result was stability. In an era where many clubs struggle with debt and management wrangles, Trident operated with a clear chain of command and a development plan.

With Mvula stepping down, Trident has moved quickly to ensure continuity.

General Secretary Jones Mwiza will assume the role of Acting Chief Executive Officer until the end of the current season. The club says a permanent appointment will be communicated in due course.

Club President Mainza Mazuba thanked Mvula for his service.

“On behalf of the Club, I extend sincere appreciation to Mr. Mvula for his service and contribution, and wish him every success in his future endeavours,” Mazuba said.

The statement added: “The Club remains committed to ensuring a smooth transition and maintaining continuity in its operations as it prepares for the next phase of its development.”

World.title: UPND Spokesperson Tells UN To Stop Calling Treason Suspects Political Detainees
World.content:
United Party for National Development (UPND) spokesperson Mark Simuuwe has called on the United Nations to stop classifying individuals facing treason-related charges in Zambia as political detainees, arguing that the label misrepresents the nature of cases currently before Zambian courts.

Simuuwe’s remarks come after UN Special Rapporteur Gina Romero urged Zambian authorities to release political detainees and restore democratic accountability following the post-election period, part of a wider wave of international commentary on the arrests of senior opposition figures on treason charges.

Simuuwe argued that the UN Charter does not condone terrorism or insurgency, and said the UN should therefore be the first to encourage the arrest of anyone found to be engaged in insurgent activity rather than framing such arrests as political persecution.

He said Zambia, as a member state of the UN and a signatory to the Charter’s provisions on sovereignty and the fight against terrorism, expects the UN to respect both the country’s sovereignty and the credibility of its legal institutions in presiding over criminal matters relating to treason or insurrection.

“It is not the first time the Zambian courts are handling treason related matters,” Simuuwe said, pointing to the Captain Solo case under former President Frederick Chiluba, the Shamwana case, and the earlier Mushala matter as precedent for the courts’ role in handling such cases.

The UPND spokesperson also raised concern about reports that some opposition political parties in Zambia have sent members for military training in other countries, saying this is a matter the UN should be equally concerned about.

Simuuwe was critical of the UN’s broader record on the continent, saying the organisation has been ineffective in addressing political violence in several African states. He cited Sudan, where he said the UN had allowed the situation to deteriorate with limited intervention, and eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, where he said the UN had appeared more a spectator and media commentator than a body founded on universal human rights.

He said Zambia, by contrast, has extensive experience in peacekeeping and has often demonstrated some of the best peacekeeping practices internationally. Drawing on that experience, Simuuwe warned that other countries have descended into civil war after heeding calls from international bodies to release suspected terrorists framed as political detainees.

“Releasing such persons without trial is basically endorsing terrorism,” Simuuwe said.

He said the UN should not be seen to prioritise public relations messaging while armed civilians are alleged to be illegally acquiring military weapons in Zambia, and urged the organisation to centre its efforts on calling for trial as established by law, rather than release without trial.

Simuuwe commended members of Zambia’s security services for their handling of the post-election situation.

World.title: Constitutional Court’s silence on presidential petition risks repeating 2016, warns legal scholar
World.content:
Constitutional law expert Prof Cephas Lumina has warned that the Constitutional Court’s failure to issue a reasoned decision on whether the so-called “People’s Presidential Petition” was validly or timeously submitted risks repeating the damaging situation of 2016 in Zambia.

His concerns stem from events surrounding a petition purportedly challenging the outcome of last month’s presidential election in Zambia. On 25 August, the Judiciary confirmed that Chief Justice Dr Mumba Malila had received documents designated as “The People’s Presidential Petition” through his private email address. He himself described that mode of transmission as “highly irregular.”

The Chief Justice did not, however, state that the irregular transmission had legally invalidated the petition. In what the Judiciary called an exceptional exercise of his administrative powers, he instead forwarded the documents to the Constitutional Court for consideration of the filing question, telling the parties concerned they would hear from the court in due course regarding the situation in Zambia.

That promised judicial decision has yet to be publicly disclosed, according to Lumina. The following day, the Judiciary’s communications office announced there was “no Presidential petition before the Constitutional Court” because none had been received by the Registry. President Hakainde Hichilema was subsequently inaugurated for his second term on 1 September.

An administrative statement, Lumina argued, cannot substitute for the judicial decision to which the Chief Justice had specifically referred.

Constitutional courts exist precisely for difficult moments of this kind, he said, tasked with safeguarding the supremacy of the Constitution and providing definitive answers where disagreement between institutions or persons might endanger legal or political stability. Zambia’s Constitution assigns the court both original and final authority over interpretation of the Constitution, presidential election disputes, and questions of its own jurisdiction. Lumina described this responsibility as especially significant given Article 45’s requirement that electoral disputes be resolved not merely quickly, but fairly.

Drawing a direct line to history, he recalled that in Hichilema and Another v Lungu and Others, the 2016 presidential petition was terminated after a majority of the court held that the constitutionally prescribed period had expired, without the substantive allegations ever being adjudicated. The political consequences of that unresolved petition endured well beyond the litigation itself. At the time, the UPND refused to recognise then-President Edgar Lungu’s presidency and boycotted presidential appearances for months.

Parliament itself later recognised the problem. A 2025 constitutional amendment inserted the words “and determine” into Article 103(2), making it a requirement that the Constitutional Court “hear and determine” a presidential election petition within fourteen days, rather than allowing disputes to vanish into procedural limbo as happened in 2016.

Turning to the current matter, Lumina examined the Chief Justice’s response to the emailed petition. The 2026 Rules establish a structured filing system in which electronic filing is expressly permitted, but documents are normally processed, reviewed and stamped through the Registry’s system. Petitioners cannot simply claim that sending an email amounts to valid filing, he said, but equally the Judiciary cannot say that an empty Registry record means there is no legal question at all.

He raised particular concern about the role played by the Chief Administrator, whose letter of 25 August reported that no petition had been filed in the Registry as at a stated time. Under the Judiciary Administration Act, Lumina noted, the Chief Administrator’s functions do not extend to any matter assigned by law to a judge or judicial officer. This, he said, raises the question of what legal authority permitted an administrative statement to effectively supersede the Chief Justice’s own referral of the matter to the Constitutional Court.

Procedural rules matter, Lumina acknowledged, and election petitions require discipline, certainty and speed. He cited the Kenyan Supreme Court’s insistence that constitutional election timelines are not negotiable. But Zambia’s own Constitution, in Article 118, states that judicial power comes from the people and that justice must be done to all without undue regard to procedural technicalities. Article 267, he added, requires constitutional interpretation to promote the Constitution’s purposes and help achieve good governance.

An unresolved question over computation of time under the 2026 Rules also remains, he said, given that Article 269 excludes the day of an event when calculating short deadlines. Lumina questioned whether the Constitution’s seven-day right for election petitions had been properly computed against the Judiciary’s holiday-filing provisions.

Comparisons with Kenya and Malawi were instructive, in his view. Both countries’ courts have weighed the principle of substantive justice against procedural technicality by issuing reasoned judgments on what requirements are jurisdictional and what defects can be cured, rather than remaining silent. In Malawi’s landmark 2019 presidential election litigation, the courts did not avoid an intensely political dispute, ultimately nullifying the presidential result and ordering a new election. The significance of that outcome, Lumina said, lay not in which candidate benefited, but in the fact that the dispute was settled by the courts.

His own optimism about Zambia’s judicial preparedness, built during his participation in the Judiciary’s Electoral Dispute Resolution training programme ahead of the August elections, is now being tested, he said

President Hichilema’s inauguration is a legal and political fact, Lumina was careful to note, and no court has established that allegations against his election are true. Legitimacy, however, has both legal and public dimensions. A President who emerges from an independent judicial examination of serious electoral complaints emerges stronger, not weaker, he argued, whereas unresolved doubt over access to the courts can turn into lasting grievance, as it did after 2016.

The Constitutional Court’s silence answers none of the outstanding questions, Lumina concluded. The country deserves an official and reasoned explanation of what became of the Chief Justice’s referral, whether the court considers itself to have jurisdiction, and the legal reasoning behind its position, rather than unresolved suspicion being left to invite competing political narratives.

By Prof Cephas Lumina

Source: The Mast

World.title: China Stands With HH, Pledges Deeper Cooperation On TAZARA And Trade
World.content:
Chinese President Xi Jinping has commended President Hakainde Hichilema’s call for national unity and commitment to improving people’s wellbeing, pledging continued Chinese support for Zambia’s development agenda as the two countries move to accelerate work on the Tanzania-Zambia Railway corridor.

President Xi conveyed the message through his special envoy, Xian Hui, vice-chairperson of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference, who called on President Hichilema at Community House on Wednesday.

She said President Hichilema’s inauguration speech on Tuesday was “very good,” particularly his emphasis on peace, development, people’s wellbeing and the One Zambia, One Nation motto.

Xian said China will continue supporting Zambia’s development and attaches great importance to the long-standing friendship between the two countries, which was established during the leadership of Zambia’s founding President Kenneth Kaunda and China’s Mao Zedong.

President Hichilema echoed that history in a Facebook post following the meeting, describing the relationship as one “forged by our founding fathers, Dr Kenneth Kaunda and Chairman Mao Zedong.” He conveyed his gratitude to President Xi for sending a special envoy to attend his inauguration.

President Xi said the TAZARA line is another symbol of the historic friendship between China and African countries, and that the Chinese government is pleased with the launch of the TAZARA revitalisation project and will continue supporting the initiative. In September 2025, Zambia, Tanzania and China signed a US$1.4 billion agreement to revitalise TAZARA and enhance regional connectivity.

President Xi said he had also met Tanzanian President Samia Suluhu Hassan and exchanged views on the railway project, expressing satisfaction with the progress being made. He commended President Hichilema for his efforts to strengthen bilateral relations through visits to China in 2023 and 2024, and congratulated him on his re-election, saying the outcome demonstrates the trust Zambians have placed in his leadership.

President Hichilema reaffirmed government’s commitment to accelerating work on the revitalised TAZARA corridor, calling for increased investment from China and other cooperating partners. He said that, following his inauguration, attention should now shift towards expediting the implementation of the TAZARA project and unlocking its wider economic potential.

He said the project should not be viewed simply as a railway line but as a transport and growth corridor capable of stimulating economic activity and opening up new investment opportunities. In his Facebook post, the President put it directly: “With our renewed mandate, we have reaffirmed our commitment to accelerate work on the Tanzania–Zambia Railway (TAZARA) corridor. We are committed to facilitating trade and growing the businesses that move along it.”

He added that foreign trade diplomacy remains central to the Grow Zambia agenda.

President Hichilema said Zambia wants to see increased Chinese investment not only in railway infrastructure but also in businesses and industries along the corridor. He said the country is satisfied with progress made so far on the TAZARA revitalisation and investments in the mining sector, but believes more can be achieved. The President asked Xian to convey to President Xi his desire for greater momentum in developing the corridor.

The trade relationship, both sides noted, is already delivering measurable results. President Hichilema said in his Facebook post that through recently enhanced cooperation, exports to China have doubled over the past five years to a record US$4.2 billion.

President Hichilema also pointed to cooperation in the renewable energy sector, particularly solar energy development, as a further area of growing partnership. He said the TAZARA revitalisation project was among the areas of cooperation discussed with President Xi during his State visit to China in 2023.

“The TAZARA is part of the culmination of what we discussed with President Xi during our State visit to China in 2023, and we would like to see more traction on the project in terms of it being accelerated and expedited. Yes, a lot of work has been done, but we can certainly do more,” the President said.

He also said Zambia valued China’s cooperation in the mining sector, where investors such as CNMC were expanding operations in the country.

President Hichilema reaffirmed his commitment to strengthening Zambia-China relations and expanding cooperation in sectors such as mining and energy. He said engagements with various Chinese provinces have demonstrated significant improvements in bilateral relations, particularly in the energy sector, including solar power.

The President stressed that foreign trade diplomacy remains central to the country’s growth agenda, as government seeks to attract investments and expand economic opportunities. He also expressed gratitude to President Xi for sending a special envoy to attend his inauguration, describing the gesture as a demonstration of the importance China attaches to its relationship with Zambia.
