World.title: Meet Ana Valdez, a Forbes ’50 over 50′ illuminating the Latino narrative in the United States
World.content:
At MND, we’re always looking for new perspectives on the United States-Canada-Mexico relationship from leaders and organizations working to improve trilateral relations through fact-based data and reporting.

One of those leaders is Ana Valdez of the Latino Donor Collaborative (LDC), a non-profit organization and think tank she has led as president and CEO since 2014.

Valdez, a Mexico City native, emigrated to the United States in the 1990s and got a volunteer job in the White House when Bill Clinton was president. Fast forward to today, and she is on Forbes’s “50 over 50” list — a selection of women aged over 50 who are doing ambitious, influential and powerful work in the United States.

The LDC, according to the organization’s website, is “dedicated to reshaping the perception of Latinos as part of the American social mainstream.”

This is very important work, Valdez told Mexico News Daily during a recent interview.

“When I [first] came here, I saw a huge disconnect between the perception of who Latinos are in the United States and the reality of who they are,” she said.

“One misconception is that everybody is an immigrant. That matters because about 70% of Latinos in this country have been here for many generations. Some were here even before this [land] was the United States,” Valdez said.

CDMX to LA via Spain and Switzerland

“Since taking the helm of the Latino Donor Collaborative in 2014, Ana Valdez has led an organization that represents the economic interests of all Latinos in the U.S,” states a brief profile of the 64-year-old that Forbes published as part of its “50 over 50” list.

“In 2023 she launched the nonprofit’s Latino Data Collective, which puts economic data and market information about Latinos into the hands of more than 650,000 CEOs, politicians, board directors and media executives.”

Before moving to the United States close to 30 years ago, and joining the Los Angeles-based LDC more than a decade ago, Valdez studied and worked in Europe for a period. Before that, she completed a bachelor’s degree in business and marketing at Mexico’s Tec. de Monterrey university.

“I was born and raised in Mexico City,” she told MND, beginning a highly condensed version of her life story.

Valdez noted later in our interview that she completed a master’s degree in international relations in Spain and subsequently worked with the United Nations in Switzerland.

“After living in Europe for four years, I came to the United States and found the Latino community. I didn’t know about it growing up in Mexico City, and I didn’t know about it in Europe,” she said.

Valdez explained that she traveled to the United States to work on a PhD thesis, but ended up getting a volunteer job at the White House, “and after three months they hired me.”

“I stayed and never finished my PhD,” she said.

In addition to working at the White House in both a volunteer and paid capacity, Valdez held positions at Nielsen and Banamex before her appointment as CEO of LDC.

“My first job was at Nielsen, so I’m a nerd — [I love] using data … to do anything [related] with business,” she told MND.

“I’ve been madly in love with data ever since,” Valdez said before correcting herself to note that her passion for statistics actually dates back to her college days.

The LDC’s mission and vision

The LDC, the organization says on its website, “was founded in 2010 after a group of national business leaders identified a critical gap: the lack of an accurate narrative about Latinos, resulting in the perpetuation of harmful stereotypes.”

“This gap in understanding about U.S. Latinos was particularly troubling, as some states began passing laws that allowed for the arbitrary arrest of individuals based on these stereotypes,” the LDC says.

“In response to these alarming developments, co-founders and national leaders Sol Trujillo and Henry Cisneros [a former U.S. secretary of housing] recognized the urgency of creating a bipartisan non-profit organization and producing reputable data and statistics that accurately reflect the identity of Latinos in America and their contributions to the nation.”

The LDC says it “produces the most reputable data on Latinos in the United States,” much of which is compiled from official U.S. government stats, according to Valdez.

The organization says that the statistics it presents are “critical to the U.S. economy, workforce, business development, entertainment, and several other key aspects of American prosperity” given that members of the U.S. Latino community account for 20% of the entire U.S. population and more than one-quarter of Americans aged 18 and under.

The organization says its mission is to “reframe and advance an accurate perception, portrayal, and understanding of the important contributions that American Latinos make to American society,” while its vision is for “American Latinos to be recognized as valued, patriotic Americans in all facets of American life.”

A central element of the LDC’s strategy to reframe perceptions of Latinos in the United States — including some 40 million people of Mexican origin — is the publication of data-heavy reports focusing on the Latino population’s contributions to the U.S. economy and society. Among the more than 60 reports the organization has published are the “2026 LDC U.S. Latino Economic Impact Report” and “Data Beyond Demographics: U.S. Latinas’ Economic Power, Influence, and Growth.”

Mexico News Daily will soon begin presenting some of the key data in LDC reports in articles with an easy-to-read, visually engaging format.

“For us, collaboration is amplification,” Valdez said, referring to a partnership with MND.

“We believe from the bottom of our hearts and minds that this information helps everybody. It helps Americans in Mexico, too. There are so many Americans living in Mexico right now, and it would be a blind spot not to inform them about people who are doing exactly the opposite,” she said.

Changing Latinos, changing perceptions

Valdez told MND that Latinos made up around 7% of the U.S. population in 1960, whereas they account for 20% today, an increase attributable to both immigration and the birth in the United States of millions of Latino babies.

“People didn’t know Latinos before because they were only 7% [of the U.S. population],” she said.

“The preconceived idea of Latinos was perhaps someone seen as a valet parker, a housekeeper or a gardener.”

Valdez acknowledged that many Latinos worked — and continue to work — such jobs. However, she emphasized that many Latinos are now business owners or work in professional fields. In a 2025 infographic, the LDC highlights that there are “approximately 5.7 million U.S. Latino enterprises in the U.S.”

Valdez noted that many recent — and in some cases undocumented — Latino immigrants to the United States have attempted to maintain a low profile while the Trump administration carries out an aggressive deportation agenda. However, U.S.-born Latino “kids” are “completely different,” she said.

“…[Market research company] Kantar calls these young people ‘200 percenters,'” Valdez said.

“They feel 100% American and 100% Latino too. Contrary to their parents, they are not ashamed or embarrassed. They are unapologetic about being Latino. They’re proud, comfortable and confident. Their friends and peers want to know more [about Latino culture], want to learn Spanish, want to dance to Bad Bunny,” she said, providing one example of how U.S. perceptions of Latinos, and Latino culture, have changed.

“… Every year, thousands or hundreds of thousands of Latinos turn 18. They vote. They go to college. If they don’t go to college, they work in much better environments than the fields where their parents worked. They are assertive [and] speak English perfectly,” Valdez said.

She subsequently noted that her husband is Mexican-American, “from one of the families that came to what is now the United States when it was still Mexico.”

“… The border crossed them when the United States took over New Mexico and many other states,” Valdez said.

“… When my husband was growing up in Colorado, people were bullied for speaking Spanish. He remembers his mother putting burritos in his lunch. He was embarrassed when he opened it and it smelled, so he would put it away, not eat it and throw it out. He was bullied because of it,” she said.

“Fast-forward to our kids in a school on the west side of Los Angeles. We realized that one of them was charging his friends to bring them home for lunch because everyone wanted real Mexican food. His white friends wanted it,” Valdez said.

“So it is a complete change,” she said.

Beyond greater acceptance in the U.S. of Mexican food and the cuisines of other Western Hemisphere countries — and indeed increased desirability and “trendiness” of such food — there is growing recognition of the immense contribution Latinos make to the United States.

Unfortunately, however, there is still discrimination against Latinos in the U.S., while certain stereotypes and misconceptions persist. The LDC, as it has done since its foundation, will continue to work to counteract those enduring problems.

It’s not just Forbes taking notice of Valdez’s work

Forbes is by no means the only prominent media organization that has taken notice of LDC’s work under Valdez’s leadership. Among the others are CBS News, CNBC, Variety and Axios.

Valdez has also come to the attention of the Mexican government, leading to invitations to speak at President Claudia Sheinbaum’s morning press conferences.

At Sheinbaum’s May 22 mañanera, the LDC CEO presented a range of data about women of Mexican origin in the United States, including one particularly striking statistic — that those women contribute US $1.1 trillion to U.S. GDP on an annual basis.

When we asked Valdez why she — a Los Angeles-based data expert focused on Latinos in the U.S. — had been invited to speak at the president’s mañanera on numerous occasions, she noted that Sheinbaum is a scientist who “likes numbers.”

“When a scientist realizes that there are almost 40 million nationals or people with Mexican national background living in the United States, and that Mexico was not in touch with them, she wanted to know more about them and begin engaging them,” Valdez said, noting also that Sheinbaum has been a strong supporter of Mexican deportees and the Mexican community in the U.S., including people at risk of deportation.

World.title: Sheinbaum again gripes about the US meddling in her government: Wednesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🇺🇸 Sheinbaum claims US is seeking to “weaken” and “divide” her government : Sheinbaum said the Trump administration is trying to “create divisions” within her Security Cabinet and cabinet, calling it a longstanding U.S. tactic against “independent governments that defend sovereignty.” She linked the criticism to November’s U.S. midterm elections, saying that U.S. politicians often use Mexico as part of their election campaigns.

: Sheinbaum said the Trump administration is trying to “create divisions” within her Security Cabinet and cabinet, calling it a longstanding U.S. tactic against “independent governments that defend sovereignty.” She linked the criticism to November’s U.S. midterm elections, saying that U.S. politicians often use Mexico as part of their election campaigns. 🚫 Sheinbaum dismisses claims that AMLO is pulling the strings : Responding to talk of “Obradoristas” and “Claudistas” within Morena, Sheinbaum said former President López Obrador has been “extremely respectful” and has never told her what to do. She called the idea that a man is really governing behind her a “sexist” one.

: Responding to talk of “Obradoristas” and “Claudistas” within Morena, Sheinbaum said former President López Obrador has been “extremely respectful” and has never told her what to do. She called the idea that a man is really governing behind her a “sexist” one. 🎢 Sheinbaum reflects on a “complex” year with Washington: Asked about the hardest moment of her second year, Sheinbaum pointed to tensions over U.S. tariffs on steel and vehicles and Washington’s extradition request for 10 officials, including Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya. However, she said that friction with the US hasn’t caused a “major problem” overall.

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Claudia Sheinbaum presided over her Wednesday morning press conference a day after delivering her second annual government report in a lengthy speech at the National Palace.

Sheinbaum largely avoided criticizing the U.S. government during her address on Tuesday, but less than 24 hours later, she reiterated her view that the Trump administration is meddling in Mexican affairs.

Her assertions on Wednesday that the U.S. is seeking to “weaken” and “create divisions” in her government were among the most significant remarks of the press conference.

Also of note at today’s mañanera was Sheinbaum’s dismissal of claims that former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador is pulling the strings in her administration. She has previously described such claims as “misogynistic,” and expressed a similar view on Wednesday.

Sheinbaum asserts that the US is seeking to ‘create divisions’ in her government

A reporter noted that DEA Administrator Terry Cole’s has spoken out against Mexico and her government, highlighting that he said last week that there are “high-level officials that are working directly with the cartels.”

The reporter also noted that Cole recently described Security Minister Omar García Harfuch as a “trusted partner” and “good friend of the United States.”

She asked Sheinbaum whether Cole’s remarks about García Harfuch amounted to an endorsement of him as a candidate in upcoming elections. Her suggestion was that the U.S. government — or at least the DEA chief — would like García Harfuch to be the next president of Mexico.

Sheinbaum responded that “they” — i.e., U.S. officials — “seek in one way or another to weaken [foreign] governments, because that’s one of their objectives.”

They “particularly” seek to weaken “independent governments that defend sovereignty,” she said.

They seek to “divide us internally,” Sheinbaum said.

“It’s one of their strategies,” she said, adding that it’s not a new tactic but rather one that U.S. governments have “always” used.

#MañaneraPresidenta | SOBERANÍA ANTE CUALQUIER INTENTO DE INJERENCIA Claudia Sheinbaum afirmó que mantener los principios y la autoridad política y moral es fundamental ante intentos de injerencia extranjera como la red de Fernando Cerimedo y Javier Negre. Reiteró que con EU… pic.twitter.com/JXsmZcKVtQ — Juncal Solano (@juncalssolano) September 2, 2026

Sheinbaum asserted that the current U.S. government is seeking to “create divisions” within the federal Security Cabinet and her cabinet.

“They are tactics of interference that they use,” she said.

“What happens is that they run into a wall because the Security Cabinet of the government of Mexico is highly coordinated and very united,” Sheinbaum said.

“… There are no divisions,” she said.

“… They think that by speaking well about one person and ill of others they’re going to create divisions inside [the Security Cabinet], but they fail,” Sheinbaum said.

She also asserted that recent remarks made by U.S. officials about Mexico are politically motivated given that midterm elections will be held in the United States this November.

“They remember they have elections in November. So they often use Mexico as part of their election [campaigns],” Sheinbaum said.

Pushed as to whether the U.S. government was giving its “vote” to García Harfuch, the president responded:

“No. What they seek, also, is to influence our elections. It’s the same old story.”

Sheinbaum: AMLO has been ‘extremely respectful’ toward our government

Sheinbaum said that opposition politicians and government critics are claiming that there is a “deep division” between her and López Obrador.

“Now [they’re talking about] the Obradoristas and the Claudistas, that’s the way they put it,” she said, referring to broader alleged divisions within the Morena party.

“It’s completely absurd. Firstly, it’s important for everyone to know, President Andrés Manuel López Obrador has been extremely respectful toward our government. Extremely respectful,” Sheinbaum said.

“He hasn’t sent any message saying, ‘Do this’ or ‘Do that’ or ‘I don’t agree with what you did,'” she said.

“… This idea that, behind the president, López Obrador is governing is a very sexist idea,” Sheinbaum said.

“… It has to do with an idea that women can’t govern,” she said.

Sheinbaum acknowledges ‘situations of tension’ with US

A reporter asked the president whether she had identified the most “critical” and “complicated” moment of her second year in office. He also asked Sheinbaum about the most “satisfying” aspect of her presidency.

“Well, I think the relationship with the United States has been complex,” Sheinbaum said.

“We’ve sought a good relationship, but there have been times of difficulty,” she said.

Sheinbaum said that the United States’ imposition of tariffs on Mexican products such as steel and vehicles created “times of tension” in the bilateral relationship.

She asserted that the U.S. government also “wanted to provoke a moment of tension” when it sent a request for 10 current and former officials, including Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya, to be detained for the purpose of extradition to the U.S. to face drug trafficking charges.

“There were times of tension with the U.S. government, or with some people of the U.S. government,” Sheinbaum said.

She said that friction between her government and the Trump administration hasn’t created a “major problem” for Mexico. But there have been “situations of tension,” Sheinbaum said.

“The truth is that we’ve been able to move on very well,” she added.

Sheinbaum subsequently said that she very much enjoys her “tours” of Mexico on weekends, during which she travels around the country to inspect progress on infrastructure projects and inaugurate completed ones, among other activities. During the tours, she gets up close and personal with Mexicans from all walks of life.

Sheinbaum said that her trips “fill” her with “happiness and energy.”

“… It’s the most beautiful thing,” she added.

World.title: MND Local: Gorillaz, mariachi festival, immersive dining and more in Guadalajara
World.content:
This week, we share details on the 33rd annual International Mariachi and Charrería Encounter, the Gorillaz’s upcoming concert in Zapopan, and an immersive dinner inspired by the indie French film “Amélie.” But first, let’s meet the new U.S. consul general in Guadalajara.

Elizabeth Hoffman Franolich begins new role as US consul general in Guadalajara

Earlier this month, Elizabeth Hoffman Franolich became the new consul general of the United States in Guadalajara. She replaces Amy Scanlon, who finished her term last July.

A career foreign service officer with more than two decades of diplomatic experience, Hoffman Franolich is well-versed in Latin American affairs, with previous postings in El Salvador, Venezuela and Colombia.

Prior to her current post, Hoffman Franolich was director of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement, and deputy chief of mission at the U.S. Embassy in El Salvador.

A fluent Spanish speaker, the new consul general arrives in Guadalajara with prior diplomatic experience in Mexico as well, having served as trade and investment counselor at the U.S. Embassy in Mexico City.

Originally from Ohio, Hoffman Franolich holds a Bachelor of Science in Public Policy from Vanderbilt University and a Master of Science in Geography from SUNY at Albany.

With reporting from the University of Guadalajara and El Informador.

The 33rd annual International Mariachi and Charrería Encounter is underway

Guadalajara is currently filled with the sound of trumpets, vihuelas and guitarrrones, courtesy of the 33rd edition of the International Mariachi and Charrería Encounter, which runs through Sept. 6.

Over the 11-day event, there will be live concerts, charro contests (Mexican rodeo) and free activities for the whole family, with 95% of the events free and accessible to all.

Mariachi, declared by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, is the soul of this gathering. Year after year it brings together diverse audiences spanning generations.

Performances feature some of Mexico’s most iconic groups and musical collaborators from more than 20 countries, including Croatia, Italy, France, Greece, Canada, Colombia and Australia.

Some of the highlights include:

Mariachi Galas at the Degollado Theater : The best mariachis in the world will join the Jalisco Philharmonic Orchestra for several unforgettable themed nights on Sept. 2, 3, and 5 at 8 p.m.

A concert with Natalia Jiménez at Telmex Auditorium : Natalia Jiménez is set to perform with the Mariachi Internacional CHG and the Jalisco Philharmonic Orchestra on Sept. 4.

A closing concert in the Children’s Park in Zapopan: A closing concert featuring a performance by Jalisco’s own Azucena on Sept. 6.

To see the full program, check out this page. Tickets are available at the venue box offices or through Ticketmaster Mexico.

With reporting from Telediario.

Gorillaz to perform at new GNP Seguros Coliseum in December

The legendary British band Gorillaz will bring “The Mountain Tour” to Guadalajara this December. The show is scheduled for the newly revamped GNP Seguros Coliseum on the UAG campus in Zapopan on Dec. 9.

For the uninitiated, Gorillaz’s music spans trip-hop, hip-hop and lo-fi indie rock that really gets a crowd moving. The band burst onto the indie scene more than 25 years ago with their irresistible single “Clint Eastwood,” which blended the hip-hop vocals of Del the Funky Homosapien over electronic music with a heavy bassline.

Gorillaz came into being as British frontman Damon Albarn’s previous indie band, Blur, was dissolving in the late 1990s.

“The Mountain,” the band’s ninth studio LP, is the product of Albarn’s dig through years of Gorillaz recordings, in search of unused material from former collaborators who have now passed. Albarn was able to get approval for all the artists he wished to include on the album — except for one notoriously difficult cat, Lou Reed.

In all, more than two dozen performers, living and dead, appear on “The Mountain,” which took inspiration from Albarn’s visit to India following the death of his father. Live shows on this tour have included a wide cast of characters, including Little Simz, Mos Def and The Smiths’ Johnny Marr.

When : Dec. 9, 2026

Where : Coliseo GNP Seguros, Zapopan, on the UAG campus.

Tickets : Tickets starting from 2,827 pesos are available at Ticketmaster Mexico .

A culinary adventure inspired by the classic French indie film ‘Amélie’

The creative team at Efímero Lab in Colonia Americana is back at it, preparing the latest installment of its “The Taste of Movies” series. This time, the lab is hosting an immersive dinner to celebrate the beloved French film “Amélie,” directed by Jean-Pierre Jeunet and starring the adorable Audrey Tautou.

The film tells the story of a Parisian waitress who plays small pranks that improve others’ lives while searching for a romance of her own.

Diners can expect a three-course meal with cocktail pairings that deliver a sensory experience inspired by the film’s characters, plot and unique sensibility.

Created by a collective of architects, artists, designers and mixologists, Efímero Lab is a cozy and sophisticated lounge exploring craft cocktails, gastronomy and immersive experiences.

When : The Amélie immersive dinner is on Sept. 5. The “Taste of Movies” series is a recurring event at Efímero Lab.

Where : Juan Manuel 1575, Colonia Americana, 44600 Guadalajara.

Tickets: Tickets for the dinner are 1,600 pesos per person. To reserve your spot, contact Efímero Lab on Instagram . Seats are limited.

MND writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: Peru Urges the OAS to Act on the Nicaragua Reform
World.content:
Nicaragua · DIPLOMACY

Key Facts — Communique Peru’s foreign ministry issued Official Communique 015-26 on 3 September 2026.

— Reform Nicaragua’s parliament approved the change on 1 September 2026, in the first of two votes.

— OAS The Permanent Council approved a resolution on 19 August 2026.

— Charter The Inter-American Democratic Charter is the OAS instrument that defines democracy as an obligation.

Peru’s move follows an OAS resolution that declared representative democracy in Nicaragua no longer exists.

The OAS building in Washington. Peru’s Communique 015-26 asks the OAS and the UN to activate all available mechanisms. (Photo: Carol M. Highsmith, Public domain, Wikimedia Commons.)

The Nicaragua reform has drawn a formal rejection from Peru. Peru has called on the OAS and the UN to act.

The aim, it says, is to prevent a dictatorship consolidating. The call came in an official communique issued by Peru’s foreign ministry on 3 September 2026.

Peru’s Official Communique

Peru’s foreign ministry issued Official Communique 015-26 on 3 September 2026, rejecting Nicaragua’s constitutional reform. The note says the reform seeks to liquidate democratic institutions and warns of the perpetuation of the Ortega and Murillo dictatorship.

Peru calls the Nicaragua reform a flagrant violation of the Inter-American Democratic Charter and of Nicaragua’s human rights commitments. In the same communique Peru urges the international community to act.

It names the organs of the United Nations and the Organization of American States.

The OAS Resolution

On 19 August 2026, the OAS Permanent Council approved a resolution convening an urgent meeting of foreign ministers on Nicaragua. It declared that representative democracy no longer exists in the country.

That resolution was political and diplomatic. It did not itself impose sanctions or authorise force.

The Nicaragua Reform

On 1 September 2026, Nicaragua’s Sandinista-controlled parliament approved a constitutional change in a first vote. The text says the country prohibits the extraterritoriality of foreign laws.

The exception is treaties Nicaragua has signed. That move came immediately after the OAS resolution and was reported as a direct reaction to international pressure.

Therefore, the Nicaragua reform is seen as a direct challenge to external oversight.

The United States pushed the OAS resolution. It asked for an urgent ministerial meeting to consider collective measures against Managua’s plan.

However, the OAS resolution itself did not impose new sanctions.

The Inter-American Democratic Charter

The Inter-American Democratic Charter is the OAS instrument that defines democracy as an obligation of member states. Invoking it is the formal route to suspending a member.

Peru’s communique explicitly references this charter, highlighting the gravity of the Nicaragua reform. As a result, the call for action carries significant diplomatic weight.

International Reaction

Peru’s call is part of a broader international response to the Nicaragua reform. The OAS resolution had already set the stage for a ministerial meeting.

Meanwhile, the United States continues to push for collective measures against Managua. Still, no suspension from the OAS has occurred.

What the Reform Means

The Nicaragua reform effectively blocks foreign laws and resolutions from having domestic effect. This could undermine international pressure and human rights commitments.

In short, the reform aims to shield the government from external accountability. Peru’s communique warns that this could perpetuate the dictatorship.

Potential Consequences

If the international community activates mechanisms under the charter, Nicaragua could face suspension from the OAS. However, that step has not been taken yet.

Next Steps

The OAS has convened an urgent meeting of foreign ministers to discuss Nicaragua. Peru’s communique adds momentum to that process.

The UN and OAS organs are now urged to act on the Nicaragua reform. Overall, the situation remains fluid, with diplomatic and economic tools on the table.

What Peru Actually Said

Peru’s note opens with what it calls deep concern and firm rejection. It refers to the reform approved by Nicaragua’s National Assembly in a first vote.

The text says the change seeks to liquidate democratic institutions in the country. It names the removal of free elections and the end of the rule of law.

It also warns of the perpetuation of what it calls the Ortega and Murillo family dictatorship. Peruvian outlets including Andina, RPP and Infobae reproduced the wording.

A Second Vote Still Has to Come

Constitutional changes in Nicaragua need two votes in the National Assembly. The first one passed on 1 September 2026.

The second vote has to happen in a later legislative session. Until it does, the reform is not in force.

That timing matters for the diplomatic response. Governments are reacting to a text that can still be stopped in law, even if few expect it to be.

The Resolution Behind the Ministers’ Meeting

The OAS Permanent Council resolution of 19 August 2026 is recorded as CP/RES. 1317 (2601/26). It convenes a consultation meeting of foreign ministers on Nicaragua.

A consultation meeting of foreign ministers is the level above the Permanent Council. It is where the organisation weighs collective measures.

Peru’s communique asks both the OAS and the United Nations to use the mechanisms they already have. It does not name a specific measure.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Nicaragua reform?

The Nicaragua reform is a constitutional change approved by parliament in a first vote on 1 September 2026. It prohibits the extraterritoriality of foreign laws, meaning foreign resolutions will not have domestic legal effect.

Why did Peru issue a communique?

Peru issued Official Communique 015-26 on 3 September 2026 to reject the reform. Peru calls it a flagrant violation of the Inter-American Democratic Charter and urges international action.

What did the OAS resolution say?

The OAS Permanent Council approved a resolution on 19 August 2026 convening an urgent meeting of foreign ministers. It declared that representative democracy no longer exists in Nicaragua.

Sources: Peruvian foreign ministry; OAS; Reuters; US Trade Representative.

World.title: Colombia Budget Debate Suspended as Ministers Skip
World.content:
Colombia · GOVERNMENT

Key Facts — What happened Joint economic committees suspended the 2027 budget debate on September 2, 2026.

— Who was absent Finance, education, and housing ministers, plus the planning director, sent delegates instead.

— The catch Even government-allied lawmakers objected to the absence, not just the opposition.

— What they said Senator Carlos Meisel said ministers must show their face before Congress.

— Context The budget debate comes during a fiscal crisis and earthquake reconstruction needs.

— What comes next No new date has been set for the budget debate in Congress.

Colombia’s Congress suspended the 2027 budget debate on September 2, 2026, because key ministers did not show up. Lawmakers from all parties objected.

Colombia’s Congress suspended the 2027 budget debate on September 2, 2026, after key ministers failed to appear. Lawmakers from across the political spectrum walked out of the session.

Ministers Skip Budget Session

The joint economic committees suspended the 2027 budget debate on September 2, 2026. Several ministers were absent from the session in Bogota.

Finance Minister Miguel Gomez, Education Minister Viviane Morales, and Housing Minister Jaime Andres Beltran were expected. National Planning Director Julian Buitrago was also cited, but all sent delegates instead.

The joint committees combine the third and fourth economic committees of Colombia’s Senate and House of Representatives. Together, they normally handle budget matters for Congress.

Lawmakers From All Parties Object

Lawmakers from several parties, including government allies, objected to the ministers’ absence during the budget debate. They demanded direct engagement by cabinet-level officials.

Cambio Radical, a party that backs the government, also registered its disapproval. Representative Carlos Cuenca said his party’s lawmakers would withdraw from the budget debate.

Senator Meisel’s Criticism

Senator Carlos Meisel of the Centro Democratico party criticized the absence of ministers from the budget debate. He said, ‘This in no way can be the kind of relationship the Government has with us.’

Meisel stressed that Colombia is going through an enormous fiscal crisis. He said Congress cannot deal with delegates on such serious matters.

What Meisel Demanded

Meisel insisted each minister must ‘show their face’ before the commissions to defend their own budget. He said, ‘For every peso given to a ministry, we need certainty that a lead official is showing their face.’

Other lawmakers echoed the complaint during the budget debate. Senator Sara Castellanos warned that ministers’ absence ‘sends the wrong message’ to Congress.

Fiscal Crisis Context

Colombia’s fiscal crisis means the government has limited money for new spending. This makes the 2027 budget debate more contentious than usual.

The government must decide how to divide scarce resources among ministries. Ministers are normally expected to justify their own spending requests in person.

Earthquake Reconstruction Needs

A 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia’s Choco region on August 10, 2026, killing hundreds and injuring thousands. Colombia’s disaster risk agency, UNGRD, says the quake destroyed 31,540 homes.

Government estimates put total losses near COP 30 trillion (US$9.6 billion), according to The Rio Times. Valle del Cauca department alone accounts for COP 19.5 trillion (US$6.3 billion) of the losses.

Scale of the Earthquake Damage

UNGRD also recorded 178,555 damaged homes and 603 collapsed buildings by August 25, 2026. The earthquake affected 494 municipalities across 16 departments.

Five cities, Cali, Manizales, Pereira, Armenia, and Quibdo, accounted for about 75% of the deaths. Rebuilding those cities is now central to the 2027 budget debate.

Reconstruction Cost Estimates

Investment bank BTG Pactual put the initial reconstruction cost at COP 20 trillion (US$6.35 billion). Government estimates put total earthquake damage near COP 30 trillion (US$9.6 billion).

Reconstruction is expected to take up to six years, according to The Rio Times. The 2027 budget debate must weigh these costs against other spending needs.

UNDP Assessment of the Damage

The United Nations Development Programme released an earthquake assessment on August 28, 2026. It recorded 331 deaths, 4,449 injuries, and 143 people missing.

More than 406,000 people were affected, and over 225,000 structures were damaged. Vatican News cited these UNDP figures in its own coverage.

Government Figures on Impact

On August 31, 2026, Colombia’s president announced the start of the reconstruction phase. Government figures showed 452,782 people affected in 213,400 families across 16 departments.

The president said emergency operations and searches for missing people would continue. These figures came a week before the budget debate was suspended.

Political Reactions

The Historic Pact, now in opposition, also criticized the ministers’ absence from the budget debate. Senator David Racero called it a bad precedent for Congress.

He suggested the government wanted to avoid debate over the size of the proposed budget and Colombia’s debt levels.

Representative Cathy Juvinao of the Green party pushed back on parts of the criticism. She still called for better communication between Congress and the government during the budget debate.

No Fiscal Room, Officials Say

Colombia’s national planning director said earlier in August that the government has little fiscal room left. He said private and regional funding will also be needed for reconstruction.

That warning adds pressure to the 2027 budget debate. Congress must weigh reconstruction costs alongside the government’s other spending plans.

What Happens Next

The joint economic committees will need to reschedule the budget debate. Ministers are expected to appear in person to avoid further delays.

No new date has been announced yet for the budget debate. Colombia’s constitution requires the 2027 budget to be approved by Congress and the government before October 20, 2026.

Role of the Planning Department

Colombia’s National Planning Department, or DNP, helps prepare the national budget. Its director, Julian Buitrago, was also absent from the September 2 session.

The DNP is a technical agency that sets development priorities. It works with the finance ministry to draft each year’s budget.

Colombia’s Peso and the Earthquake Bill

On September 2, 2026, Colombia’s central bank set its official exchange rate, the TRM, at 3,184 pesos to the US dollar. That was down slightly from the previous trading day.

That volatility affects the cost of imported materials needed for reconstruction. It is one more factor lawmakers must weigh in the 2027 budget debate.

Historical Budget Process

In Colombia, the government submits a budget proposal to Congress each year. The joint economic committees review it before a full vote.

Ministers usually appear in person to defend their portfolios. This is a key part of the legislative oversight process behind every budget debate.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why was the budget debate suspended?

The budget debate was suspended because key ministers did not attend the session. They sent delegates instead, which lawmakers objected to.

Who were the absent ministers?

Finance Minister Miguel Gomez, Education Minister Viviane Morales, and Housing Minister Jaime Andres Beltran were absent. National Planning Director Julian Buitrago also did not attend.

What did Senator Meisel say?

Senator Carlos Meisel said the absence cannot be the relationship the government has with Congress. He insisted each minister must show their face.

What is the context of the earthquake?

The August 10 earthquake caused extensive damage, with losses estimated near COP 30 trillion (US$9.6 billion). Reconstruction is a major need in the 2027 budget debate.

Sources: El Pais America – Colombia; El Colombiano; La Silla Vacia; Infobae Colombia; El Tiempo; The Rio Times; UNGRD; Vatican News; The City Paper Bogota; Banco de la Republica.

World.title: Bolivia Diesel Quota Raised, YPFB Intervened
World.content:
Bolivia · ENERGY

Key Facts — What happened Bolivia raised the subsidized diesel quota for small farmers to 2,500 liters a month.

— How big The price stays at 9.80 bolivianos (US$0.81) per liter under Supreme Decree 5698.

— The catch The YPFB intervention is temporary, up to 180 days, extendable once by 90.

— Who it hits Large consumers lost their diesel subsidy on August 17, now paying 18 bolivianos (US$1.49).

— What comes next YPFB is meant to exit fuel sales and focus on exploration, production, and refining.

Bolivia expands subsidized diesel for small farmers and takes over its state oil company, YPFB. The moves aim to end protests and fix fuel supply.

La Paz, Bolivia. The government raised the subsidised diesel quota and placed YPFB under a temporary intervention. (Photo: The Rio Times archive.)

Bolivia raised its diesel quota for small farmers on September 2, 2026. The government also intervened in state oil firm YPFB to fix fuel supply.

New Diesel Quota for Farmers

Bolivia’s government expanded the subsidized diesel quota for small agricultural producers on September 2, 2026. Under Supreme Decree 5698, they can now buy between 121 and 2,500 liters a month.

The price stays at 9.80 bolivianos (US$0.81) per liter. The diesel is for the producer’s own use and cannot be resold.

About the Dollar Conversions

This article converts bolivianos to dollars at 12.06 bolivianos per dollar. That is the open-market rate from open.er-api.com on 3 September 2026, close to Bolivia’s parallel-market rate that week.

Bolivia’s old official peg of 6.96 bolivianos per dollar is no longer used in most everyday transactions. Bolivians now buy and sell dollars closer to the market rate used here.

How Producers Qualify

Producers must show a national ID card to buy diesel under the new quota. They must also be registered in Bolivia’s Unified Agricultural Regime, known as the RAU.

The RAU must send updated lists of eligible producers by the 10th business day of each month. Regulators had three business days to write rules for Supreme Decree 5698.

President Paz Signs the Decree

President Rodrigo Paz promulgated Supreme Decree 5698 on September 2, 2026. It followed producer rejection of an earlier measure, Supreme Decree 5676.

Producers had blocked roads over the terms of Decree 5676 before the government revised its approach. The new decree raised the diesel quota rather than reversing the August subsidy split.

Protests in Beni Over Diesel

On August 26, producers from Marban province in Beni blocked the San Pablo bridge. Their demand was the repeal of the decree that had split the diesel subsidy.

The government expected the new, larger quota to end these protests. Officials announced the quota increase on September 2, 2026.

Producers had briefly lifted the San Pablo bridge blockade earlier, after the government pledged to guarantee diesel supply. They later resumed the blockade over continued shortages.

YPFB Intervention Decree

Supreme Decree 5697, promulgated on September 1, orders an extraordinary intervention of the state oil company. The intervention lasts up to 180 calendar days, extendable once by 90 more days.

The goal is to review the company’s commercialization, logistics, and fuel traceability. It also aims to strengthen the import and distribution chain.

The commission will look for fuel smuggling networks, hoarding, and diversions in the supply chain. The decree says the intervention does not abolish the state oil company or change its legal structure.

Commission Members Named

The the company intervention commission has six members. They include Fernando Aramayo of the Presidency, Christian Morales of Economy, and Oscar Mario Justiniano of Production.

Also on the commission are Marcelo Blanco of Hydrocarbons and Mauricio Zamora of Public Works. Vice-Minister of Transparency Yamil Garcia completes the six-person the state oil company commission.

YPFB to Leave Fuel Sales

Public Works Minister Mauricio Zamora said the company should leave fuel commercialization and focus on exploring for and producing hydrocarbons. He used a strong metaphor to make his point.

Zamora said, ‘We have to remove this cancer that YPFB has, and that cancer is called commercialization.’ He added, ‘We are going to do like a chemotherapy to remove this cancer that is harming Bolivians.’

Blanco on YPFB’s Natural Role

Hydrocarbons Minister Marcelo Blanco said YPFB should return to its natural role. He said YPFB was not created to sell fuel to the public.

Blanco said YPFB should instead focus on exploration, production, and refinery work. Both ministers made their comments at a press conference on September 2, 2026.

Subsidy Split in August

On August 17, the government removed the diesel subsidy for large consumers. It set a new reference price of 18.00 bolivianos (US$1.49) per liter.

Public and private transport with minimum consumption, plus small agricultural producers, kept paying 9.80 bolivianos (US$0.81) per liter.

Government Response to Fuel Shortages

The government also doubled the Treasury funds backing the fuel subsidy, to 2,000 million bolivianos (US$165.8 million). This followed reported shortages and roadblocks around the country.

The YPFB intervention is a separate step to address inefficiencies and alleged corruption at YPFB. Officials say the goal is a stable fuel supply.

Minister Explains Decree in the Field

Production Minister Oscar Mario Justiniano traveled to Cuatro Canadas with YPFB technicians on September 2. He went to explain Decree 5698 and review local fuel supply.

Cuatro Canadas is a farming area in Santa Cruz department. Producers there also rely on the subsidized diesel quota set by YPFB and the government.

Bolivia’s Broader Fuel Crisis

Bolivia has faced fuel shortages and long lines at gas stations for months. A shortage of US dollars has made it harder for YPFB to pay foreign fuel suppliers.

The dollar shortage has also pushed Bolivia toward multiple exchange rates. That is why this article uses the open-market rate rather than Bolivia’s old official peg.

Background on YPFB

YPFB is Bolivia’s state oil company. Officials now criticize its role in selling fuel directly to the public.

The government argues YPFB was not created for that purpose. The current intervention aims to correct this, according to ministers.

What Led to the Intervention

The YPFB intervention follows months of fuel shortages and protests around Bolivia. The government has faced criticism over how it manages YPFB.

Officials allege corruption and inefficiency inside YPFB’s fuel distribution business. The intervention commission is meant to investigate and fix these problems.

Next Steps for Fuel Supply

The intervention commission will oversee YPFB’s operations for up to 180 days, extendable once by 90 more days. Small farmers can now buy up to 2,500 liters of diesel a month at 9.80 bolivianos (US$0.81).

Officials have not given a timeline for when YPFB will fully exit fuel commercialization. The government says the intervention itself is a temporary, not permanent, measure.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the new diesel quota for small farmers in Bolivia?

Small farmers can now buy between 121 and 2,500 liters of diesel a month. The price is 9.80 bolivianos (US$0.81) per liter.

Why did Bolivia intervene in YPFB?

The government wants YPFB to leave fuel sales and focus on exploration and refining. The YPFB intervention aims to fix fuel supply and address alleged corruption.

How long will the YPFB intervention last?

The YPFB intervention lasts up to 180 calendar days. It can be extended once for an additional 90 days.

What caused the protests in Beni?

Producers in Marban province blocked a bridge on August 26. They demanded repeal of the decree that had split the diesel subsidy.

Sources: eju.tv; Vision360; El Mundo; Jornada; Enfoque News; Urgente.bo; El Dia; open.er-api.com; The Rio Times.

World.title: US Urges Partners to End Business With Nicaragua
World.content:
Nicaragua · DIPLOMACY

Key Facts — What happened Nicaragua’s Congress passed a constitutional reform on 1 September 2026.

— The reform It bars opposition parties from elections and extends most official terms to seven years.

— US response Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged partners to stop business with Nicaragua.

— What comes next Washington will bring specific measures to the next OAS foreign ministers meeting.

— The catch The US did not call for a trade halt or name any trade measures.

— Trade pact Nicaragua has been part of CAFTA-DR, a free trade deal with the US, since 2006.

Washington wants allies to stop normal dealings with Nicaragua after a vote that locks out the opposition. The next step goes to the Organization of American States.

Avenida Bolivar in Managua, lined with the city’s illuminated metal trees. Washington has urged partners to stop business as usual with the government. (Photo: The Rio Times archive.)

The United States has called on international partners to stop business with Nicaragua’s government. Secretary of State Marco Rubio made the appeal after Nicaragua’s Congress passed a constitutional reform that locks out the opposition.

Rubio’s Statement

On 2 September 2026, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the country’s National Assembly had ‘eroded the fiction of Managua’s democracy.’ He said the vote entrenched an ‘illegitimate dynasty’ in the country.

He urged partners to ‘immediately stop business as usual operations with this brutal dictatorship.’ Rubio added that dictatorships should not get the same benefits as democratic governments.

Nicaragua’s Constitutional Reform

the country’s Congress passed the constitutional reform on 1 September 2026. It was the first of two votes required for such changes to take effect.

The reform bars opposition parties from Managua’s elections. It also extends terms for co-presidents and other top officials from six to seven years.

Terms grow to seven years for deputies, mayors, judges, and the heads of the army and police. Officials already in office keep their longer terms automatically.

Inside the Reform Text

The reform bars anyone labelled a ‘traitor to the homeland’ from holding elected office in the country. That label has already stripped nationality from at least 452 critics and opponents, per the Tico Times.

Among them are the writers Sergio Ramirez and Gioconda Belli. The reform also lets the country’s Supreme Electoral Council cancel parties it says received foreign funding.

A Vote Staged in Leon

Managua’s Congress passed the reform unanimously by a show of hands on 1 September 2026. Lawmakers met in Leon, a city roughly 90 kilometers from Managua.

The session opened the government’s self-declared Patriotic Month. Assembly president Gustavo Porras laid a copy of the text at the tomb of poet Ruben Dario.

the country’s official gazette, La Gaceta, published the amendment’s certification the next morning. That step gave the first vote on Nicaragua’s constitution full legal effect.

Ortega’s Long Rule in Nicaragua

Daniel Ortega is 80 years old and has led the country since 2007. Rosario Murillo has stood at his side for most of that time.

Managua’s government has faced years of criticism over democracy and human rights. The September reform is the latest change critics say weakens checks on power in the country.

Ortega and Murillo’s Role

Daniel Ortega and Rosario Murillo pushed the reform through the country’s Congress. Murillo has been co-president since an earlier constitutional change in 2024.

That 2024 change extended the presidential term from five to six years. It also pushed Managua’s presidential election back to late 2027.

US Calls for Action

Rubio said Washington remains committed to addressing human rights violations in the country. His statement did not spell out what actions partners should take.

It named no specific companies, industries, or countries in the country. It called only for a broad end to normal dealings with Managua’s government.

OAS Meeting Next

Rubio said the United States will bring specific measures to the next meeting of OAS foreign ministers on the country. He did not describe those measures.

The OAS Permanent Council voted on 19 August to call that meeting. Brazil opposed the vote and Mexico abstained, and no date has been set.

No Trade Measures Announced

The State Department statement does not call for a halt to trade with the country. It does not name any trade measures, such as suspending CAFTA-DR.

The Tico Times and other outlets confirm the call was to end ‘business as usual,’ not to start an embargo.

Trade Pact Context

Managua belongs to CAFTA-DR, a free trade pact linking the US, five Central American nations, and the Dominican Republic. It removes tariffs on most goods.

The pact entered into force for the United States and the country on 1 April 2006. Nicaragua gained duty-free access to US markets, especially for textiles and farm goods.

How CAFTA-DR Works

The United States is the country’s largest trading partner, according to Britannica. Exact current trade figures for Managua are not publicly available right now.

CAFTA-DR also includes investment protections and a dispute process. Suspending it for the country would require formal steps by both the US and Nicaragua.

Reform and Nicaragua’s Trade Obligations

the country’s new constitution says foreign laws do not apply inside Managua. Havana Times reported this rule on 31 August 2026.

Legal experts say the change has no practical effect on treaties. Nicaragua remains bound by CAFTA-DR and its other international agreements.

Ortega’s Earlier Comments

On 19 July 2026, Daniel Ortega said ‘there won’t be any more elections’ in Nicaragua. He said this would stop the opposition from ‘seizing the government’ again.

Reuters reported the comment ahead of the constitutional reform’s first vote. It came weeks before Rubio’s statement on Nicaragua.

International Reaction

The US call is aimed at international partners, not only OAS members. It seeks to isolate Nicaragua’s government both diplomatically and economically.

Responses from other countries are not yet known. The OAS meeting on Nicaragua will be a key moment to watch, and Nicaragua’s government has not yet replied to Rubio.

What Comes Next

A second vote on the reform is required under Nicaragua’s constitution before it takes effect. It is expected after Nicaragua’s new legislative session opens in January 2027.

No exact date has been set for that second vote in Nicaragua. The US will present its own measures at the coming OAS meeting.

Understanding the OAS

The Organization of American States is a regional body with 35 member states, founded in 1948. It includes the United States and most Latin American countries.

Its charter promotes democracy, human rights, and regional security. Nicaragua itself withdrew from the OAS in November 2023.

Resolutions can condemn actions or suspend a member state. Enforcement still depends on member states acting on their own.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the US call for regarding Nicaragua?

The US urged international partners to stop business with Nicaragua’s government. Secretary of State Marco Rubio made the call after a constitutional reform.

What does Nicaragua’s constitutional reform do?

The reform bars opposition parties from elections and extends most official terms to seven years. It passed a first vote in Nicaragua’s Congress on 1 September 2026.

Will the US stop trade with Nicaragua?

No, the US did not call for a trade halt with Nicaragua. It only urged an end to business as usual and will bring measures to an OAS meeting.

What is CAFTA-DR?

CAFTA-DR is a free trade agreement linking the US, Central America, and the Dominican Republic. It has applied to Nicaragua since 2006.

Sources: The Tico Times; U.S. Department of State; Reuters; Havana Times; Britannica; Divergentes.

World.title: Brazil Vorcaro Testimony Had No Federal Police, Folha Says
World.content:
Brazil · JUSTICE

Key Facts — What happened Banker Daniel Vorcaro gave testimony without Federal Police present.

— How big The statement was taken before an auxiliary judge in Justice Mendonça’s chambers.

— The catch Mendonça’s office says he met Vorcaro once, in March 2025, and only listened.

— Who it hits The case involves messages between Vorcaro and Justice Alexandre de Moraes.

— What comes next The full Supreme Court will analyze the material, and the prosecutor-general will comment.

A Brazilian banker’s statement to a Supreme Court justice’s office was taken without Federal Police present, a newspaper reported. The justice says he only listened to the banker once.

Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court in Brasilia, lit at night. Daniel Vorcaro gave his statement to Justice Andre Mendonca’s office. (Photo: The Rio Times archive.)

Brazilian banker Daniel Vorcaro gave testimony without Federal Police present, Folha de S.Paulo reported. The statement was taken before an auxiliary judge in Justice André Mendonça’s chambers.

Testimony Details

Folha de S.Paulo reported on 2 September 2026 that Vorcaro’s statement was taken without the Federal Police. The statement itself was given on 27 August 2026, before an auxiliary judge in Mendonça’s office.

Vorcaro said Federal Police leaders were reluctant about his cooperation proposal. The newspaper attributed this to his own account in the statement.

Mendonça’s Office Response

Mendonça’s office said he received Vorcaro once, in March 2025, at Vorcaro’s initiative. He limited himself to hearing him, the office said.

For the later statement, the office said Federal Police were kept away to protect Vorcaro. He had reported serious intimidations, and court rules allow this for a deponent’s safety.

Secrecy Lifted

On 1 September 2026, Mendonça lifted secrecy on the case. He called the full court the inevitable path.

He asked the court’s president to schedule a public, in-person plenary session. The court later would hear the case in plenary.

A plenary session is a meeting of all 11 Supreme Court justices. This is different from a decision made by a single justice in chambers.

Prosecutor-General Involved

The material was sent to prosecutor-general Paulo Gonet for comment. No direct reaction from Gonet to the testimony is verified.

The prosecutor-general is Brazil’s top federal prosecutor. His role is to give a legal opinion on the case before the court decides.

What Is Banco Master

Banco Master is a Brazilian bank. Daniel Vorcaro is a former banker associated with it.

The case involves messages between Vorcaro and Justice Alexandre de Moraes. The Federal Police flagged these messages.

Justice Moraes is a member of the Supreme Court. The messages were found during a police investigation.

Background of the Case

The broader case involves reports and messages involving Moraes and Gonet. The Supreme Court is reviewing the material.

Mendonça sought plenary, public review rather than handling it only in chambers.

Vorcaro’s Cooperation Proposal

Vorcaro said the Federal Police were unwilling with his proposal of collaboration. This is according to his testimony.

The Federal Police have not given a direct quoted reaction to this point. Their resistance is mentioned in reports.

Timeline of Events

Mendonça met Vorcaro once in March 2025. Vorcaro’s formal statement, without Federal Police present, was given on 27 August 2026.

Secrecy was lifted on 1 September 2026, and the statement was reported on 2 September 2026. The plenary session has not yet been scheduled.

Legal Significance

The absence of Federal Police during a formal statement is unusual. Mendonça’s office says court rules justify it when a witness reports intimidation.

A representative of the Public Ministry was present, since that is required by law. The formal statement is separate from Mendonça’s single March 2025 meeting with Vorcaro.

What Comes Next

The full Supreme Court will analyze the Federal Police material. The prosecutor-general will comment.

The plenary session will be public and in-person. No date has been set yet.

Understanding the Supreme Court

Brazil’s Supreme Court is called the Supremo Tribunal Federal, or STF. It is the highest court in the country.

It has 11 justices, called ministers. They are appointed by the president and approved by the Senate.

The STF handles cases involving the constitution and high-ranking officials. This case falls under its jurisdiction.

A single justice can make urgent decisions, but the full court usually decides major issues. Mendonça wants the full court to review this case.

Role of the Federal Police

The Federal Police, or PF, is Brazil’s national police force. It investigates crimes against the federal government and public officials.

In this case, the PF produced reports and messages involving Moraes and Gonet. These were sent to the Supreme Court for review.

The PF also rejected Vorcaro‘s cooperation proposal, according to his testimony.

What Is a Plea Deal

A plea deal, or cooperation proposal, is a legal agreement. A suspect agrees to provide information in exchange for a reduced sentence.

Vorcaro offered a cooperation proposal to the PF. The PF was unwilling to accept it, according to his testimony.

Public Interest

The lifting of secrecy allows the public to see the evidence. This is a step toward transparency.

The plenary session will be open to the public. This ensures that the decision is made in the open.

Mendonça’s Meeting with Vorcaro

Justice André Mendonça’s office said he met Daniel Vorcaro once, in March 2025, at Vorcaro’s initiative, and only listened to him. This statement was reported by Poder360 on September 2, 2026.

For the later statement, the office cited court rules that protect a witness who reports intimidation. That is separate from the single 2025 meeting.

Vorcaro’s Testimony Without Federal Police

Folha de S.Paulo reported on September 2, 2026, that Vorcaro’s statements were taken without the Federal Police present. They were before an auxiliary judge in Mendonça’s cabinet.

The Federal Police had been reluctant about Vorcaro’s cooperation proposal, according to his own account.

The statement itself was given on 27 August 2026, ahead of the September 2 reports. Mendonça’s office cited court rules meant to protect a witness who reports intimidation.

Mendonça’s Request for Plenary Session

On September 1, 2026, Mendonça asked STF President Edson Fachin to schedule a public, in-person plenary session.

It would analyze Federal Police material on Vorcaro and Alexandre de Moraes. He called the plenary ‘the inevitable path’, as quoted by Folha de S.Paulo.

The court would later hear the case in plenary, but the report does not say Vorcaro testified that day.

Prosecutor-General’s Role

After Mendonça lifted secrecy, the prosecutor-general, Paulo Gonet, was sent the Federal Police material for comment. The retrieved sources do not include a direct reaction from Gonet to the testimony itself.

The material is part of a broader case involving Banco Master and messages with Moraes and Gonet.

Timeline of Events

Key dates: March 2025 for the single meeting. August 27, 2026, for the formal statement without Federal Police present.

September 1, 2026, for lifting secrecy and seeking plenary review. September 2, 2026, for news reports on the statement and Mendonça’s office comment.

Mendonça’s office said court rules protect a witness after a report of serious intimidation. It said this justified keeping Federal Police away from the August 27 statement.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why was the Federal Police absent from Vorcaro’s testimony?

Mendonça’s office said court rules protect a witness who reports intimidation. Vorcaro had reported serious intimidations before the statement.

What did Mendonça say about his meeting with Vorcaro?

He said he met Vorcaro once, in March 2025, and only listened. He did not take testimony.

What is the role of prosecutor-general Paulo Gonet?

He was sent the material for comment. He has not yet reacted publicly.

What happens next in the case?

The full Supreme Court will analyze the material in a public session. The date is not set.

Sources: Folha de S.Paulo; Poder360.

World.title: Argentina Country Risk Dips Below 500 Points
World.content:
Argentina · MARKETS

Key Facts — What happened Argentina’s country risk fell below 500 points on September 2, 2026.

— How big Intraday low was 493 points, lowest since August 17.

— The catch Closing levels varied by outlet, from 496 to 500 points.

— Who it hits Investors in Argentine bonds and shares benefit from lower risk.

— What comes next Markets watch if the index stays below 500 in coming days.

Argentina’s country risk index slipped under 500 points on Wednesday, a level not seen since mid-August. Local shares and dollar bonds extended gains for a third straight session.

The Obelisco on Avenida 9 de Julio in Buenos Aires. Argentina’s country risk index dropped below 500 points on 2 September 2026. (Photo: The Rio Times archive.)

Argentina’s country risk fell below 500 points on September 2, 2026, for the first time in over two weeks. The index, which measures the extra interest Argentina pays over US debt, touched an intraday low of 493 points.

Country Risk Drops Below 500

Argentina’s country risk index, compiled by JP Morgan, fell below 500 points on Wednesday, September 2, 2026. The index measures the extra interest Argentina pays over United States government debt.

According to Infobae, the index touched an intraday low of 493 points, the lowest since August 17, 2026. Different market screens put the close between 496 and 500 points, depending on the outlet.

Intraday Low and Closing Levels

Infobae reported the intraday low of 493 points and said the index closed at 500 points, down four units. BAE Negocios and Misiones Online both reported a close of 496 points.

La Nacion also reported 496 points, down five units on the day. iProfesional and a separate Infobae report both gave 498 points.

What Country Risk Measures

Country risk shows the extra interest Argentina must pay on its debt compared to the United States government.

A lower number means investors see less risk in lending to Argentina. This can reduce borrowing costs for the government and companies.

The index is based on the yield spread of Argentine bonds over US Treasuries. A spread of 500 points means Argentina pays 5% more interest than the US.

Shares and ADRs Rise

Argentine shares listed in New York, known as ADRs, rose for a third straight session on September 2. Infobae reported gains led by Edenor (+5.1%), Central Puerto (+4.7%), and Cresud (+4.5%).

La Nacion gave a different set of leaders: YPF up 4%, Transportadora Gas del Sur up 3.7%, and Tenaris up 2.7%. Other outlets reported ADRs up as much as 5% that day.

The differences come from the time of day each outlet checked the prices, and which shares each one tracked.

Dollar Bonds Also Gain

Sovereign dollar bonds rose about 0.2% on average on September 2, according to Infobae. This helped push the country risk index lower.

The Bonares and Globales bonds, which Argentina uses to borrow, were among those that gained. The average gain was broad but gentle.

Third Consecutive Session of Gains

The local stock market, the Merval, also rose for a third consecutive session on September 2. Infobae said the Merval gained 1.9% that day, matching La Nacion’s report of a third straight positive session.

The Merval closed at 3,106,216 points on September 2, according to Infobae and The Rio Times’ own market snapshot.

On September 1, Infobae reported the Merval up 0.5%, closing at 3,049,455 points.

Reversing August’s Picture

The recent decline in country risk reverses the picture from most of August, when the index moved higher. By 2 September, it had fallen back to levels last seen in mid-August.

The drop below 500 is symbolic for markets. It signals a partial return of the investor confidence that August had eroded.

Market Reactions and Outlook

The country risk fell below 500 points on September 2, 2026, reaching an intraday low of 493 points. It closed between 496 and 500 points, according to different sources.

This was the first time it went below 500 since August 17, 2026. The stock market and ADRs rose for a third consecutive session on that day.

How Country Risk Is Calculated

The JP Morgan EMBI index tracks the yield spread of emerging market bonds over US Treasuries. For Argentina, it reflects the extra return investors demand for holding its debt.

A spread of 500 points means Argentina pays 5 percentage points more than the US government. This compensates investors for the higher risk of default.

The index is updated in real time during trading hours. It reacts to news, economic data, and changes in global risk appetite.

Why the Level Matters

A country risk below 500 points is often seen as a positive signal. It suggests that investors consider Argentina less risky than before.

This can lower the cost of borrowing for the government and companies. It may also attract foreign investment.

However, the level is still high compared to investment-grade countries. Argentina has a long way to go to regain full market confidence.

The Role of the Merval

The Merval is Argentina’s main stock exchange index. It tracks the performance of the largest companies listed in Buenos Aires.

On September 2, the Merval rose 1.9%, adding to gains from the previous sessions.

Understanding ADRs

ADRs are shares of foreign companies traded on US stock exchanges. They allow US investors to buy Argentine companies without dealing with local markets.

Argentine ADRs include companies like Edenor, an electricity distributor, and Cresud, an agricultural firm. Their price movements reflect investor sentiment toward Argentina.

What the Numbers Mean

Country risk is a measure of how safe it is to lend to a country. The JP Morgan index is a common way to track it, and a lower number means less risk.

On 2 September 2026, the index fell to 496 points, according to BAE Negocios. This was a drop of eight points from the previous day, as reported by Misiones Online.

How the Index Is Calculated

The index compares the interest rate on Argentina’s dollar bonds with the rate on US Treasury bonds. The difference, in percentage points, is multiplied by 100 to get the index number.

For example, if Argentina’s bonds pay 5% more than US bonds, the index would be 500. A lower number means investors are more confident in Argentina’s ability to repay its debts.

What Happened Before

In August 2026, the country risk had been above 500 points. On 17 August 2026, it was at a level that was later seen as a recent high.

The drop below 500 on 2 September was the first time in over two weeks, according to La Nacion. This was a sign of improving investor sentiment.

What Comes Next

Investors will watch to see if the country risk index stays below 500 points or if it goes even lower. The next few days will show if this is a lasting change or just a short-term move.

The move came after months of higher country risk readings during August. A steady run below 500 would mark a real shift in sentiment.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Argentina’s country risk?

Country risk measures the extra interest Argentina pays on its debt compared to US government bonds. A lower number means less perceived risk.

Why did country risk fall below 500 points?

The fall was driven by rising dollar bonds and shares. Investors showed increased confidence in Argentine assets.

What does it mean for Argentina?

Lower country risk can reduce borrowing costs for the government. It also signals improved investor sentiment.

Will country risk stay below 500?

It depends on economic and political developments. Markets are volatile, so the index could rise again.

World.title: Venezuela Cash: A Country of 28 Million Is Running Out of Banknotes
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

VENEZUELA · ECONOMY

Key Facts —Cash per person: Venezuela’s physical bolívar cash is worth roughly US$3 to US$5 per inhabitant. Brazil holds about US$300 per person in notes and coins, Mexico about US$1,500. —Highest note: The largest banknote in circulation, 500 bolívares, is worth about US$0.63 at the official rate of 798.33 per dollar on 1 September 2026. —Vault claim: A July research memorandum says some 750 million unused banknotes printed in 2016–2018 sit in central bank vaults. The Rio Times could not verify that figure independently. —The law: The old note families were formally demonetized in 2018 and 2024. Reviving them would require an affirmative central bank decision with almost no international precedent. —Expired forecast: The memorandum predicted a “recirculation” of old notes by 22 July, later “early August.” No announcement came; the exchange rate kept crawling upward. —Disclosure: The memorandum is published by MIGP Capital Corporation, a firm with a commercial interest in Venezuelan foreign exchange.

Venezuela cash has nearly vanished: a country of roughly 28 million people runs on about US$3 to US$5 of physical bolívares per person — and a much-circulated theory that the central bank would simply reissue its old banknotes has now failed its own deadline.
