Visit Caribbean Tire this September.

World.title: Former Minister Edmund Castro pleads not guilty to charges stemming from dog attack on 5-year-old
World.content:
Former Minister Edmund Castro pleads not guilty to charges stemming from dog attack on 5-year-old

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Former Belize Rural North Area Representative and former Minister Edmund “Clear the Land” Castro, 61, pleaded not guilty on Wednesday to two criminal charges stemming from an alleged dog attack that left a five-year-old boy injured in Maskall Village.

Castro appeared in Court #5 alongside his attorney, Norman Rodriguez, where he was arraigned on one count of negligent wounding and one count of permitting an unmuzzled ferocious dog to be at large.

The charges arise from an incident on August 24 in which five-year-old Kevin Young Jr. was reportedly attacked by several dogs while walking past Castro’s residence in Maskall.

Police said the child suffered bites to his face, head, neck, ears, back and stomach. Public reporting following the incident indicated that the boy was taken to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where wounds were treated and he received two stitches behind one ear before being prescribed antibiotics. His mother later said his face and neck became swollen and that he remained in considerable pain.

During Wednesday’s arraignment, the sitting Magistrate questioned the charges presented by the prosecution, stating, “The charges seem to be duplicitous,” and noting that, based on the facts presented, it did not appear that Castro himself had inflicted the wounds.

The prosecutor indicated that the issue would be addressed when the matter returns to court.

Rodriguez also told the court that the animal in question was a “pup” and said he intends to make several submissions regarding the charges at Castro’s next appearance.

Castro, who had initially been granted police bail, was offered court bail of $500 plus one surety in the same amount, which he met. He is scheduled to return to court on November 10, 2026.

Outside the courthouse, Castro declined an on-camera interview but questioned why he had been charged, maintaining that the dogs involved did not belong to him.

“I nuh understand how deh could charge me when the dogs don’t even belong to me,” Castro said.

That position is consistent with Castro’s response immediately following the August incident. When contacted by 7News Belize at the time, the person identified by the child’s family as the owner denied that the dog belonged to him.

The case remains before the Magistrates’ Court, and the allegations against Castro have not been proven.

World.title: Give youth a seat at the table: Town Councils should follow Belize City’s lead
World.content:
Give youth a seat at the table: Town Councils should follow Belize City’s lead

By Zoila Palma: The Belize City Council’s Youth Shadow Council is an initiative that other municipalities across Belize should seriously consider adopting. As the council launches its 2026–2027 cohort, the program provides a strong example of how local governments can actively prepare young people for leadership, civic participation and future public service.

Rather than limiting youth involvement to occasional events or consultations, a Youth Shadow Council gives young people an opportunity to gain firsthand knowledge of how municipal government operates. Participants can learn about the responsibilities of the Mayor and councillors, observe decision-making processes, take part in community initiatives and develop communication and leadership skills.

Youth Shadow Councillor Avery Young recently described the experience as an important step in becoming a better communicator and leader within his community. Following a 36-hour training session, Young commended the Belize City Council and Mayor Bernard Wagner for creating the opportunity, highlighting the value of learning, mentorship and working alongside other young leaders.

“It is my honor to be apart of something bigger than myself. I have been blessed with the knowledge and discernment to be positioned in places of high importance. I have completed the first step of becoming a better communicator and leader within my community, whilst adapting the professional approach from Dr. Dionne Chamberland,” Young said.

The success of the initiative should encourage other town councils to follow suit.

Municipalities in Cayo, Orange Walk, Corozal, Stann Creek and Toledo could establish their own Youth Shadow Councils, giving young people in places such as San Ignacio and Santa Elena, Benque Viejo, Orange Walk Town, Corozal Town, Dangriga and Punta Gorda similar opportunities to become involved in local government.

The program could be structured around actual council portfolios, allowing young participants to shadow councillors responsible for areas such as infrastructure, sanitation, finance, sports, tourism, youth development and community affairs.

They could attend council meetings, participate in projects and consultations, and learn about the day-to-day responsibilities involved in running a municipality. This would provide valuable preparation for those who may one day seek elected office or other leadership positions.

Belize City has shown what is possible.

Now, other town councils should embrace the initiative and make youth participation in local government a broader national effort.

Preparing future mayors, councillors and community leaders should begin long before election day.

World.title: Crisis in the classrooms
World.content:
The 2026 Global School-Based Student Health Survey has painted an alarming picture of the state of Jamaican children surveyed with the data showing “an increase in suicidal ideation and attempts” by students in grades nine to 11 with girls outstripping boys in both thinking about the act and attempting it.

According to researchers, in comparing the 2010, 2017 and 2026 survey results, “mental health indicators have worsened over time with more students reporting suicidal thoughts, suicidal planning, suicide attempts, anxiety and depression”.

With a sample size of 3,058 students between grades 7 and 12 the survey administered questionnaires where the children were quizzed on their behaviours over the past seven days, the past 30 days, and the past 12 months.

The study, which was officially released on Wednesday morning by Health Minister Dr Christopher Tufton in collaboration with representatives of the National Council and Drug Abuse, found that suicidal thoughts were highest among grade 11 students with 36.6 per cent of girls saying they had thought about killing themselves as against 23.1 per cent of boys.

Chillingly it said, 32.4 per cent of grade nine girls, 21.8 per cent of grade eight boys, and 21.5 per cent of grade eight boys reported that they attempted to end their lives since this year.

In the meantime anxiety was highest among grade 10 girls with 46.2 per cent experiencing this, and 16.8 per cent of their grade 11 male peers.

Girls again led the way in reporting depression, with the highest numbers being among grade 11 students where 47.8 per cent of girls and 23.8 per cent of boys said they experienced this.

According to the experts, “If current trends persist, several critical challenges threaten adolescent well-being” across three primary areas.

“First, rising adolescent mental health crises involve escalating rates of emotional distress, feelings of hopelessness and self-harm risk indicating that early action matters,” the experts said.

Secondly they said, “Untreated distress negatively affects school engagement, interpersonal relationships, and substance use risks, demonstrating that untreated problems today lead to greater harm tomorrow”.

“Third, stigma and limited services delay professional help-seeking due to barriers like social judgement, restricted access and long wait times emphasising that early support saves lives” the experts said.

According to researchers, to address the issues several questions must be raised including about the extent to which school-based mental health initiatives address early screening and timely referrals, the clarity of suicide prevention pathways between home, school and community and the impact and scope of the expansion of access to adolescent mental health services.

In the meantime an assessment of social media use and screen time found that “most students have a mobile phone and use it for online activities”. According to the data 87.4 per cent of students surveyed have a mobile phone, 77.5 per cent use their devices for social media/online communication or Internet browsing, while 67. 2 per cent spend three-plus hours of screen time on an average school day. Interestingly, only 39 per cent said their parents or guardians have rules about social media use.

The researchers, in noting that the “high levels of screen time highlight the importance of digital balance and supportive rules” said this was so as “excessive screen time can impact physical, social and mental health”.

In addition they warned that excessive social media use can affect relationships and in-person interactions, and also “increases exposure to risky content and online pressures”.

“If current trends persist, several digital-related challenges emerge across multiple areas. First, there is reduced sleep, activity and family engagement as screen time displaces healthy habits,” the canvasser said, while noting that individuals experience greater exposure to online harms and social pressures, including negative comments, fake news and unrealistic comparisons.

“Thirdly, widening gaps in parental digital supervision appear between technologically confident families who maintain open conversations, privacy settings and screen time limits and parents lacking knowledge or time who are unfamiliar with risks, unclear about settings or have little time to monitor,” the experts declared.

They said to guide future efforts the extent to which health digital habits are promoted in schools must be determined.

In addition the experts said the parenting initiatives in existence for social media provision and monitoring must be known as well as the way in which cyberbullying, online exploitation and harmful content are built into adolescent mental health services.

The GSHS is an international gold-standard survey developed by World Health Organization, in collaboration with United Nations Children’s Fund; United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization; United States Agency for International Development; and the United States-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

It measures self-reported health behaviours and protective factors among youth 13-17 years old in the area of alcohol, tobacco and drug use, dietary behaviour, physical activity, sexual behaviours, violence and unintentional injury and protective factors.

It also establishes trends, and facilitates international comparison, develops priorities, establishes programmes, facilitates resource advocacy for school and youth health programmes/policies.

World.title: ‘Wake The Town And Tell The People’: U Roy celebration set for Sep 19
World.content:
U-Roy

Five years after pioneer deejay U Roy’s death, his family has taken steps to ensure the songs that made him famous are in the right hands. His daughter, Dionne Beckford, made this clear in a recent interview with the Jamaica Observer.

U Roy (given name Ewart Beckford) died in February 2021 at age 78, leaving a solid catalogue of songs and albums that are still in demand, especially in Europe where he had a lasting following.

“As far as his catalogue being secure and his music being properly distributed, we’re working with a team of lawyers to get things in place. He had 13 to 15 children, and there are about nine to 10 who are alive, and we should keep his legacy going,” said Beckford.

A dance dubbed ‘Wake The Town And Tell The People’ is one of the ways to salute U Roy’s role as an artiste, sound system kingpin and mentor. It takes place on September 19 at Cling Cling Oval in Olympic Gardens, Kingston, and features his Stur Gav sound system.

Some of the artistes who helped make Stur Gav dominant during the 1980s will perform. They include Josey Wales, Little John, Little Twitch and Lone Ranger.

At the peak of its popularity in the 1980s, Stur Gav fielded the biggest names in dancehall music. Among them were Sugar Minott, Charlie Chaplin, Super Cat, Tenor Saw, Tiger and Early B.

Wake The Town And Tell The People is U Roy’s signature phrase. It is also the title of his most famous song, released in 1970 by producer Duke Reid’s Treasure Isle label.

It marked the toaster’s transition from sound system selector to recording artiste. Wake The Town And Tell The People hears him deejaying to Girl I’ve Got Date, a hit for Reid and singer Ellis four years earlier.

U Roy had similar success toasting The Wailers’ Soul Rebel (as Natty Rebel) and The Paragons’ Wear You To The Ball.

Dionne Beckford, who lives in New York City, says she has been aware of his musical influence since childhood.

“I travelled with him on tours, so I got a bird’s-eye view of what’s going on the international scene with dad. That proved to me that our father was a legend.”

World.title: Leon Bailey to move to Olympiacos — reports
World.content:
In this file photo Reggae Boyz winger Leon Bailey attempts a cross in his AS Roma debut against Inter Milan in the Serie A on Saturday October 18, 2025 at the Stadio Olimpico. .

Reggae Boy Leon Bailey is expected to leave Aston Villa for Greek Club Olympiacos, according to international reports.

The move from the English Premier League club is said to be permanent, with a contract until June 2029. It follows Bailey’s loans from Villa to various clubs, including Roma.

Bailey had several rough, injury-plagued seasons with Villa and did not feature at all for the club this season.

An £8 million Hull City move had been in the works but fell through before the close of the EPL transfer window. Several other clubs had shown interest in the 29-year-old, including Saudi-based Al Ittihad and Diriyah Club.

With over 100 titles across national, regional and youth competitions, Olympiacos is the most successful Greek Club on record and consistently dominates its league.

The club’s home ground is the 33,000-capacity Karaiskakis Stadium, in Piraeus near Athens.

Reports are that Bailey is travelling to Athens for medical testing.

World.title: Harbour View FC salutes academic stars’ exceptional CSEC results
World.content:
Harbour View FC's 2026 Academic stars from left Dominic Thompson, Jelani Harvey Jaden Smith Tristan Riley and Emmanuel Donalds

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Harbour View Football Club is celebrating an academic feat after five of its young players excelled in the classroom, with General Manager Clyde Jureidini challenging them to become role models for the next generation of footballers.

Dominic Thompson, Jaden Smith, Jelani Harvey, Tristan Riley and Emmanuel Donalds were singled out by Jureidini for their outstanding academic achievements, which he said demonstrated that success in football and education can go hand in hand.

Thompson of St George’s College achieved 10 CSEC subjects with nine distinctions; Smith of Wolmer’s Boys has nine subjects with seven distinctions; Campion College’s Harvey has nine subjects and six distinctions; Donalds of Jamaica College has eight subjects and six distinctions; and Riley of St George’s College has nine subjects and five distinctions.

Jureidini heaped praise on the youngsters for their “focus, hard work, diligence and discipline”, while making it clear that their accomplishments were largely the result of the support provided by their parents, teachers and school communities.

“We really want to credit them for their focus, for their hard work, for their diligence, for their discipline and even more so for their achievement,” Jureidini said.

“We know they didn’t do it without the strong guidance, assistance and support of their peer group at school, of course their parents and at home. The club did a little bit but could not in any way take credit for what they and, by extension, their parents and their teachers have put in.”

Jureidini believes the achievement could be a significant moment for the Harbour View programme, noting that it is a rare feat.

“We think it’s one of the few times, if not the first, that so many Harbour View youngsters have excelled at the same time,” he said.

The achievement is also a reflection of Harbour View’s long-term youth development programme, with most of the five players progressing through the club’s ranks from the Under-11 level.

“Many have done it over the years, and these have done it because the majority of them have been in Harbour View from Under-11 through Under-13, Under-15, Under-17, Under-18,” Jureidini said.

Harvey’s progression has been particularly notable. After advancing through the Harbour View youth system, he moved into the Under-20 programme and senior Premier League squad before earning an overseas scholarship.

Jureidini wants the five high achievers to set an even higher bar for those following behind them.

“Set the highest standard for yourselves, for your teammates, for the football fraternity and the many youngsters from our Under-11, Under-13, Under-15 and Under-17 who are behind them,” he said.

For Jureidini, the message is bigger than football.

He believes combining academic excellence with sporting ambition gives young athletes a stronger foundation for life beyond the pitch.

“Go after the academic excellence as well as the football dominance because it’s a good mix that gives you a good opportunity in life, not just in the game of football or in sports,” he said.

And with five Harbour View youngsters leading the way, Jureidini is hoping their success will become contagious.

“So big up and congratulations, and we hope many more will exceed, follow their example and achieve greater heights,” he said.

— Howard Walker

World.title: $500m more for drought fight
World.content:
Minister of Water, Environment and Climate Change Matthew Samuda looks on at pipe-laying works being carried out by the National Water Commission on Old Hope Road in St Andrew on Tuesday. (Photo: Joseph Wellington)

AHEAD of next week’s reopening of schools, an additional $500 million has been allocated to ease Jamaicans’ torment caused by drought and severe heat brought on by Super El Niño weather conditions. Cabinet approved the measure Monday and Minister of Water, Environment and Climate Change Matthew Samuda provided an update to the media yesterday.

“We’ll see $150 million being sent to the National Water Commission (NWC) for them to dedicate trucks to schools, [for] back-to-school; to health centres and hospitals; and indeed to critical infrastructure, including police stations, with a priority on those that are places of detention. From the approved $500 million we will see $200 million being channelled through the offices of the Members of Parliament to provide support in their constituencies, and it will see $150 million of support going to all municipalities to ensure that they’re able to respond in areas where the utility footprint is not,” Samuda announced.

He was speaking during a tour of a multi-billion-dollar pipe-laying and rehabilitation project on Old Hope Road in St Andrew.

The minister stressed that if weather conditions improve, the funds will not be spent. However, he acknowledged that meteorological forecasts indicate that the situation is not likely to improve any time soon.

Brutal heat, reduced rainfall, and drought are some of the conditions that accompany what is on track to be the strongest El Niño on record. The weather pattern has been unleashing extreme weather across the globe, and Jamaicans have been reeling from the impact.

“Because the forecast has said we’re unlikely to see a major change in our current rainfall levels until early next year, we’ve made this provision to ensure that we’re able to respond to those most in need, and to critical infrastructure needs and, of course, support back-to-school as best as possible,” Samuda shared.

He said it is clear the drought is having a terrible impact on social stability and economic activity as well as the general comfort of citizens, and sought to assure that the Government is doing everything within its power to shore up its emergency response to the situation.

Samuda said he is aware that nothing makes people feel better than when they have water running through their pipes at home.

“The Government is spending over $15 billion this year alone on infrastructure work to upgrade the pipes. For those who find themselves in dire straits, we’re clear that we have to provide a particular level of support in a number of ways. It’s important to note that the Government already, since the start of this drought, has expended $86 million in trucking of water to those critically affected and to critical infrastructure,” the minister said.

Turning his attention to adherence to water restrictions imposed by Government, Samuda said generally there is a great consciousness within the society that the country is experiencing a weather crisis, and there is support for the push to get citizens to conserve.

“We are seeing that [conservation] in stabilisation and reduced rate of decline at major storage facilities. We always have errant ones, but generally we are getting compliance. We deal with weather crises annually, sometimes rainy seasons and sometimes dry spells. I think the consciousness related to this particular drought is there,” he added.

World.title: Learning the game
World.content:
Casino Gaming Commission Director of Human Resources Shainee Myles speaking at this week’s Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange. (Photo: Joseph Wellington)

THE Casino Gaming Commission (CGC) says it has been preparing its regulators to face a new challenge, not only learning how casinos operate, but knowing enough about roulette, blackjack, and other games to spot when something is going wrong.

With much of the specialised expertise not readily available locally, the commission has partnered with overseas bodies and international regulators to train its staff and expose them to established casino operations.

Director of human resource and administration at the CGC, Shainee Myles said the training push was driven by the need to establish the level of expertise required to regulate the new sector to international standards.

“One of the first things that we needed to do was to establish what the requirement is for that First World standard, and we had to work closely with the operational team to also understand what the training gaps are and the type of people that we need,” Myles said at this week’s Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange.

She said the commission recognised early that simply transferring knowledge from Jamaica’s existing gaming environment would not be enough, given the specialised nature of casino regulation.

“A lot of the expertise does not reside locally in Jamaica so we had to create these persons. We partnered with overseas bodies and also looked keenly on what other international regulators are doing so that they can effectively manage the sector, and we identified several training opportunities that are needed. Our persons had to be very keen on upskilling as well so they can bring in that information and be fully prepared for the regulatory rules that they will fill,” she explained.

The preparation comes as Jamaica moves towards the launch of its first licensed casino under the Casino Gaming Act, 2010.

The CGC granted Jamaica’s first casino operator’s licence to Adamas Grand Casino Limited on July 29. The casino is proposed for Princess Grand Jamaica Resort in Green Island, Hanover, where it will operate under a management agreement with Spanish gaming and hospitality entity Grupo Orenes.

Myles said the commission has already completed training in table games and slot machines, while investigations training is ongoing and further practical exposure is planned.

That practical component is particularly important because casino regulation requires officials to understand the mechanics of the games they will be responsible for overseeing.

Asked specifically about table-game training, Myles said regulators must be able to distinguish ordinary play from manipulation or cheating.

“They need to understand how a roulette is played, how a blackjack is played, and also identifying when cheating is happening. You’ll have people coming in who know what they’re doing so we cannot sit and say we don’t know as yet — we have to know as well. So, we need to know how to play those games and to detect when cheating is taking place,” she explained.

According to Myles, the commission has also launched an online academy offering staff and partner agencies access to specialised regulatory courses, with areas including surveillance, risk management and anti-money laundering.

She noted that the aim is to ensure that knowledge does not become concentrated in a handful of employees who could leave the organisation and take that expertise with them.

“The Casino Gaming Commission is ready to regulate that difficult sector. It’s [going to be done] through continuous development as well of our people and upskilling them, and also continuous learning and institutionalising that knowledge, because it cannot reside in a single individual,” she expressed.

She said the academy currently offers 29 courses and is also designed to strengthen the capabilities of agencies that will work alongside the CGC.

“We also have to train our partner agencies. You have Customs, you have BGLC [Betting, Gaming and Lotteries Commission], MOCA [Major Organised Crime and Anti-Corruption Agency] — all those other areas that will be a part of the process. If there’s an investigation, if there are machines coming in, they need to know what to look for and how they can be a part of what is happening,” she explained.

The emphasis on training is part of a broader effort by the CGC to establish a regulatory system for a sector that is new to Jamaica in its full casino form.

Th country has long had gaming lounges regulated by the BGLC but those establishments are not casinos in the legal sense. Gaming lounges generally offer gaming machines while a CGC-licensed casino can offer full casino gaming including live table games such as blackjack, roulette, baccarat, craps and poker, as well as gaming machines.

Casino gaming is also restricted to approved integrated resort developments (IRDs), rather than standalone premises. The model ties casino gaming to larger tourism developments anchored by hotels and other amenities.

The CGC’s regulatory framework was completed with the Casino Gaming (General) Regulations, 2025, which set out detailed requirements covering licensing, management qualifications, record keeping, inspection, enforcement, and responsible gaming. The House of Representatives approved the regulations in February 2026 and the Senate affirmed them on April 17, completing the legal framework for licensing.

World.title: The Building Returns: Kartel leads dancehall back to the club
World.content:
The National Arena was jam-packed for The Return of the Building on Saturday night.(Photo: Ashb Media)

HUNDREDS poured into the National Arena on Saturday for the highly anticipated Return of The Building. Promising patrons a trip down memory lane, organisers transported eager partygoers back to an era when Kingston’s nightlife was ruled by its hottest clubs.

Headlined by Vybz Kartel, the event leaned heavily into the unpredictability and movement that once defined places such as The Building, Fiction and Quad. Instead of unfolding as a traditional concert, with one performance neatly following another, the evening was a mix of music, artistes, selectors, dancers and familiar faces, all operating inside a space transformed by disco lighting, liquor and a heavy dose of nostalgia.

Ahead of the event, organisers outlined that today’s party scene is increasingly being driven by patrons following brands, promoters, and concepts from venue to venue. They argued that Jamaica’s entertainment landscape has shifted away from the era when the nightclub itself was the destination. Still, Saturday’s event proved that though much has changed, Jamaica’s love for music remains unshakeable, and with that love comes unwavering support for an active nightlife, no matter the venue.

For much of the night, music remained at the centre of the experience. Selectors moved patrons through a slew of dancehall hits, including a host of tracks from Kartel’s early days.

“When Building did deh bout, a lot of unnu inna fifth grade, sixth grade and seventh grade. You were in school when Gully/Gaza war did active,” DJ Escobar said as he riled up the crowd during his brief juggling session.

“All who know say a Gully/Gaza make you know fi defend yuhself a school, buss a blank,” he continued, with the crowd willingly following his instructions.

ZJ Chrome, Ricky Platinum and a host of others also enjoyed brief juggling stints as they got the crowd ready for the man of the moment.

Before long, Vybz Kartel had full command of the National Arena.

“Long time me nuh deejay fi me people dem from dem levels yah,” he said.

Perched atop a raised platform overlooking the jam-packed crowd, Kartel served up songs such as Touch A Button, Send A Hell, Dumpa Truck, One Man, Was Dat Jah and others, catering to both his female fanbase and his ‘thugs’.

Leaning into the kind of unpredictability that once governed the club scene, Kartel treated patrons to several guest appearances throughout the night. Shawn Storm, Harry Toddler, Future Fambo, Jamal, Ishawna, Pamputtae and Laden were among those who joined the festivities, serving up energetic performances of their own.

Of course, it would hardly be a Vybz Kartel showcase without a moment that underscored his own legacy. Encouraging the men in attendance to commit to their responsibilities as fathers, the entertainer handed over the microphone to his son, Likkle Vybz.

“Mi father never rich, but him was a good father. Always remember, ghetto youths: From you man enough to get a girl pregnant, be man enough fi take care a di yute. Memba yuh babymadda know seh you is a trying yute so just be there for her and the child…in a few years, you might get a son like mine,” he said before turning things over to his son.

“The entire experience was phenomenal. We saw how patrons were in complete awe that the arena could indeed be transformed into a club for one night. They enjoyed themselves as Kartel interacted with them in such a genuine way, which was what The Building experience was,” said Kennika Johnson, one of the organisers of The Return of The Building.

“I’m happy he was able to bring that energy back to the people and just revive the club culture for one night. It was exactly what we wanted it to be.”

Whether Jamaica’s nightclub culture is poised for a full-scale comeback remains to be seen but for the hundreds who packed the National Arena on Saturday, that question could wait.

For a few hours the selectors juggled, the dancehall faithful answered every call, familiar faces appeared without warning, and Kartel once again held court over a crowd gathered to experience the music up close.

The Building may no longer stand at its old New Kingston address but on Saturday night its energy found a new home.

World.title: China trade surge
World.content:
CHINA is closing in on a milestone in its trade with Jamaica.

After selling a record US$878.6 million worth of goods to the island last year, the Asian manufacturing giant is now within striking distance of becoming a US$1-billion-a-year supplier to Jamaica. And it has got there quickly.

In 2021, Jamaica imported US$463.8 million worth of goods from China, according to official data compass, the Statistical Institute of Jamaica (Statin). Four years later, that bill had climbed by almost US$415 million, with China’s share of the island’s imports moving from 7.8 per cent to 11.7 per cent.

The increase last year alone was steep. Imports from China jumped by US$181.8 million, or just over 26 per cent, from US$696.8 million in 2024.

But look beyond the clothes, shoes, furniture, and other finished goods for which China is well-known and a large part of the business is in machinery, equipment, industrial supplies, and building materials.

Detailed trade tables supplied to the Jamaica Observer by Statin show imports of machinery and transport equipment from China rising from US$321.3 million in 2024 to US$416.2 million last year, accounting for almost half of everything Jamaica bought from the Asian country.

Manufactured goods classified mainly by material, a category that includes industrial supplies and building materials, climbed even faster, from US$196 million to US$271.3 million. Together those two categories accounted for more than three-quarters of Jamaica’s imports from China last year.

Chemicals and related products increased from US$39.8 million to US$44.2 million, while miscellaneous manufactured articles moved from US$125.9 million to US$132.8 million.

Statin said some of the leading individual products imported from China over the five-year period included new pneumatic rubber tyres for motor cars, parts for air-conditioning machines, and lithium-ion and other electric accumulators. Its broader machinery and transport category also covers vehicles, industrial machinery, telecommunications equipment, and other technical components.

The data have renewed a much older debate about what Jamaica should be importing and what it should be trying to make, assemble or otherwise add value to itself.

Businessman and manufacturer Metry Seaga does not believe the answer is to attempt to replace imports wholesale.

“Truth is, we’re an island and we don’t have a great supply chain here in the island. So because of that, we are going to import product. There’s no doubt about that. And we have to import various things,” Seaga, a former Jamaica Manufacturers and Exporters Association president said in a recent interview with the Business Observer.

“However, what we need to do is, we need to start realising that our policies need to have the ability to force people to buy with a local component,” he continued.

He wants Government to start with industries that already benefit from tax concessions, arguing that the support should come with a greater effort to keep some of the spending and production in Jamaica.

“If you’re giving an industry — the hotel industry, the BPO industry — if you are giving them benefits, tax benefits, then what you need to ask Government to say to them is, ‘listen, you need to have some value-added production for the import of your products’,” Seaga said.

“If you buy furniture, if there’s no capacity here, which there is, then buy from a local furniture manufacturer or one that’s in and does semi-production here. We need to add more value to the industries that are getting benefits from the Government,” he argued.

Seaga has long pushed local production, but his thinking on what that should look like has changed over the years. Full-scale manufacturing of a finished product is not always necessary, he reasoned. Jamaica could import inputs and undertake part of the production process here, particularly where the finished goods can then be sold into much larger markets.

“The opportunities are endless, and I’ll tell you why; because Jamaica is located in the best place in the Caribbean, in the Americas actually. Where Jamaica is located in the Americas is like where Singapore is located in Asia,” added Seaga, who also sits as chairman of JFP Limited, a manufacturer of custom-built commercial contract furniture.

“We have the ability to use our location as an asset… and we have to develop our economy as a logistics-centred economy where people can come in, add value to products here, and then distribute them throughout the Americas. We have never taken advantage of that,” he added.

China was not always so far ahead of Jamaica’s other suppliers.

In 2021 Jamaica imported US$463.8 million worth of goods from China, according to official data compass, the Statistical Institute of Jamaica (Statin). Four years later, that bill had climbed by almost US$415 million, with China’s share of the island’s imports moving from 7.8 per cent to 11.7 per cent.

Statin’s tables show that in 2021 Brazil sold US$514.3 million worth of goods to Jamaica, more than China’s US$463.8 million. China moved ahead the following year and has continued to pull away.

By 2025 it was Jamaica’s second-largest source of imports, behind only the United States. US goods entering Jamaica were valued at US$2.83 billion last year, compared with China’s US$878.6 million, Brazil’s US$396.8 million, Japan’s US$299.7 million and Trinidad and Tobago’s US$279.1 million.

Responding to queries from the Business Observer about China’s growing share of Jamaica’s import market, the Planning Institute of Jamaica (PIOJ) said the pace of the increase mirrors a wider global trend, particularly in Chinese exports of manufactured goods and capital equipment.

PIOJ also pointed to evidence in Statin data that China’s share of machinery and electrical goods has been increasing while the US share has declined.

“Statin trade data show declining US share in machinery and electrical goods, while China’s share has risen,” the PIOJ said.

It listed lower costs and China’s economies of scale, financing linked to Chinese investment projects and the country’s place in global supply chains for intermediate goods among the factors behind the change.

Importantly, PIOJ noted that products featured heavily among China’s imports line up with demand from construction, tourism, renewable energy, and infrastructure projects locally. While electronics and appliances bought by households remain part of the trade, the institute said “investment-driven demand is the primary driver of the import surge.”

PIOJ, however, sees some risk in Jamaica becoming increasingly reliant on a handful of countries for important imports.

“China’s growing role in Jamaica’s trade is both an opportunity and a risk. It supports investment and growth but raises concerns about over-reliance and trade imbalance,” PIOJ said, adding that stronger domestic production, export development, and greater diversification would be important to improving Jamaica’s economic resilience.

It calculated Jamaica’s import concentration index at 0.303 in 2025 and pointed out that China was already supplying 19.9 per cent of the country’s capital imports in 2023, compared with 42.3 per cent from the United States.

“Supply shocks, such as shipping disruptions, geopolitical tensions [and] tariff changes, could significantly affect transport, construction and energy sectors, where Chinese inputs dominate,” PIOJ said.

For Jamaica to capture more of that spending locally, however, Seaga believes some longstanding problems have to be addressed.

He named poor productivity, bureaucracy, and labour arrangements among his biggest concerns, putting electricity costs lower down the list than is often heard in discussions about manufacturing.

“Our lack of productivity is a huge one. Bureaucracy is a huge one. The cost of electricity to me is less important,” he said. “People can do solar, there are opportunities to deal with electricity in many industries, not all. There are some that are very electricity intensive, and we can’t do those here.”

Seaga also wants it made easier for overseas workers with specialised skills to work alongside Jamaicans and pass on technical knowledge, while arguing that delays within the public sector continue to frustrate businesses trying to invest and expand.

“Productivity is key. Our labour laws are key. Relaxing the importation of labour is key; and bureaucracy, I don’t want to diminish that in any way. Bureaucracy in the Government, it is too difficult to get anything done,” he said.

“To move a document from one civil servant desk to another, the same office can take months. It is not right.”

The special economic zone programme, in his view, should be doing more to marry overseas investment with businesses already operating locally.

Seaga, who previously chaired the Jamaica Special Economic Zone Authority (JSEZA), said the structure built for the SEZ regime is sound, but its development has been too slow.

“We do have a very good system with a good structure around it that international companies can live by and live in and operate in. Now, we need to move faster,” he said.

SEAGA… we have the ability to use our location as an asset… and we have to develop our economy as a logistics-centred economy where people can come in, add value to products here, and then distribute them throughout the Americas

That includes deliberately seeking investors whose operations could create more business for companies already producing in Jamaica.

“We need SEZ to be a vibrant organisation that’s looking to bring companies here to twin with manufacturers here and to bring industries that are relevant to the manufacturers here,” Seaga said.

“So if you have a box manufacturer here, you want to bring people who will use the box manufacturer here and increase their business tenfold. So those are the types of businesses you need to look for. Look for what is in your ecosystem now that’s efficient and effective, and then bring companies that come to Jamaica,” he argued.

While Jamaica’s purchases from China have been racing towards US$1 billion, the flow in the opposite direction remains small.

Exports to China were valued at US$25.9 million in 2025, up sharply from US$5.2 million a year earlier but still equal to only 1.6 per cent of Jamaica’s total exports. Jamaica bought almost US$34 worth of Chinese goods for every US$1 of goods it sold to China last year.

The detailed Statin tables show US$16 million of those exports falling under crude materials, inedible, except fuels; another US$5.9 million under mineral fuels, lubricants, and related materials; and US$3.9 million under food and live animals.

Statin describes the crude-materials category as raw, unprocessed commodities used as manufacturing inputs, while its food category covers products for human and animal consumption. The mineral-fuels category covers organic energy sources and petroleum-based products.

PIOJ sees room for Jamaica to tackle the imbalance from several directions, including more agro-processing and light manufacturing at home and some production of renewable-energy components. It also pointed to opportunities to grow sales to China.

“Target niche areas such as rum, coffee, seafood, cultural products, and services [tourism, education]. The World Trade Organisation data show China’s applied Most-Favoured-Nation tariff average is 7.5 per cent, but for many agricultural and cultural goods there is duty-free access,” the institution told the Business Observer.

Seaga, though, does not believe Jamaican manufacturers need to look halfway around the world first.

When asked how Jamaica could sell more to China, he quickly turned the conversation towards the United States.

“We don’t need to go so far as China. As I said, our location in the Americas allows us access to the richest market in the whole world, which is the United States of America,” he said.

“If most companies in Jamaica — which every company is a small company, even the greatest that Wisynco that we think of is a small company — if they get into one city in America with their products, it changes the shape of their business.”

“Whilst we want to sell to everywhere in the world — China, Africa, Europe, Asia, the rest of Asia — we don’t want to concentrate on far away yet. Let’s concentrate on who is beside us, America,” Seaga argued.

His idea of production is broad enough to include some of the relatively simple work that takes place between importing a product and selling it.

“Bring rice, package it here, label it here, use the packaging and the labelling from here. Use the labour that’s here to store it, to do the value-added,” Seaga said.

“Our economy is too small; and we need to grow that outside of Jamaica.

“It may not be that we’re manufacturing — complete manufacturing — but you may be doing semi-manufacturing or screwdriver industry or some form of value add.

“I don’t care what it is, just add some value here,” Seaga said.

The Business Observer also asked JSEZA about efforts to attract more manufacturing and assembly operations, including Chinese investment, and whether the SEZ framework is already helping Jamaica capture more value from imports through local production. See the companion story in this edition for JSEZA’s response

(Pages 10 & 11).

World.title: Poland calls for stricter controls on EU visas for Russians
World.content:
Sikorski called for restricting Russian diplomats’ freedom of movement to the countries where they are accredited, limiting the issuance of Schengen visas to Russian citizens, requiring biometric passes for Russians entering the EU, and capping the number of Russian diplomats stationed within the bloc.

“We still have far too many Russian diplomats throughout the European Union. We estimate there are over 2,000, and we estimate that at least 40 percent of them are performing tasks that are inconsistent with their diplomatic status. They work for agencies that also carry out terrorist activities in our countries,” he said. “Therefore, in solidarity with Germany, we should implement all the necessary safeguards for our population.”

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said Paris was ready to support further steps “if circumstances require it.”

Europe, and Germany specifically, have recently been confronted with a series of hybrid attacks. Only this week, there have been two attacks on power facilities in different parts of the country and one on a defense company — all of which are currently being investigated and have not been attributed by authorities.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul did not respond to a question on whether Russia was behind the arson attack on the defense company in Munich.

“I can’t say much about this publicly. After all, the security of Germany and the security of our allies take priority,” he said. “But we are always in a position to investigate these matters. The incident in Leipzig demonstrated this, and we are also always in a position to provide a response. This will continue to be the case in the future.”

World.title: Teresa Ribera schlägt eine Ölsteuer und gemeinsame Schulden vor, um Europa klimaresistent zu machen
World.content:
Ribera hielt sich mit konkreten Vorschlägen zurück, fügte jedoch hinzu: „Es ist an der Zeit, die Debatte darüber zu eröffnen, wie wir die Herausforderungen bewältigen können. Eine klare Antwort ist noch nicht in Sicht. Ob wir mehr finanzpolitischen Spielraum oder einen größeren gemeinsamen Haushalt benötigen, den weiteren Einsatz grüner Eurobonds und/oder die Wiederbelebung des Vorschlags von [UN-Generalsekretär António] Guterres, große Ölkonzerne zu besteuern, um einen Resilienzfonds zu speisen.“

Die Vorschläge werden wahrscheinlich auf gemischte Reaktionen stoßen. Höhere Ausgaben und eine höhere Verschuldung sind für die sparsameren Länder der Union, wie beispielsweise Deutschland, ein Gräuel ; Deutschland plädiert bereits für einen EU-Haushalt, der unter dem von der Kommission vorgeschlagenen liegt.

Gleichzeitig drängen Deutschland, Portugal, Italien, Polen, Österreich und Riberas Heimatland Spanien angesichts des jüngsten Energiepreisschocks auf eine Sondersteuer für Ölkonzerne. Seit Beginn des Krieges im Iran haben Unternehmen der fossilen Brennstoffbranche Milliarden an Mehrgewinnen eingestrichen. Auch Guterres hat wiederholt ähnliche Vorschläge unterbreitet.

Ribera verwies auf die Auswirkungen des extremen Wetters in diesem Sommer als Warnsignal dafür, dass der Kontinent dringend in Maßnahmen investieren muss, um besser mit dem Klimawandel umgehen zu können, und schloss sich damit den Worten des Klimabeauftragten der Kommission, Wopke Hoekstra, an. Die EU-Kommission schätzt, dass die Union jährlich 70 Milliarden Euro benötigt, um sich auf die Gefahren einer wärmeren Welt vorzubereiten.

„Der Klimawandel wirkt sich auf die Wirtschaft und das Wohlbefinden der Menschen aus“, sagte sie und wies darauf hin, dass „das BIP Frankreichs aufgrund der Hitze stagniert; die Notdienste in den Krankenhäusern sind mit der Nachfrage überfordert … Staudämme müssen gesprengt werden, um Kernkraftwerke zu kühlen, während Waldbrände und Ernteausfälle Leben und die Ernährungssicherheit bedrohen.“

Mit Blick auf die verheerenden Überschwemmungen in Nepal fügte sie hinzu: „Und weit entfernt sehen wir die erschreckenden Bilder von Gletschern, die zusammenbrechen und Hunderte Menschen das Leben kosten.“

World.title: Sánchez dismisses police claim that Morocco instigated Ceuta crisis
World.content:
“No one can deny that this government is not afraid to confront other foreign powers when the situation has required it,” the prime minister added, alluding to his frequent clashes with U.S. President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. “If solid evidence existed, we would act accordingly.”

Sánchez is facing mounting political pressure over the Ceuta crisis. Tens of thousands of people took to the streets across Spain on Wednesday to protest the government’s handling of the situation, and even members of Sánchez’s coalition government are challenging the prime minister’s narrative.

Ignoring jeers of protest from opposition lawmakers, Sánchez insisted that Spain must “continue cooperating with Morocco” and maintain “a good neighborly relationship” in order to deport the unauthorized migrants that remain in Ceuta and prevent future surges.

Prior to entering the parliament Thursday, Youth Minister Sira Rego, a member of the left-wing Sumar group, the junior partner in the government, said it was “hard to imagine that 80,000 people could have been moved to the border without Moroccan authorities knowing about it.”

She also questioned Sánchez’s long-term “policy of appeasement with Morocco,” adding the strategy had not been beneficial for Spain.

Sovereignty defense

While defending neighborly relations with Rabat, Sánchez took an unusual swipe at Morocco and for the first time publicly condemned the country’s “unacceptable” statements challenging Spain’s sovereignty over Ceuta and Melilla.

World.title: Green Leader Zack Polanski pitches for Keir Starmer’s old seat
World.content:
Starmer stood down from the House of Commons this week, saying he wanted to devote more attention to international affairs. He quit as prime minister earlier this year after losing support in his own party, and has been succeeded by Andy Burnham. No date has yet been set for the contest.

Polanski will still need to be selected by local Green Party members. That selection is expected to take place next week.

In a taste of his campaign pitch, Polanski said “voters will have someone who will always fight their corner — never scared of big donors or the party whip.”

And he charged: “Too often Labour has stood up for corporations and big money. I will stand up for people struggling to pay their bills.”

Polanski has overseen a boost to the Green Party membership and led his party to a strong performance at the local elections in May, but has faced scrutiny around the vetting of candidates and his social media posts. He has been a member of the London Assembly scrutinizing Mayor Sadiq Khan since 2021.

Starmer held the Holborn and St Pancras seat in 2024 with an 11,572 majority, but faced a strong challenge from a left-wing independent and the Greens.

World.title: German economy will grow more than expected, think tank says
World.content:
“The recovery of the German economy is continuing,” said Timo Wollmershäuser, ifo’s head of economic forecasts. He pointed to signs of improvement, particularly in the crisis-hit industrial sector.

The forecast is more optimistic than an assessment by Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel, who said in an interview published by Le Monde on Wednesday that Germany was on track to grow by around 1 percent this year — twice the Bundesbank’s June forecast of 0.5 percent.

Ifo also raised its 2027 growth forecast by 0.4 percentage points. The revisions reflect updated historical data from Germany’s Federal Statistical Office and a more positive assessment of the economy’s underlying momentum.

Inflation is expected to reach 2.8 percent this year and 3 percent next year before easing to 2.3 percent in 2028, bringing it closer to the European Central Bank’s target.

World.title: Can ‘ratty’ Farage get his mojo back?
World.content:
As Reform UK kicks off conference season in Birmingham, Nigel Farage appears to have some work to do.

The party has gone from dominating the political conversation to facing a fall in polling numbers, mounting scandals and fresh questions over Farage’s leadership.

Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy preview a crucial three days for Reform, with major announcements expected on migration and the economy – while a French connection could be significant.

Elsewhere, the Conservatives are ramping up the pressure on Andy Burnham over defence spending, unveiling their own plan on how they would cut welfare to fund more money for the military.

Plus, ahead of Sunday’s state elections in Germany, Anne reports from the campaign trail on the rise of the far-right AfD party and her dramatic encounter at a rally in Lutzen.

Sam and Anne will return on Sunday afternoon for a special de-brief episode to reflect on the Reform party conference.

World.title: Dublin tests Europe’s budget red lines
World.content:
At the informal General Affairs Council in Dublin today, the EU’s next 7-year budget is set to dominate the agenda.

The talks are still in deadlock over the size of the money pot … but the red lines of various capitals are starting to take shape. On today’s episode, host Zoya Sheftalovich and Ian Wishart explain why — counterintuitively — that’s actually a step forward for the negotiations.

Next, the pivotal regional election in Germany’s Saxony-Anhalt is just days away … and the far-right AfD party is poised to win big. But just how big? And what would the party do if it manages to come to power?

Finally, the EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, is considering a council of elders to help with the reform of the bloc’s foreign policy arm, the EEAS. Who do you think should be part of an expert group like this? Get in touch on WhatsApp here, or at +32 491 05 06 29.

World.title: Brussels to open door to curbing Airbnb and second homes in bid to ease housing burden
World.content:
The European Commission will propose new housing rules that would give national and local authorities clearer rules for restricting short-term holiday rentals and the purchase of homes or land that are not used as someone's main home, according to a document seen by Euronews.

 

The prospect of a tougher crackdown comes as prices have skyrocketed faster than local incomes across most European capitals, rising 64.9% between 2015 and 2025 and rents 21.8%, according to EU data.

Even people who cannot afford to buy are facing rising rents, which consume 40% of household income, and middle-class families are also increasingly facing a reality where they can't afford to buy or rent, but also aren't eligible for social housing.

Many residents in cities like Lisbon, Barcelona and Prague complain that short-term rental platforms like Airbnb have removed homes from the market and pushed prices up, often forcing them to move. EU data from 2024 reveals that nearly 10% of people living in EU cities spend more than 40% of their disposable income on housing.

Short-term rentals represent only 1.2% of the EU's total housing stock, but they can account for up to 20% in some tourism hotspots. With too few homes being built where demand is strongest, Brussels estimates it needs more than 2 million new homes every year to fix the problem.

However, the Commission's upcoming restrictions would be allowed only in areas with clear evidence of serious housing pressure.

For Airbnb-style rentals, the EU is particularly concerned about commercial operators running several properties as holiday lets, rather than people occasionally renting out their own home. Under the proposal, cities would be able to target professional multi-property operators, but a person's ability to rent out their main residence would be protected.

"In order to limit the negative impact on the internal market of any measure restricting access to, or the provision of, short-term accommodation rental services or restricting acquisition and use of land and residential property, such measures should be limited to areas where the acute pressure on the availability and affordability of residential property justifies action to safeguard affordability and availability of residential property," reads the document.

The rise of housing prices across the EU between 2014 and 2025. Eurostat and House Price Index.

However, the Commission acknowledges that short-term rental restrictions and limits on second homes can't solve Europe's structural housing shortage. Other challenges include high construction costs, expensive land, planning restrictions and lengthy permitting processes.

According to Housing Europe, the Brussels-based European Federation of Public, Cooperative and Social Housing, housing needs far exceed supply. Latest data show that France requires 518,000 homes annually (198,000 social), Germany 400,000 (140,000 social), the Netherlands nearly 1 million by 2031, and Sweden over 500,000 by 2033 – yet new provision consistently falls short of need, often by as much as 50%.

The Commission is working on a "Housing Simplification Package" aimed at cutting administrative barriers that slow down construction due in 2027.

Housing has also become an investment asset, making it increasingly difficult for younger people and middle-income households to buy.

EU lawmaker Leïla Chaibi (The Left/ France) told Housing Commissioner Dan Jørgensen on 2 September that financialisation and the widespread use of housing as an asset are among the main drivers of the lack of affordable housing in EU cities.

"It is time for the EU to act, and we know short-term rentals have an impact on the housing crisis, in our city centres, in our neighborhoods, as well as in the countryside everywhere in Europe now," Chaibi said.

The Commission is also considering encouraging national governments to step in when a particular area has house prices at least eight times higher than incomes, prices have risen over the previous decade, and the situation is not expected to improve within the next three years.

Housing is a national and local responsibility, leaving the Commission powerless to order member states or cities to build more of it. Instead, Brussels is trying to use EU funding, state-aid rules, investment and legislation to influence the market.

Commenting on a 2025 S&D study on short-term rentals, EU lawmaker Gaby Bischoff (S&D/Germany), vice-president for Sustainable Economy and Social Europe, warned that too many Europeans are facing evictions or are even at risk of homelessness. She attributed the crisis to growing socio-economic inequality and unsustainable housing systems that "prioritise profit over people".

An estimated 1.2 to 1.3 million people experience homelessness across the EU on any given night, driven heavily by the deepening housing crisis and rising living costs, according to the European Federation of National Associations on Homelessness (Feantsa).

The Commission is set to present its housing plan on 9 September.

World.title: Gloria Steinem, feminist icon, writer and pioneering journalist, dies aged 92
World.content:
Gloria Steinem, the celebrated author, feminist activist and one of the most famous voices of the US’ women’s movement, has died aged 92.

 

She died on Wednesday at her home in New York City, according to her and her foundation’s social media pages.

“Gloria’s near-century on earth were years well-lived, and she continued working for equality until the very end,” read the statement. “Gloria’s greatest gift was her ability to listen to others, to make others feel seen and heard. Her words, actions, and example gave people permission to be their truest selves. Gloria lived true to her independent spirit, always with curiosity and a great sense of humor.”

The statement continued: “She spent her recent years doing the two things she loved most: being in community with others and writing. She has welcomed hundreds of guests into her living room for Talking Circles, a tradition she insisted will continue long after she is no longer with us. As Gloria wrote in her forthcoming book, 𝘈𝘯 𝘜𝘯𝘦𝘹𝘱𝘦𝘤𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘓𝘪𝘧𝘦, “I have now lived for more than fifty years in this brownstone, in rooms that have witnessed lives before mine, and will know others after I am gone.” This book, along with her commitment to her home becoming a center for social justice movements, are among the many gifts Gloria has given the world with the hope they have ripple effects for generations to come. Gloria often quoted the adage: “The flap of a butterfly’s wing can change the weather hundreds of miles away.”"

It concluded: “In lieu of flowers, Gloria has asked that those wishing to honor her with a gift, may make a donation to Gloria’s Foundation.”

Our journalists are working on this developing story. Please check back for updates.

World.title: ‘Even I can’t mess this up’: Behind the lens in Iceland with the ‘really bad photographer'
World.content:
As the old adage goes, a picture is worth a thousand words. Light, shadows, depth of field and colour can all be used to capture a sense of place and tell a destination’s story. Icelandair, however, decided to turn that theory on its head.

 

And typically, when an airline launches a search for a new photographer, you’d expect a pristine portfolio to be part of the application. That was not the case with Blanche Mortemard, who had something rather different: a “camera roll of bad photos”, as described to Euronews Travel.

Out of 127,642 people who came forward to share their, well, lack of photographic talent in the hopes of being crowned the “world’s worst photographer”, it was Mortemard’s collection of snaps that stood out.

The carrier set out to prove that even someone with zero photography skills can take great photos of the Nordic island as part of its "Really Bad Photographer" campaign.

“This is part four of our 'Real Unreal' umbrella,” Gísli S. Brynólfsson, Icelandair's director of global marketing, told Euronews Travel, adding that since 2025, the carrier has been emphasising the country’s authenticity and realness as a destination of choice against the rise of AI-generated images and spread of misleading travel information.

“When it comes to representing Iceland in images, there simply is no need for AI.”

Real Unreal started when Icelandair shared photographs on its social media platforms of eruptions in the volcanic Reykjanes Peninsula as well as scenes from the Northern Lights.

“This sparked conversation about whether the photos were real or not, and we realised people had just stopped trusting images on the internet related to Iceland,” Brynólfsson said.

So, when it came to their latest campaign, the idea was simple: the real Iceland doesn’t need filters to impress, nor a skilled photographer either.

“We believe that Iceland is that real and that beautiful that even the worst photographer is able to take a beautiful photo in Iceland,” he added.

What made Mortemard’s portfolio stand out? Well, as you might imagine, choosing one bad photographer out of a mountain of applications was no easy task.

In Mortemard’s case, however, her “lack of talent isn’t something you can imitate”, Brynólfsson said.

A photo of Iceland's Berserkjahraun lava field by Blanche Mortemard, featuring her fingers in the frame Icelandair

Ten days in Iceland

Over the course of 10 days, Mortemard, a Paris native who until recently had never visited Iceland, took as many as 7,000 photos of the island.

“I knew what the country looked like, thanks to there being so many photos of Iceland online,” she told Euronews Travel.

“Before ever visiting, I had seen the landscapes, the glaciers, mountains and waterfalls, but I never would have believed there would be so many different landscapes all around me that I would see during such a short period of time.”

Her excursion began fresh off the plane, in Reykjanes, around 50 kilometres away from the capital, Reykjavik, as she launched her unconventional career as a bad photographer.

With her trusty camera in hand, she saw the peninsula’s lava fields, the geothermal water of the Blue Lagoon, met locals and even challenged a fellow tourist to a worst photographer battle to see who could snap a terrible picture.

After working up an appetite, she was treated to freshly baked rye bread, which reminded her of French “pain de campagne” – a rustic sourdough loaf.

The rest of her photography expedition took her to Icelandic attractions such as the picturesque Seljalandsfoss waterfall, Jökulsárlón glacier lagoon and the Hverfjall volcano.

Along the way, she also had a bingo card of challenges, which included taking an “iconic selfie”, witnessing a geyser erupt, taking a photo with a funny road sign, and seeing 20 waterfalls.

Exploring the country’s remarkable landscapes, however, didn’t shake her bad photographer crown, even an inch.

“There were lots of times where I would see the mountains and waterfalls and think, ‘even I can’t mess this up', but I’m still credible as a bad photographer,” she said.

Perusing through a sneak preview of her recent portfolio, this travel journalist did spot her finger occasionally making an appearance in the frame.

“As time went on, I did improve,” she said. “I started thinking more about what I wanted to capture and where my fingers are – in fact, most of my photos had my fingers in them,” she said, adding that there ought to be at least one award-winning snap in the bunch.

While a coveted photography award may not be in the bag just yet, what’s for certain is she is leaving the experience with her own personal favourite snaps.

“I feel the best photo of the trip was at Kerlingarfjöll,” she said, adding that the colours of the mountain range, plus her newly found composition skills, showed up so well on her camera.

“The second would be at Vestrahorn – here I think was a turning point for me,” she said.

“I managed to capture the atmosphere: the mountain had a crown of clouds and the sand was gliding across the ground. This was one of the first times I didn’t just press ‘click’, I decided the angle and what I wanted to share with everyone through my picture.”

Not only does she leave the experience with new-found photography skills, Mortemard said she’s now a different traveller, too.

After her road trip through Iceland, where she got to see and experience different things in one trip, she sees herself doing that in the future: “I’ll think more about road tripping, rather than just staying in one place for too long.”

If, like this travel journalist, you’re eager to see the final product of Mortemard’s unique style of photography and meet her in person, her photos will be gracing the walls of London’s White Rabbit Studios from 11-12 September. There are also future plans to showcase her talents across other cities in Europe and North America.
