World.title: Poland grants Ukraine permission to search for remains of Ukrainians massacred by Polish partisans
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has granted permission for Ukraine to conduct a search for the remains of Ukrainian civilians killed by Polish resistance fighters during World War Two. The decision marks the latest step towards reconciliation between the two countries over their difficult shared history. Following a diplomatic breakthrough last year, Kyiv has also granted Poland permission to search for and exhume the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists. On Tuesday, Ukrainian deputy culture minister Ivan Verbytskyi announced that the Polish authorities had granted a permit for a Ukrainian group to conduct exploratory work in the village of Łasków in southeastern Poland, around 10km from the border with Ukraine. The search aims to uncover the remains of Ukrainian civilians killed by the Peasant Battalions (Bataliony Chłopskie), a major underground resistance movement that emerged in Poland during the German occupation of World War Two. Łasków, which had a predominantly ethnic Ukrainian population, was attacked by a Peasant Battalion unit on 10 March 1944, with some estimates suggesting around 300 civilians were killed. Among those who died was a local Orthodox priest, Lev Korobchuk. On the same day, members of the Home Army (Armia Krajowa), Poland’s largest armed resistance movement, also attacked the nearby village of Sahryń. According to estimates, they killed hundreds more Ukrainians. Ukraine has also submitted an application to carry out exploratory work there. Dariusz Kopciowski, the conservator of monuments in the Lublin province where Łasków is located, confirmed to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that a permit for exploration work in Łasków had been granted. The issue had recently begun to cause tension, with Ukrainian media reporting last week that Ukraine has been waiting over a year for permission to carry out searches in Łasków. By contrast, Kyiv has granted permission for Poland to conduct such searches on its territory. Those Polish efforts are focused in particular on finding and exhuming the remains of victims of the so-called Volhynia massacres, in which Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Poles, mostly women and children, as part of an ethnic cleansing operation. Poland regards those massacres as a genocide. However, Ukraine strongly rejects that label and also points to the fact that Polish partisan units killed Ukrainian civilians during the war. Poland, in turn, argues that many such incidents were acts of reprisal for the massacres carried out by Ukrainians. Long-simmering tensions between Poland and Ukraine over WWII massacres have finally boiled over, prompting a diplomatic crisis.@danieltilles1 looks at how we got here and what it may mean for the two countries and Europe more broadly https://t.co/a8tiYJJHRr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 22, 2026 In 2017, Ukraine introduced a moratorium on search and exhumation work on its territory in response to the dismantling of a monument in Poland dedicated to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA). The UPA led the Volhynia massacres but is still celebrated by many in Ukraine for its role in fighting for independence from Moscow-backed Soviet rule. Last year, following negotiations with Poland, Ukraine lifted that moratorium and again began issuing permits for searches and exhumations of Polish victims on its territory, a number of which have already taken place. Last Sunday, Verbytskyi attended a funeral ceremony for 55 Polish massacre victims, around half of them children, whose remains were recently found and exhumed in a former Polish village located in what is now Ukraine. The remains of 55 Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII have been reburied at a ceremony in Ukraine attended by political and religious figures from both countries. The victims, around half of them children, were exhumed this summer https://t.co/4q3giZhBAL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 31, 2026 However, as well as those moves towards reconciliation, there have also been regular clashes between Warsaw and Kyiv over World War Two history, in particular following President Volodymyr Zelensky’s decision in May this year to name a military unit after the UPA. That triggered strong protests from Poland, whose president, Karol Nawrocki, stripped Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour, the Order of the White Eagle. Poland has also expressed concern over a new national pantheon being established by Ukraine. It has warned that, if figures associated with the massacre of Poles are included, that could have consequences for Ukraine’s ambitions to join the European Union. President Zelensky has signed a law establishing a national pantheon to commemorate Ukrainian heroes, prompting Poland to again warn that Ukraine "will have a huge problem" integrating into the EU if it honours figures associated with massacres of Poles https://t.co/fN7Zgbovvu — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 24, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poles eating more meat but drinking less alcohol
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poles are eating more meat but drinking less alcohol, continuing a long-term trend, the latest data from Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, show. The average person in Poland ate 82 kilograms of meat in 2025, which was 7.5% more than a year earlier. It also marks an increase of 15.7% since 2015 and 22.7% since 2005. Likewise, consumption of eggs rose 8.5% in 2025 to an average of 218 per person. The increases have come amid rapidly rising incomes, which make such products more affordable. A separate GUS study earlier this year showed that the proportion of Poles who cannot afford to eat meat at least every other day fell from 8.2% in 2015 to 3% in 2025. By contrast, vegetable consumption has changed little, with the average Pole eating 108 kg in 2025, compared with 107 kg a year earlier and 110 kg in 2005. However, consumption of potatoes, a starchy staple of the Polish diet presented by GUS separately from other vegetables, has fallen sharply over the longer term, despite a slight increase last year. The average Pole ate 96.5 kg of potatoes in 2025, down 23.4% since 2005. Meanwhile, alcohol consumption last year continued its recent decline. In 2025, the average Pole drank 81.7 litres of beer, down 4.9% from the previous year and 18.7% from the peak of 100.5 litres per person in 2018. Likewise, consumption of spirits and liqueurs fell 5.9% year-on-year in 2025 to 3.2 litres per person. That was 13.5% down from a peak of 3.7 litres in 2019. In 2025, the amount of wine drunk per person, at 4.9 litres, fell even more, by 9.3% year-on-year. However, alcohol consumption is still higher than it was two decades ago, with the average Pole drinking 28% more spirits and 1.2% more beer in 2025 than in 2005. A 2023 study by ProVeg, an NGO, conducted in partnership with the University of Copenhagen and Ghent University, found that Poles were the most carnivorous among ten European countries surveyed. Three quarters of Poles (74%) said they ate meat frequently, compared to an average of 62% across all countries. Italians and Spaniards (both 69%) were the next biggest meat eaters, while Germans (45%), Austrians (48%) and the Dutch (53%) were the least likely to eat meat frequently. Meanwhile, 7% of people in Poland said they were either vegan (2%), meaning consuming no animal products at all, or vegetarian (5%), meaning they do not eat meat or fish. That was just below the European average of 8%. In terms of what kinds of meat are favoured by Poles, GUS’s most recent such breakdown, from 2017, showed that pork was most popular, with the average Pole consuming 39.8 kg that year, followed by poultry (26.kg) and beef (2.3 kg). Poland's first company to produce cultured meat – which is grown in a lab from animal cells without the need to raise and kill livestock – has received a state grant to support its work. LabFarm this year presented a prototype of its chicken meatball https://t.co/pezABciGU6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 7, 2024 Earlier this year, Poland’s current government, a coalition ranging from left to centre right, announced new rules intended to improve the quality and variety of school meals, including offering less meat. From the start of the new school year, which began today, school canteens are expected to serve meat no more than twice a week, offer fish at least once per week, and offer a plant-based option at every meal. They should also limit fried food to no more than twice a week, use seasonal and locally sourced products, and include fruit and vegetables with meals. However, an attempt by the government to further raise taxes on alcoholic, sugary and sweet drinks was vetoed by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki last December. A fundraiser for an eight-month-old baby who survived an accident in the Polish city of Kraków in which his parents were killed by a speeding driver has reached more than 1 million zloty (€231,000). The tragedy has prompted widespread anger, with calls from residents and local politicians for the authorities to take action to deal with dangerous driving in the city. To będzie jedna z najtrudniejszych zbiórek, jakie wspólnie przeprowadzimy.💔Proszę o RT🙏 Kilka dni temu rozpędzony kierowca w Krakowie wjechał w młode małżeństwo. Mateusz i Klaudia zginęli. Ich kilkumiesięczny synek, Oliwier, trafił do szpitala. Mam dla Was dobrą wiadomość.… pic.twitter.com/R8L1xgEBPn — Damian Żurawski (@damian_zurawski) August 26, 2026 On 22 August, a married couple, Mateusz and Klaudia, both 32, were walking with their baby on Solna Street, close to the southern bank of the Vistula river, when a car driven by 26-year-old Hubert B., whose surname is masked under Polish privacy law, mounted the pavement, killing both parents. The child, eight-month-old Oliwier, survived the accident but was hospitalised. His condition is continuing to improve, reports broadcaster TVP Kraków. According to prosecutors, the car was travelling around 40 km/h (25mph) faster than the speed limit in the area. Hubert B. has been charged with unintentionally causing a fatal accident, for which he could face up to eight years in prison. “The suspect pleaded not guilty to the offence he was charged with, explaining, among other things, that the car skidded due to the uneven road surface,” prosecutors said, adding that the suspect has been placed in pretrial detention. An online fundraiser set up last week to provide Oliwier “with financial security for years to come” shared the news that the baby’s condition is now stable, although “his arm and leg are in plaster”. “We can’t give Oliwier back his mum and dad,” reads the fundraiser’s description. “However, we can do everything we can to ensure he has the resources for his education and a peaceful start to adult life.” At the time of writing, the fundraiser has reached more than 1.05 million zloty, over double its initial target. There have been more than 23,300 donations so far. Meanwhile, Oliwier’s grandfather, Andrzej, told newspaper Fakt that the family had given its consent for the fundraiser and was very grateful for those who had donated. A court in Kraków has granted Mateusz’s brother custody of the child. As well as sympathy for the victims, the accident aroused anger from residents. Several hundred people attended a protest at the site, holding signs reading “How many more people must die for something to change?” and “Stop road killers”. They installed their own mock-up pedestrian crossing and speed bumps. “Such tragedies are not isolated incidents,” said the organisers, quoted by news website Interia. They cited police figures showing that Kraków had the most road accidents of all Poland’s provincial capitals in 2025. Its figure of 941 was over 100 more than in Łódź and over 250 more than in Warsaw. Local councillor Rafał Zawiślak told news website Onet that he was filing a complaint with the prosecutor’s office, saying the city authorities had been negligent, failing to respond to warnings from 2024 that the site of the accident was dangerous. World.title: Fire During C-Section at Bulovka Hospital Leaves Woman Seriously Burned
World.content:
A woman suffered serious burns during an emergency cesarean section at Prague’s Bulovka Hospital on Aug. 25, hospital spokeswoman Eva Stolejda Libigerová said.

The cesarean was performed because of an acute obstetric complication. The woman’s condition is now stable and she does not require intensive care, the hospital said. She is recovering in a standard ward with her newborn.



The hospital is investigating the incident as part of its internal procedures for reviewing patient safety and the quality of medical care. It said it would take appropriate measures once the investigation is complete.

Fire broke out during surgery

According to information obtained about the incident, medical staff were attempting to control bleeding toward the end of the operation when a fire broke out involving a surgical device.

The device was reportedly being used shortly after the patient’s skin had been treated with a disinfectant.

The woman suffered second- and third-degree burns to her inner thighs, sides, lower abdomen and genital area, according to the available information.

Two days after the operation, she was transferred to the Burns Medicine Clinic at University Hospital Královské Vinohrady for treatment. She was later returned to Bulovka Hospital’s postpartum ward.

The circumstances surrounding the fire, including how it started and whether established safety procedures were followed, are being examined by the hospital.

Previous incident at Bulovka maternity clinic

The hospital’s gynecology and obstetrics clinic was also the site of a serious medical error in March 2024.

In that case, staff mistakenly identified two patients of Asian origin. A pregnant woman who had arrived for a routine examination was incorrectly subjected to a curettage procedure, resulting in the loss of her pregnancy.

An internal investigation concluded that two employees had violated established procedures and internal rules. The hospital subsequently ended its cooperation with one of them.

Police also investigated the case on suspicion of negligent bodily harm but ultimately brought no charges.

The woman later reached a settlement with the hospital worth 2.3 million Czech crowns. One of the employees involved lost her job.

World.title: Ambiente to Open Its 35th Prague Establishment This September
World.content:
Restaurant group Ambiente is preparing to open its 35th establishment, with a second location of its Pult beer concept set to launch in Prague’s Holešovice district in mid-September.

The new venue will be located on Tusarova Street and will follow the concept of Pult in Prague 1, which opened in the Celnice building in 2021.



While both locations will focus on Czech lager, the new Holešovice branch will introduce a different food concept and its own selection of beers.

The original venue serves beers from six breweries, with an emphasis on precise storage, serving and temperature control.

A different approach to food

Food will be one of the main differences between the two Pult locations.

The original Pult in Celnice focuses largely on smaller dishes and snacks. The Holešovice restaurant will instead offer a more substantial menu designed specifically to accompany beer.

The menu is expected to focus heavily on Czech beef, including several versions of steak tartare and steaks. Unlike many restaurants where the kitchen closes earlier than the bar, the new Pult plans to serve food until closing at 1 a.m.

The restaurant will have space for around 130 guests.

Another new destination for Holešovice

The opening comes as Holešovice continues to attract new restaurants, cafés and cultural venues. The area has become home to places including Vnitroblock, Mexická, Slice Slice Baby, Eatery, Ema, Typika, Osada and Polepšovna.

Ambiente itself has expanded its presence in Holešovice this year. At the Holešovice Market, the group has opened a second location of its Myšák confectionery and Naše maso butcher shop, as well as Skô, a Slovak-focused restaurant concept.

World.title: 7 Autumn Bike Trips to Take Around Czechia
World.content:
With cooler temperatures and autumn colours arriving, September and October are among the best months for cycling in Czechia.

The country’s extensive network of marked trails makes it easy to plan anything from a relaxed day trip to a multi-day adventure.

Here are seven routes worth considering this autumn.



1. Prague–Mělník–Litoměřice

One of the easiest options for Prague residents is to head north along the Elbe. The route passes through Mělník, known for its vineyards and historic centre, before continuing towards Litoměřice.

Along the way, cyclists can see Roudnice Chateau, Mount Říp and the historic fortress town of Terezín. Mělník is particularly appealing in September, when its wine season is in full swing.

2. Znojmo Wine Route

For a combination of cycling and wine, South Moravia is hard to beat in autumn. The 63-kilometre Znojmo Wine Route connects vineyards and villages around Znojmo and is suitable for cyclists of different abilities.

September and October are also the region’s main wine-harvest season, with numerous wine and burčák events taking place.

3. Mikulov and Pálava

The Mikulov Wine Trail offers another relaxed way to explore South Moravia. The route takes cyclists through vineyards and the countryside around Mikulov, with the Pálava hills providing one of the region’s most distinctive landscapes.

It is particularly attractive in September, when the annual Pálava Wine Festival takes place.

4. Singltrek pod Smrkem

If road cycling isn’t your thing, head towards Liberec. Singltrek pod Smrkem has more than 60 kilometres of purpose-built mountain-bike trails, ranging from easier sections for beginners to more challenging routes.

The surrounding Jizera Mountains also make it a good destination for a weekend trip.

5. Bečva Cycling Trail

The almost 160-kilometre Bečva Cycling Trail follows the Bečva River across Moravia. The route can be completed over several days and is largely downhill when ridden from the river’s source towards its confluence with the Morava.

Highlights along the way include Helfštýn Castle, the Zbrašovské Aragonite Caves and the open-air museum in Rožnov pod Radhoštěm.

6. Ploučnice Cycle Path

The nearly 100-kilometre Ploučnice Cycle Path runs from the river’s source near Ještěd to Děčín. It passes through Česká Lípa, the Ralsko area and the Kokořínsko-Máchův kraj landscape before reaching the Elbe.

7. Prague–Vienna Greenway

For a more ambitious trip, the Prague–Vienna Greenway stretches 368 kilometres between the two capitals. The route passes through historic towns, castles and monasteries, including Tábor, Znojmo and Mikulov.

It takes roughly a week to complete with stops, making it better suited to a longer autumn holiday than a weekend ride.

World.title: How to Buy TikTok Followers Without Risking Your Account
World.content:
Building a TikTok audience from zero can be frustrating. Even well-produced videos may struggle to attract attention when an account has only a handful of followers.

This slow beginning encourages some creators and businesses to purchase followers in the hope of making their profiles appear more established. Follower count can influence first impressions. When visitors discover a profile with an existing audience, they may be more willing to watch its videos, explore older content, or follow the account themselves. However, purchased followers cannot replace engaging videos or genuine interaction. Low-quality services may also deliver inactive accounts that disappear quickly or create an unnatural gap between follower numbers and actual engagement. Anyone considering this approach should understand how follower services operate, what they can realistically provide, and which warning signs suggest that a seller should be avoided.

Why Creators Purchase TikTok Followers

New accounts frequently face a credibility problem. Viewers have little information to judge whether the creator is worth following, so the visible follower count becomes one of several signals they use to make that decision. A larger audience can make a profile appear more established. This is particularly relevant for businesses, influencers, musicians, and other new TikTok creators trying to build authority in a competitive category. Some creators also purchase TikTok followers to reach eligibility thresholds for particular TikTok features. TikTok commonly applies age, location, and follower requirements to features such as LIVE, although the exact conditions may differ between markets and can change over time. The important distinction is that purchased followers mainly affect appearance. They may strengthen the profile’s initial social proof, but they do not guarantee greater reach, more sales, or stronger engagement.

What Purchased Followers Can and Cannot Do

Follower count is visible to anyone who visits a TikTok profile, which means it can shape the visitor’s first impression. A profile with several thousand followers may look more credible than an otherwise similar account with fewer than 100. TikTok’s recommendation system, however, evaluates much more than audience size. Signals such as watch time, completion rate, rewatches, shares, comments, saves, and viewer satisfaction are generally more important when determining whether a video should reach a wider audience. This creates a potential problem. If an account displays 30,000 followers but its videos consistently receive only a few dozen views, the imbalance may look unnatural to both TikTok and real visitors. Brands evaluating the creator for a partnership may notice the same discrepancy. Purchased followers should therefore be understood as a limited form of social proof. They cannot:

Make weak videos more entertaining

Guarantee placement on the For You feed

Produce meaningful comments or conversations

Create loyal customers

Replace a consistent publishing strategy

Automatically generate revenue

The greatest risk comes from purchasing followers that are obviously automated, inactive, or created only to inflate account statistics. These profiles add little value and may be removed during platform cleanups.

How to Evaluate a TikTok Follower Provider

The market contains everything from established social media marketing platforms to temporary websites selling automated accounts. A professional design alone does not prove that a service is dependable, so each provider should be evaluated carefully. Platforms such as SocialWick offer clearly defined TikTok packages and a conventional ordering process. Regardless of which company is being considered, several basic checks should be completed before placing an order.

Check the Website’s Security

A provider should use HTTPS encryption to protect information submitted through its website. This can usually be confirmed by checking for the padlock symbol beside the address in the browser. Secure payment methods are equally important. Credit cards and reputable payment processors normally offer better consumer protection than cryptocurrency transfers, gift cards, or other payment methods that are difficult to reverse.

Never Provide a TikTok Password

A follower delivery service generally needs only the public username or a link to the TikTok profile. It should not require the account password, email login, recovery code, or two-factor authentication details. Requests for private credentials are a serious warning sign. Sharing this information could allow an unknown company to access the account, change its settings, publish content, or lock out the owner.

Review the Delivery Time

Instant delivery may sound convenient, but an enormous follower increase within minutes can look unnatural. A newer account is unlikely to gain tens of thousands of followers suddenly without a viral video or another clear reason. More credible providers commonly offer gradual delivery. This spreads the order across several hours or days and makes it easier to monitor the quality of the accounts being added.

Understand the Package Quality

Follower packages are often divided into labels such as standard, high quality, active, real, or premium. These terms are not standardized, so they can mean different things on different websites. A higher-priced package may include accounts with profile photos, usernames, existing posts, or more complete activity histories. Cheaper options frequently consist of empty or inactive profiles. Before paying extra for a so-called premium tier, buyers should read the description carefully and determine what the seller is actually promising. Independent comparisons of TikTok follower providers and package quality may provide additional context, but customer reviews and seller claims should still be treated cautiously.

Look for Accessible Customer Support

A legitimate business should provide a clear way to request assistance. Live chat, email support, or a functioning contact form gives customers somewhere to report missing followers, delayed orders, or payment problems. Support availability does not automatically prove that a provider is trustworthy. However, a website with no contact information, unanswered messages, and no stated resolution process presents a much greater risk.

Warning Signs That Should Not Be Ignored

Very low pricing is one of the most common signs of poor-quality delivery. Maintaining accounts that look authentic requires more resources than operating a large collection of disposable bots. Consequently, offers promising thousands of “real and active” followers for a few cents are unlikely to match their description. Other warning signs include:

Requests for passwords or security codes

Guaranteed viral results

Promises of automatic monetization

No terms of service or privacy policy

Prices far below comparable providers

Only irreversible payment methods

Broken pages or copied website content

No delivery estimate

No refund or replacement policy

Large numbers of identical customer reviews

Claims of guaranteed engagement also deserve scrutiny. No external provider can honestly promise that purchased followers will watch every video or become paying customers.

Why a Refill Policy Matters

Follower losses can occur after an order is completed. TikTok may remove suspicious accounts, users may deactivate their profiles, or low-quality followers may simply disappear. A refill policy allows customers to request replacements when the follower count drops within a specified period. Depending on the provider, this protection may last for several days or a month. The conditions should be reviewed before checkout. Some companies refill only when the loss exceeds a minimum amount, while others exclude certain packages. Buyers should also check whether the replacement is automatic or must be requested manually. A refill guarantee cannot eliminate every risk, but it shows that the provider has at least acknowledged the possibility of follower loss and established a process for addressing it.

Avoid Unnatural Growth Patterns

Sudden, unexplained growth can draw unwanted attention. An account that gains 10,000 followers overnight without publishing anything new may appear suspicious, particularly if its views and interactions remain unchanged. Gradual delivery is generally less disruptive than receiving an entire order immediately. However, spreading out a purchase should not be treated as a method for bypassing TikTok’s enforcement systems. Buying followers may still conflict with platform rules, and no delivery method can guarantee that an account will avoid restrictions or removals.

Creators who choose to purchase followers should keep the order proportionate to the profile’s existing size. Adding a modest number to an active account is less conspicuous than transforming a nearly empty profile into a large one overnight. Content should also continue to be published consistently. A larger number beneath the profile image will have little effect if visitors arrive and find outdated, irrelevant, or poorly produced videos.

Keep Engagement and Follower Numbers Balanced

Follower count is only one part of a TikTok profile. Views, likes, comments, shares, and posting frequency provide a broader picture of its actual performance. If follower growth significantly outpaces every other metric, the account may lose credibility. A profile with 20,000 followers and almost no interaction may look less trustworthy than one with 2,000 followers and an active community. Maintaining a reasonable balance requires genuine content work. Creators should continue to:

Publish videos on a consistent schedule

Capture attention within the opening seconds

Respond to real comments

Participate in relevant trends

Use searchable captions and keywords

Test different formats and video lengths

Review analytics to identify strong topics

Collaborate with creators in the same niche

These activities provide TikTok with behavioral signals that purchased followers cannot produce.

Turning Social Proof Into Organic Growth

The most practical reason to purchase followers is to improve the profile’s initial presentation. If that stronger appearance encourages more people to explore the content, it may indirectly support organic growth. This effect depends entirely on what visitors find after opening the profile. A clear bio, recognizable niche, strong video covers, and a useful collection of content can convert curiosity into a genuine follow. An inflated number without quality content is unlikely to accomplish the same result. Creators should prepare their profiles before purchasing anything. A complete profile should include:

A memorable username

A clear profile image

A concise description of the account

Several high-quality published videos

Pinned content that represents the creator’s best work

A consistent subject or visual identity

An appropriate call to action

Purchased followers may bring the profile closer to the starting line, but the content determines whether real viewers remain interested.

Final Considerations Before Buying TikTok Followers

Buying TikTok followers can improve the visible size of an account, but it should never be confused with building a real community. The number may influence first impressions, yet it cannot reproduce the value of genuine viewers who regularly interact with the content. Anyone considering a purchase should choose a provider carefully, avoid sharing login information, use protected payment methods, read the refill conditions, and remain skeptical of unrealistic guarantees. It is also important to recognize that follower purchases may violate TikTok’s rules and could lead to removals or other account consequences. The strongest TikTok profiles combine credibility with content that earns attention. Purchased followers may change how a profile looks, but sustainable growth still depends on originality, consistency, audience understanding, and videos that people genuinely want to watch.

World.title: Vinohrady’s Americká Street Block Party Returns on September 12
World.content:
Americká and Záhřebská streets in Prague’s Vinohrady will turn into a pedestrian festival zone on Saturday, September 12, for the 15th edition of Zažít Americkou jinak.

From 10:30 AM to 9:30 PM, the streets will host a full-day programme of live music, dance, workshops, design, food and activities for children. The festival is free to attend.

A major part of this year’s programme will focus on Mexico and Latin American culture, including a celebration of Mexican Independence Day.



The main programme will take place on the La Calle Mexicana Stage, hosted by DJs Roxana Velasco and José. Visitors can look forward to performances by Studio Anyo, traditional Mexican music, a piñata, a dance workshop and appearances by Mexican musicians Razcarmelo and Andrea Viruega.

One of the highlights will be El Grito, the traditional ceremony marking Mexico’s Independence Day. The event has become an annual gathering point for the Mexican community in Czechia and festival visitors.

The programme will also feature Mariachi Azteca de Praga, described as the first authentic mariachi band based in the Czech Republic.

The evening will continue with international acts including Faustina Calavera, a ten-member band from Wrocław combining Latin American cumbia, Balkan brass and ska, followed by ONIXIA, an Argentine singer, dancer and songwriter based in Berlin who blends electronic music with Latin American rhythms.

More Space to Relax

This year’s festival will also feature an expanded chill-out zone at the intersection of Americká and Jana Masaryka streets, with seating, workshops and space to meet friends and neighbours.

Music will also be played at two additional locations. The Burza #4 Stage will return by the fountain at the corner of Americká and Záhřebská streets, while another stage on Záhřebská Street will focus on world and house music.

MINT Market, Food and Local Businesses

The festival will once again include MINT Market, bringing together dozens of Czech designers, independent makers and creators from Latin America. Visitors can browse fashion, jewellery, illustrations, ceramics, natural cosmetics and other handmade products.

Food will be another major part of the day, with Mexican, Latin American and international cuisine, street food and special offers from cafés, restaurants and other local businesses.

During the festival, Americká and Záhřebská streets will be closed to traffic and parking.

World.title: New Pharmacy Partnership Makes Prescription Drugs Easier for Foreigners in Czechia
World.content:
Foreigners from outside the EU insured with Maxima pojišťovna can now collect prescription medicines at selected pharmacies without paying upfront.

The Czech insurer has expanded its network of partner pharmacies through a new agreement with LÉKÁRNA U MUZEA in Prague 1.

Under the arrangement, the pharmacy and insurer handle the reimbursement directly, bringing the process closer to the system used by patients covered by Czech public health insurance.



The change is aimed at simplifying access to medicines for foreigners, who can face difficulties navigating the Czech healthcare system and understanding the costs associated with medical treatment.

According to figures cited by the insurer, nearly 900,000 people from non-EU countries have been living in the Czech Republic on a long-term basis. They account for about 8.2 percent of the country’s population.

How the new system works

Previously, foreign clients with commercial health insurance could be required to pay for prescribed medicines at the pharmacy and then submit the receipts to their insurer for reimbursement.

Under the new arrangement, this step is eliminated. Eligible Maxima clients can collect their prescribed medicines through the partner pharmacy, while the financial settlement takes place directly between the pharmacy and the insurance company.

The model has already been operating for more than a year at the pharmacy operated by Maxima’s healthcare partner Innova Healthcare at the Hůrka Polyclinic in Prague.

The data also highlights some of the most common medical needs among patients visiting the participating clinics. More than 63 percent of patients seen by general practitioners, pediatricians and gynecologists were prescribed antibiotics.

More than 37 percent required treatment for sideropenic anemia, or iron deficiency, while 20 percent received prescriptions for blood-thinning medication following injuries.

The pharmacy in Prague 1 will also stock medical equipment and rehabilitation aids. Its range includes orthoses, crutches, wheelchairs and products for convalescence, rehabilitation and everyday healthcare.

Maxima says it intends to expand the direct-settlement model to additional partner pharmacies in the future.

World.title: Dozens of Hot Air Balloons to Fill Czech Skies During September Festival
World.content:
Dozens of hot air balloons are expected to take to the skies over eastern Bohemia this week as the Balonové Nebe festival returns to Hradec Králové, Jaroměř and nearby areas.

The five-day event will run from Wednesday, September 2, through Sunday, September 6, with a program combining competitive balloon flights, mass launches and evening shows. All public events are free to attend.

Weather will play a major role in the festival schedule. Balloon flights can only take place under suitable conditions, meaning launch sites and departure times may change at short notice.



Organizers say the exact location of each flight will depend mainly on wind direction and other weather conditions. Planned flights may also be postponed or cancelled if conditions are unsuitable.

The festival has established itself as one of the country’s major hot air balloon gatherings. Last year’s event set a Czech record when 81 balloons flew into the sky at the same time.

The 2026 edition will once again feature morning competitions, during which pilots will complete a series of tasks while large groups of balloons rise over the region.

Evening programs will offer a different spectacle, with balloon shows planned for spectators. The precise locations of these events will be announced according to the weather forecast and flying conditions.

Visitors planning to attend are advised to check the festival’s official website before setting out. The organizers will publish the latest information about launch locations, times and any changes to the schedule there.

World.title: VIDEO: Golden STARLUX Lands in Prague for the First Time
World.content:
A golden Airbus A350-1000 operated by Taiwan’s STARLUX Airlines landed at Václav Havel Airport Prague for the first time on Tuesday, September 1.

The aircraft, registered as B-58554, carries the special AIRSORAYAMA Gold livery created in collaboration with Japanese artist Hajime Sorayama.

Prague is one of only three destinations where STARLUX plans to operate the specially designed aircraft on a regular basis, alongside Tokyo and Phoenix.



The arrival marks another step in the expansion of STARLUX’s new direct connection between Prague and Taipei.

The airline launched the route on August 1, initially using the smaller Airbus A350-900. From September, the carrier has switched to the larger A350-1000, which can carry up to 350 passengers in four travel classes.

STARLUX, Airbus and paint manufacturer Mankiewicz developed a multilayer coating using mica particles to create the metallic effect while meeting aviation safety requirements.

Increasing capacity on Prague route

STARLUX launched Prague as its first European destination on August 1, connecting the Czech capital directly with Taipei three times a week. The service currently operates on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays.

Flight JX101 leaves Taipei at 12:10 a.m. and arrives in Prague at 8:35 a.m. The return flight, JX102, departs Prague at 10:35 a.m. and arrives in Taipei at 7:55 a.m. the following day.

The switch to the A350-1000 increases the available capacity on the route. The aircraft has four travel classes, including First Class, Business Class, Premium Economy and Economy.

An additional Monday flight is scheduled to operate from October through November, bringing the route to four flights per week during that period.

World.title: Orbán’s son named as head of Chad medical mission in non-public government resolution
World.content:
Newly obtained documents suggest Gáspár Orbán had a far more prominent role in Hungary’s controversial Chad mission than previously acknowledged.

Former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán’s son, Gáspár Orbán, was named as the person responsible for leading a Hungarian medical mission to Chad in a non-public government resolution, according to official documents obtained by Hungarian news outlet 444.hu.

The documents shed new light on the role played by the former prime minister’s son in Hungary’s planned African mission, suggesting that his responsibilities went considerably beyond simply participating in preparations.

According to 444.hu, the documents include non-public government resolutions and records connected to the mission. They reportedly show that Gáspár Orbán was placed in a position of authority over both military personnel and the medical mission’s coordinator.

Gáspár Orbán named as head of medical mission

A medical mission travelled to Chad between 21 September and 5 October 2023. A non-public government resolution concerning the mission reportedly identified Gáspár Orbán as the person responsible for leading the entire medical mission.

The document placed both the military leadership and the medical mission coordinator under his authority. The Hungarian consul was reportedly the only person at the same level in the organisational structure, although no other officials were assigned under the consul.

The documents also point to Gáspár Orbán having played a leading role in an earlier mission to Niger.

One document reportedly states that Hungary Helps and the Hungarian University of Agriculture and Life Sciences acted according to instructions issued by the Coordination Office, headed by “Gáspár O.”

Niger mission later became Chad operation

The original plans reportedly focused on Niger, but political developments in the West African country prompted Hungary to change the destination.

Chad subsequently became the focus of the project, which was broader than a military operation. According to Telex, when then-Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó announced the initiative in December 2023, he described it as involving security, economic, humanitarian and educational cooperation.

Documents obtained by 444.hu reportedly show that Gáspár Orbán was a member of the Africa Working Group (MUCS) established in connection with the Chad mission.

However, the documents suggest his involvement went significantly beyond ordinary membership. According to 444.hu’s reporting, several internal documents indicate that activities connected to the project required his approval.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Government officials gave conflicting accounts

The newly reported documents appear to contrast with earlier statements from Hungarian government and military officials about Gáspár Orbán’s involvement.

In April, then-Chief of Staff Gábor Böröndi confirmed that the former prime minister’s son had participated in the government planning group dealing with the Chad mission. At the same time, however, Böröndi described claims that Gáspár Orbán had led the group as a “gross exaggeration”.

“We had a dedicated planning team in place, which was led by my deputy, Lieutenant General Ferenc Kajári,” Böröndi said at the time.

Former government minister Gergely Gulyás had previously claimed that Gáspár Orbán had played no role in preparing the Chad mission.

However, former Defence Minister Kristóf Szalay-Bobrovniczky had given a different account. In both an interview and a 2024 parliamentary hearing, he said Gáspár Orbán had been involved in preparing the mission after being assigned to the ministerial cabinet.

Orbán’s son had already been linked to the secret mission

Gáspár Orbán’s involvement in the African operation first attracted widespread attention in early 2024, when investigative outlet Direkt36 reported on his role. The outlet published photographs and videos appearing to show him personally taking part in negotiations involving the Hungarian delegation in Chad.

More recently, Army Captain Szilveszter Pálinkás told Telex that Gáspár Orbán had been given an office in the Karmelita complex in Budapest after graduating from the Royal Military Academy in the United Kingdom, where he held the rank of first lieutenant. According to Pálinkás, he subsequently began working on the planning of the African mission.

World.title: New Budapest neighbourhood taking shape: 324 flats and four-star hotel to rise – Photos
World.content:
A new mixed-use urban complex is taking shape in Budapest’s 13th district on the former site of the Szikra Printing Works. The Parkside Residence development has now reached its highest point, with the 43,650-square-metre site bounded by Esztergomi Road, Visegrádi Street, Süllő Street and Zsilip Street set to feature homes, a hotel, retail units and community spaces.

One of the project’s key features is the redevelopment of a site that had stood largely unused for more than 15 years, just a short distance from Vizafogó Park.

Visual plan: Parkside Residence Budapest

324 flats and a 152-room hotel planned

The development is being carried out in four phases. Plans call for a total of 324 new homes, a 152-room four-star hotel, nine retail units, 364 parking spaces and 215 storage units, Magyar Építők reported.

A major element of the complex will be a landscaped 2,000-square-metre inner garden connected to the residential buildings. Across the entire development, almost 4,800 square metres of green space will be created.

The project is being built next to Vizafogó Park, close to the Göncz Árpád City Centre area. According to the developers, the aim is to create an urban environment where residential, retail, service and community functions are combined with opportunities for recreation.

Visual plan: Parkside Residence Budapest

Four-star hotel to form part of the complex

One of the most prominent elements of Parkside Residence will be the 152-room Staybridge Suites hotel, which will become part of the portfolio of international hotel group IHG Hotels & Resorts. The four-star, apartment-style hotel will primarily target business travellers and guests staying in Budapest for medium-length periods. It will be operated by Mogotel Hotel Group.

The development will therefore go beyond a conventional residential project, bringing accommodation and commercial functions to the area alongside housing.

Visual plan: Parkside Residence Budapest

Czech developer’s first project in Hungary

Parkside Residence is being developed by Czech UDI Group, which has more than three decades of experience and operates in six countries across residential, commercial and logistics projects. The development is the company’s first project in Hungary.

Energy-efficient solutions included

Energy efficiency has also been a key consideration in the development. The flats will feature heat pump-based ceiling heating and cooling, which, according to the developer, is intended to meet the requirements of the A+ energy efficiency category.

The plans also include a rainwater harvesting irrigation system, electric vehicle charging points and preparations for the installation of smart home systems.

Visual plan: Parkside Residence Budapest

Structural works give way to next phase

The topping-out ceremony marks the completion of another major stage of the buildings’ structural works. The project is continuing according to the planned schedule. In the next phase, the focus will shift primarily to façade works, mechanical installations and interior fit-out.

Once completed, the site of the former Szikra Printing Works, which had remained vacant for more than 15 years, will have an entirely new purpose. A new complex combining residential, hotel, retail and community functions is therefore set to emerge in one of the 13th district’s sought-after areas.

Proximity to the park increasingly important

According to the developer, the area around Vizafogó Park has become increasingly attractive to homebuyers in recent years. One of the location’s biggest advantages is that residents can enjoy both the benefits of urban infrastructure and easy access to green space.

The nearby park provides opportunities for walking, exercise and relaxation, while this part of the 13th district is also well connected to the city centre and other parts of Budapest. The development is thus taking shape in an area that has seen several major property projects in recent years.

World.title: Revolut customers could face a nasty surprise even after paying their debts
World.content:
Revolut customers in Hungary could face an unexpected problem after settling a debt: an account seizure may remain active even after the bailiff has officially asked the bank to remove it.

The issue was highlighted by a Revolut customer in the Facebook group Revolut Közösség, whose account had been transferred to Revolut Bank UAB’s Hungarian branch before an enforcement order, known in Hungary as an inkasszó, was placed on it.

According to the customer’s account, the enforcement was initially legitimate, but they subsequently contacted the bailiff and settled the outstanding debt. The bailiff then officially requested that Revolut remove the account seizure on 3 August. However, the customer said that 11 days later, on 14 August, the restriction was still in place.

The customer also contacted Revolut’s support team, but was reportedly only told that the bank was working on the issue.

Why could this cause problems?

The delay could have serious financial consequences for customers who have already paid what they owe. According to the account reported by RevB, the enforcement order can remain active for 35 days. During this period, the bank’s system may automatically deduct the amount covered by the order from the account.

That means a customer who has already settled the underlying debt could still face the risk of money being taken from their Revolut account while the enforcement order remains active.

Hungarian Revolut accounts have entered a new phase

The issue has emerged following Revolut’s gradual migration of Hungarian customers to its Hungarian branch. Revolut began transferring customers to Revolut Bank UAB’s Hungarian branch in May, bringing its Hungarian accounts further into the domestic banking and enforcement framework.

Since the transition began, Hungarian customers with outstanding debts have increasingly reported receiving enforcement orders against their Revolut accounts. The change is significant because Hungarian bailiffs can now access accounts held through Revolut’s Hungarian branch for enforcement purposes.

For customers, this means that having a Revolut account is no longer necessarily separate from Hungary’s domestic debt-enforcement system.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Revolut is also rolling out a new AI assistant

The enforcement issue comes as Revolut introduces a new artificial intelligence feature to Hungarian customers. The company has begun rolling out AIR, an AI assistant designed to let users manage everyday finances through a conversational interface rather than navigating the app’s traditional menus, Revb reported.

AIR can answer questions about spending, such as how much a customer has spent on food during a particular month. It can also help manage subscriptions and temporarily freeze a lost bank card. Customers who use Revolut’s investment features can ask about their portfolio’s current performance or the performance of individual shares.

The assistant also extends to travel planning, with the ability to create itineraries, search for accommodation and suggest local activities based on a user’s budget. Revolut says the launch does not change existing privacy settings. According to the company, third-party AI partners involved in the feature do not store customers’ data or use it to train external models.

AIR is being rolled out gradually and can be accessed from the app’s home screen by swiping down, or through the Chats section under the Profile menu.

World.title: Major Budapest road closures from Friday: four bridges affected
World.content:
Budapest is set for major traffic restrictions this weekend as the 41st Wizz Air Budapest Half Marathon takes place on Sunday, 6 September. Temporary closures will affect seven districts and several major roads, including sections of four bridges: the Árpád Bridge, Margaret Bridge, Liberty Bridge and Chain Bridge.

The Budapest Police Headquarters (BRFK) has urged drivers to exercise particular caution and allow extra time for their journeys. The restrictions will be in place from Friday, 4 September, through Sunday, 6 September.

First closures begin on Saturday

Pázmány Péter Promenade in District XI will be closed between Műegyetem Embankment and Dombóvári Road from 8 AM on Saturday until 9 PM on Sunday.

On Sunday morning, further closures will affect Magyar Tudósok Boulevard, the Buda and Pest lower embankments, Műegyetem Embankment, Liberty Bridge and Szent Gellért Square. Some roads will be closed only temporarily as runners pass through.

Árpád and Margaret bridges affected

Between 6 AM and 11.30 AM on Sunday, sections of the race route will be closed intermittently. The affected route runs from Pázmány Péter Promenade along the Buda lower embankment and Árpád fejedelem Road, across the southern carriageway of Árpád Bridge, through Margaret Island and across the northern side of Margaret Bridge.

The restrictions will then continue through Jászai Mari Square, Újpest Embankment and the Pest lower embankment before reaching Fővám Square, Liberty Bridge, Szent Gellért Square and Műegyetem Embankment. The two affected bridges will not necessarily be closed for the entire period: police will impose temporary restrictions as the race progresses.

Chain Bridge also affected later in the day

A second period of intermittent closures is scheduled between 11 AM and 2 PM. The route will run from Pázmány Péter Promenade along the Buda lower embankment, Bem Embankment and Fő Street to Clark Ádám Square, before crossing Chain Bridge.

Runners will then continue via Széchenyi István Square, Eötvös Square, the Pest lower embankment, Fővám Square, Liberty Bridge, Szent Gellért Square and Műegyetem Embankment.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Exact closure times

According to the BRFK, the main full closures on Sunday are scheduled as follows:

4 AM–4 PM: Magyar Tudósok Boulevard in District XI

Magyar Tudósok Boulevard in District XI 6 AM–1.30 PM: Buda lower embankment in Districts I, II, III and XI

Buda lower embankment in Districts I, II, III and XI 6.30 AM–3.10 PM: Pest lower embankment in Districts V, IX and XIII

Pest lower embankment in Districts V, IX and XIII 8.20 AM–2.10 PM: Műegyetem Embankment in District XI

Műegyetem Embankment in District XI 8.55 AM–2 PM: Liberty Bridge and Szent Gellért Square in Districts IX and XI

The intermittent restrictions along the race routes will operate separately during the morning and early afternoon.

In case you missed it: Major shake-up in Budapest — Government bill would hand key city-centre spaces to the capital for free

Parking restrictions also in force

Drivers should also be aware that parking restrictions will begin before some of the road closures. No parking will be permitted in several locations from Friday, including parts of Magyar Tudósok Boulevard. Additional parking bans will apply from midnight on Saturday and Sunday at various locations around the Buda and Pest embankments, Árpád fejedelem Road, Műegyetem Embankment, Hunyadi János Street and Jégverem Street.

Police have advised motorists to check the altered traffic arrangements before setting off and to follow temporary signs and instructions. The BRFK has published detailed information on the affected locations and times, together with an interactive map showing the restrictions on individual road sections. The 41st Wizz Air Budapest Half Marathon will take place in the Hungarian capital on Sunday, 6 September, bringing runners through several central Budapest districts.

World.title: Budapest apartment block catches fire: 10 people taken to hospital, dozens forced to leave their homes
World.content:
A fire broke out in a multi-storey residential building in Budapest’s 18th district on Wednesday evening, forcing dozens of residents to leave their homes. Ten people, including seven children, were taken to hospital, according to reports.

The fire broke out in a building on Ráday Gedeon Street, where a ground-floor flat was engulfed in flames.

43 residents forced to leave their homes

According to the Hungarian News Agency (MTI), the building contains 32 flats and was filled with smoke following the fire. A total of 43 people had to leave the property while firefighters tackled the blaze. Máté Kisdi, spokesman for the Budapest Disaster Management Directorate, said residents would not be allowed to return to their homes until the building had been properly ventilated.

The initial reports indicated that one person had been taken away from the scene by ambulance. Later information confirmed that ten people, including seven children, were transported to hospital.

The available reports did not immediately provide details about the condition of those taken to hospital.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Firefighters prevent flames from spreading

Professional firefighters from Budapest, together with volunteer firefighters from the FOKA River Disaster Management and Special Rescue Public Benefit Association, responded to the incident. Several water jets were used to fight the flames, while firefighters simultaneously evacuated the building and worked to prevent the fire from spreading to other parts of the property.

The blaze was eventually brought under control, and firefighters began carrying out follow-up operations. The cause of the fire has not yet been reported.

World.title: PM Magyar meets Costa, sets conditions for backing EU’s next 7-year budget
World.content:
The Hungarian government will only be able to approve the European Union’s new seven-year budget if it serves the interests of Hungarian people and businesses, Prime Minister Péter Magyar told European Council President António Costa during a meeting in Budapest on Wednesday.

In a Facebook post following the meeting, Magyar said he had also told Costa that Hungary expected an early solution to the issue of the EUR 1 million-a-day fine imposed under the previous Hungarian government to be suspended.

According to Magyar, he also stressed that, particularly in light of events in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in Africa this summer, Hungary would continue to maintain the legal framework and physical border barrier needed to stop illegal migration.

“Hungary will continue to protect the European Union’s external borders. And we expect these efforts to be recognised at European level as well,” Magyar said.

The prime minister added that he had reiterated during the meeting that Hungary does not support an accelerated EU accession process for any candidate country.

Hungary opposes fast-track EU membership

The comments come as the EU prepares its next seven-year budget, with member states facing negotiations over how the bloc’s financial priorities and funding will be structured for the coming period.

Magyar’s remarks also show the Hungarian government’s position on migration and EU enlargement, signalling that Budapest intends to maintain its existing border protection measures while opposing what it considers accelerated accession procedures.

World.title: Michelin-starred chef brings a new taste of Hungary to Time Out Market Budapest
World.content:
Ákos Sárközi is bringing together the culinary worlds of Borkonyha and Textúra in a new, more relaxed concept at Budapest’s Time Out Market. Fúzió by Textúra & Borkonyha will open on 11 September, offering Hungarian-inspired bistro dishes with a creative twist.

A new restaurant concept is coming to Time Out Market Budapest this September, as Michelin-starred chef Ákos Sárközi brings his latest culinary venture to the capital’s popular food hall.

Fúzió by Textúra & Borkonyha will open on 11 September at the Corvin Palace on Blaha Lujza Square, combining the distinctive culinary identities of two well-known Budapest restaurants in a more relaxed and accessible format.

The concept is designed to introduce a wider audience to Sárközi’s approach to Hungarian cuisine, with playful, modern takes on familiar bistro dishes.

Two restaurants, one culinary vision

Fúzió has grown out of the professional collaboration between Borkonyha and Textúra, two Budapest restaurants led by Sárközi Ákos alongside co-owners Tamás Horváth and Zoltán Kalocsai.

Borkonyha has been one of the most consistent names in Hungarian gastronomy. It received its Michelin star in 2014 and has retained the distinction ever since. Its cuisine combines traditional and contemporary Hungarian flavours with influences from Transylvanian culinary traditions and international gastronomy.

Textúra, which joined Borkonyha as its sister restaurant in 2018, is now entering a new chapter of its own, moving closer to the approachable world of bistro dining in both its food and atmosphere while retaining the creativity and experimentation that define its kitchen.

Although the two restaurants have distinct personalities, they complement one another closely. Fúzió aims to capture precisely this balance, adapting it to the informal, communal setting of Time Out Market.

The new concept is also intended to reach diners who may not regularly visit traditional restaurants but are interested in high-quality food served in a quicker, more relaxed setting.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Hungarian bistro classics with a creative twist

At the heart of Fúzió will be Hungarian-style bistro cuisine, interpreted through Sárközi’s playful and inventive approach.

Several dishes will be available exclusively at Time Out Market Budapest, including duck liver with Tokaji Aszú, pear and breadstick, juicy roast pork brioche with a thyme sauce, and “Barack virág” (“Peach blossom”) Rákóczi túrós, a creative take on the beloved Hungarian cottage-cheese dessert.

The duck liver dish brings together traditional Hungarian ingredients and contemporary presentation, while the roast pork brioche takes inspiration from szalontüdő, a classic Hungarian dish traditionally made with offal.

“There is beauty in simplicity, but when it is combined with creativity, it can become something memorable. We should be proud of the diversity of Hungarian cuisine,” said Ákos Sárközi, executive chef.

For Sárközi, one of the key aims of Fúzió is to make high-end gastronomy feel less distant and intimidating.

“People often put Michelin-starred chefs in a bubble and think that I only make dishes that are difficult for everyone to understand. At Time Out Market, I have the opportunity to show that I am the same ordinary person I have always been and always will be: I love cooking and I love eating,” he said.

The experience goes beyond the plate

Márton Tibor, the manager and coordinator of Borkonyha and Textúra, will play a central role in Fúzió’s day-to-day operation. He will oversee the team, help maintain the restaurant’s professional standards and coordinate the new concept.

Preparations for the 11 September opening are already underway, with test cooking sessions taking place and the team taking shape. The aim is to create an experience that goes beyond simply having a meal.

“It is a huge source of pride for me to represent Fúzió at Time Out Market. It is another professional journey and challenge, where we are stepping outside the traditional walls of a restaurant and entering a marketplace where gastronomy and culture meet directly and create a shared experience,” Márton Tibor said.

The team will also help guests navigate the menu, offering explanations and personal recommendations so that diners can comfortably explore a new take on Hungarian bistro cuisine.

If you missed it: Gordon Ramsay chooses Budapest for first Central European restaurant – opening date revealed

A new addition to Time Out Market’s autumn line-up

Fúzió will join Time Out Market Budapest’s existing selection of restaurants and three bars, adding another culinary direction to the venue’s offering.

Located inside the Corvin Palace at Blaha Lujza Square, Time Out Market Budapest brings together chefs, restaurants, drinks and cultural experiences under one roof. Constant curation and renewal are central to the international Time Out Market concept, with new culinary partners regularly joining its venues.

Balogh Olivér, owner of Time Out Market Budapest, said Fúzió represents exactly the kind of new addition the Market is looking for: a distinctive concept offering high-quality gastronomy in a more accessible format.

The arrival of Fúzió will also coincide with a busy autumn at the Market. The venue will celebrate its first anniversary in September with special programmes and offers, while the autumn season will feature seasonal harvest-inspired dishes, wine events and cultural programmes.

Time Out Market Budapest

Address: 1 Blaha Lujza Square, Corvin Palace, 1085 Budapest

Opening hours: Daily, 11:30–23:30. Kitchens close at 22:00, while the last call at the bars is at 23:00.

Fúzió by Textúra & Borkonyha opens: 11 September

Reservations and further information are available through Time Out Market Budapest’s official channels.

World.title: Hungary could publish up to 80,000 names in Communist-era secret service files
World.content:
Hungary could soon see tens of thousands of names revealed from the country’s Communist-era secret service files, with government estimates suggesting that as many as 60,000–80,000 people could be identified.

Bálint Ruff, head of the Prime Minister’s Office, told Telex that the figure was based on professional estimates concerning the potential disclosure of names contained in the files.

“I have an idea of the number,” Ruff said, while stressing that he did not know whether the documents would include people who later became important political or economic figures after the fall of Communism in 1990.

“The agent files are a very important part of our shared past, and there will be many things in them that will cause sadness for many families,” he said.

Who could appear in the files?

The possible publication of tens of thousands of names could make the Communist-era secret service files one of the most politically and socially sensitive historical disclosures in modern Hungary.

Ruff did not say that all of the people whose names could appear were necessarily secret agents or informants. The files may contain the names of people who had various connections to the state security apparatus, meaning that the precise nature of an individual’s involvement would need to be established from the documents.

He also said he did not know whether people who went on to become prominent political or economic figures after 1990 would be among those named.

If you missed it: Hungary submits landmark bill to open Communist-era secret service files

Around 100 documents could be declassified this week

Ruff said he hoped that approximately 100 documents known as “No. 3,000 resolutions” would be declassified and published later this week. He said questions of potential criminal responsibility would have to be decided by investigating authorities.

According to Ruff, the documents concern decisions and contracts that were signed by identifiable officials. He noted that the relevant “3,000” documents were signed by the prime minister in office at the time.

The government has also indicated that it intends to make public information concerning the travels of János Lázár, who served in senior government positions under Viktor Orbán. Ruff claimed that he knew where Lázár had travelled, what he had done and why the information had previously been kept secret. He said these details would also be made public.

Government says complaints involve HUF 2 trillion

The disclosure of the historical documents comes alongside a broader government investigation into the use of public money under previous administrations.

Ruff said the government had so far filed complaints in cases involving a total value of HUF 2 trillion (EUR 5.4 billion).

One of the ongoing investigations concerns Századvég, a Hungarian think tank that Ruff said had received between HUF 20 billion and HUF 30 billion in public money over the past decade for research and studies. He said a criminal complaint would also be filed in connection with that case.

The government has already filed a complaint concerning Observer, a media-monitoring company, over what Ruff described as “exorbitant” sums paid for its services.

He also referred to the Kommentár Foundation, claiming that properties worth “twenty billion” forints had been purchased for the organisation. Ruff added that colleagues were currently calculating the sums paid to the Nézőpont Institute.

The allegations and complaints mentioned by Ruff do not in themselves establish criminal wrongdoing; any potential criminal liability will ultimately be determined by the competent authorities.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

A long-running question in Hungary

The fate of Hungary’s Communist-era secret service files has been a contentious issue for decades. Successive governments have faced pressure to make the records more accessible and clarify the activities of the former state security services. The issue is particularly sensitive because some people who were connected to the Communist-era system later became influential figures in post-1990 Hungary.

If the government proceeds with the planned disclosures, the publication of tens of thousands of names could reignite long-running debates about political responsibility, collaboration with the former regime and the extent to which the past has been fully confronted. For many Hungarian families, however, the revelations could have consequences far beyond politics, potentially exposing secrets that have remained hidden for generations.

World.title: Council of Europe report: Romania makes progress against detainee ill-treatment, but overcrowding persists
World.content:
Romania has made significant progress in preventing the ill-treatment of people held by the police and in prisons, according to a new report by the Council of Europe’s Committee for the Prevention of Torture (CPT). However, the committee warned that conditions in police detention facilities remain very poor and that prisons are operating at 119.5% capacity.

The report presented the findings of a 2025 visit to five police detention facilities, four prisons in Botoșani, Bucharest-Rahova, Craiova, and Iași, and two detention centres for children and young adults in Craiova and Târgu Ocna.

The CPT welcomed the authorities’ “zero-tolerance policy towards ill-treatment” and noted an improvement in police conduct. Most detainees interviewed said they had been treated professionally and respectfully, although the delegation also received some allegations of slaps, punches, and other physical ill-treatment, including from children.

“To further combat ill-treatment and impunity, the authorities should take additional measures such as training in non-coercive interviewing, expanding technological support, and providing prosecutors with their own investigators,” reads the press release.

Conditions in police detention facilities remained “deplorable,” according to the committee. Problems included overcrowding, humidity, poor hygiene, worn mattresses, and inadequate food, while many facilities remained below ground and offered limited access to natural light.

Detainees generally had no meaningful activities apart from one hour per day outdoors, often in small and poorly equipped spaces, the same report found. The CPT warned that prolonged detention under such conditions “could amount to degrading treatment.”

“The authorities should take urgent measures to offer appropriate material conditions and regime. Further, the CPT reiterates that persons placed in pre-trial detention should be under the authority of the National Prison Administration,” it said.

In prisons, the population has increased by 20% since 2020. Overcrowding was recorded at all four facilities visited and was highest in Iași, at 140% of capacity, and Botoșani, at 130%.

Many prisoners had only two to three square metres of living space, compared with the CPT’s minimum recommendation of four square metres in shared cells. Inspectors also found poorly maintained cells, inadequate furniture, worn bedding, and frequent infestations of bed bugs and cockroaches.

While the committee noted “significant progress” in preventing abuse by prison staff, it expressed concern about violence among detainees at Iași Prison and insufficient staffing across the facilities visited. It also called for improvements to healthcare, mental health support, work opportunities and vocational training.

Meanwhile, at the centres for children and young adults, most residents spoke positively about staff. However, the delegation received allegations of slaps and baton blows at Craiova and excessive force at Târgu Ocna, where violence among residents was described as frequent and severe and included sexual assaults.

“The CPT calls for an urgent review of violence-prevention policies and an enhancement of pedagogical approaches. Furthermore, staff working in these centres should not carry batons,” the source said.

In their response, the Romanian authorities said they planned to expand and modernise the prison system through investments between 2026 and 2030. They are also seeking to reinforce staffing within existing budget limits and plan to remove legal provisions treating self-harm and attempted suicide as disciplinary offences.

World.title: Bucharest-Ilfov dominates Romania’s IT sector, with five cities accounting for 85% of total turnover
World.content:
The Bucharest-Ilfov region has established itself as the undisputed leader in Romania’s IT sector, both in terms of the number of companies and the business generated, while Cluj, Timiș and Iași are the other IT hubs in the country, according the "Romanian IT Market Study: Evolution and Perspectives" conducted by the Romanian Economic Monitor team within Babeș-Bolyai University, in partnership with the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) and Transilvania IT Cluster.

The study includes 19,033 Romanian IT companies with recent annual turnover of more than EUR 50,000, according to the ListaFirme.ro database.

Largest counties dominate Romanian IT

In a national ranking of IT businesses, Bucharest leads by far, with a turnover of almost EUR 8.8 billion in 2024 and 6,369 companies included in the analysis, to which Ilfov’s indicators can be added: business worth EUR 1.21 billion and 406 companies. The next-ranked, Cluj, is listed with business worth EUR 2.48 billion and 2,650 companies.

Overall, the five counties (four counties and Bucharest) with the highest turnover account for 87% of total revenues, 75% of total net profit, and 85% of the total number of employees in IT companies in Romania, highlighting the unequal geographical concentration of the IT sector. These are Bucharest, Cluj, Timiș, Iași and Ilfov.

Aside from the largest players, smaller counties are also impressive. Despite the small number of companies included in the analysis (therefore not very relevant at industry level), Călărași County nevertheless ranks first in terms of productivity, having the highest average turnover per employee. Other counties with good scores are Buzău, Ilfov, Tulcea and Ialomița.

IT at city-level

The map created based on turnover at city level highlights several important IT centers that dominate Romania’s IT sector, the top five cities accounting for 85% of its total turnover and employing, in total, more than 136,000 people.

According to the analysis, IT companies in Bucharest recorded rapid growth, with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of turnover of 19.4% (2020-2024), supported by strong profit growth and a stable level of indebtedness, making this city Romania’s main IT center. IT companies in Cluj-Napoca recorded a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 19.8% in turnover (2020-2024), driven by workforce expansion and significant growth in equity, while maintaining stable profitability.

IT companies in Timișoara recorded the highest turnover growth (38% CAGR) among the major cities, with spectacular growth in net profits and significant expansion of equity during 2020-2024.

Meanwhile, IT companies in Iași recorded steady expansion, with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 19.6% in turnover and strong growth in equity, while maintaining a high profit margin.

The strong concentration of the IT sector in a few regional poles has two sides, according to Levente Szász, coordinator of the RoEM-UBB FSEGA team. “On the one hand, it is an important advantage: in university centers such as Bucharest, Cluj, Timiș and Iași, genuine IT ecosystems have formed, in which universities, the critical mass of specialists, multinational companies and local entrepreneurship mutually reinforce each other. This clustering continues to attract investment, talent and know-how and facilitates the emergence of higher value-added activities,” explained Levente Szász, coordinator of the RoEM-UBB FSEGA team, cited by Economedia.

On the other hand, concentration also represents a vulnerability. “A very large part of the industry depends on the development of a few centers and is thus exposed to the same shocks: from reduced external demand and changes in multinational companies’ strategies to the transformation of the traditional business model under the impact of AI,” the researcher added.
