World.title: Feminist activist and writer Gloria Steinem dead at 92
World.content:
Breaking CultureCelebrityVale Feminist activist and writer Gloria Steinem dead at 92 James Costa September 3, 2026 — 8:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

American journalist and second-wave feminism leader Gloria Steinem died at age 92 on Wednesday, according to a post on her official Instagram account. “Yesterday, Gloria Steinem passed away peacefully at her home in New York City, surrounded by some of the many who loved her,” the post read. Gloria Steinem speaks onstage during Visionary Women in November 2019. Getty Images for Visionary Women Steinem was a leading activist for the second-wave feminism movement in the late 1960s and 70s, which focused on sexuality, reproductive rights, and critiquing patriarchal social structures and institutions, among other issues. Former US President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2013 for her work in the women’s liberation movement.



“Gloria’s near-century on earth were years well-lived, and she continued working for equality until the very end,” the post said. Steinem also wrote and contributed to publications, including New York Magazine, Esquire, The New York Times, and Cosmopolitan, and co-founded the feminist magazine, Ms. “She spent her recent years doing the two things she loved most: being in community with others and writing,” the post read. “Gloria loved the tradition of lighting signal fires on hills to light the way to the other side of the mountain. Lighting your own candle for Gloria makes you part of this global and celestial community circle.“



Steinem’s forthcoming book, titled An Unexpected Life, is a memoir of her early life and her journey to activism. It is due to be released in late September. Gloria Steinem at a New York City gala in November 2022. Getty Images The Instagram post shared a quote from the book, “I have now lived for more than fifty years in this brownstone, in rooms that have witnessed lives before mine, and will know others after I am gone.” “This book, along with her commitment to her home becoming a centre for social justice movements, are among the many gifts Gloria has given the world with the hope they have ripple effects for generations to come,” the post said. Steinem was born in Toledo, Ohio in 1934.

World.title: Schools need to tackle the vile manosphere
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Schools need to tackle the vile manosphere September 3, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Matt Davidson To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Matt Canavan blames the “feminisation of the school curriculum” for pushing boys towards toxic online material (″⁣Contos sounds alarm on manosphere″⁣, 3/9). Does this mean that we should also blame young female teachers, many of whom are considering leaving teaching, because they are being targeted by boys making disgusting suggestions and displaying disrespectful behaviour in the classroom and school grounds? His suggestion that the school curriculum is pushing boys towards the manosphere is ludicrous. Revolting people like Andrew Tate and other online personalities use their platforms to make money by targeting young males using outrage and extreme political and misogynistic views. This is what schools need to address. As to getting more male teachers, Canavan must think he has come up with a unique idea, but that problem has been around for decades and while there are various reasons for the lack of male representation, the pay scale is a major factor. Teaching just does not pay enough compared to other professions.

Helen Ross, Northcote Parents, be the No. 1 role models

Benjamin Preiss penned a thoughtful article on parenting in today’s world (″⁣The complex task of parenting as social media reigns″⁣, 31/8). While I do not envy today’s parents with the challenges they are facing, parenting children has always been a very difficult and stressful job. Every generation has had its challenges and difficulties. As humans we grow and mature in similar ways to what we always have done and this includes significant transitions during adolescence. For most of us (and our children) maturity to adults brings a better understanding of who we are and where we fit in. Parents need to realise that they are the most influential models of their children and strive to be good parents rather than ″⁣friends″⁣ . Good role models, including examples of how to deal with modern social media, are very important.

Shaun Quinn, Yarrawonga Mentorship as a preventative action

The revelations (″⁣Schoolboys expelled for misogyny and threats″⁣, 2/9) that the influence of the manosphere ideology is infiltrating secondary schools to the extent that boys are refusing to show respect and follow directions from female teachers – culminating in the expulsion of boys from school – should ring alarm bells with all who strive to uphold gender equality and respect as a guiding principle of life. One can only imagine the effect this has on the mental health of female secondary teachers. For this reason, the actions and statements from our elite sportsmen, social influencers and music artists are so important in modelling proper respect for women.

One way to counteract this insidious counter culture would be to flood schools with high-profile young men to mentor male students and model respectful relationships. To those who receive the adulation and financial rewards of fame in our society should come the responsibility of modelling respect for women, social inclusion and the debunking of misogynist philosophies. Let’s take preventative action now rather than relying on expulsions and sanctions after the event.

Graeme Lechte, Pascoe Vale



Women and girls deserve proper response

The expulsion of two Sandringham College boys for threatening female staff comes as a recent Monash survey found nearly 80 per cent of teachers had seen or experienced gendered violence. Both indicate that hostility towards women and girls among teenage boys is worsening. Something has to change. The federal government’s instinct is to review and strengthen consent and respectful relationships programs. That may be the right thing to do. My concern is that after a decade of these programs we still have little solid evidence that they work, and there is a plausible risk that boys who feel lectured about the failings of their sex go looking for somewhere they feel welcome, and find it in the toxic online manosphere. I don’t know whether that is happening. Does anyone? That uncertainty is the thing to fix. We should fund proper trials, compare approaches, and be willing to drop what does not work. Existing programs should continue while we find out, but the girls and women bearing the cost of this abuse deserve a response built on evidence.

Paul Henry, Murrumbeena THE FORUM Power to the people

Jemena notified us in early August about “essential maintenance” works in our area (“Suburban fury stalls data centre power pole plan”, 3/9). Great we thought. Preparing to ensure supply over summer. We should have been more suspicious. There was a massacre of our street tree canopy, cutting of outdated cables left trailing in our front yards and street closures.

Maintenance day arrived. Cars were moved early, a warm alternative place to spend the day found and a women’s book group was re-scheduled.

What did Jemena define as “essential maintenance”? Fifteen-metre concrete poles to carry 22,000 volts. Ugly new poles on every corner and some extra ones in between. It’s new infrastructure, Jemena – for data centres. I know why Jemena didn’t inform us. We leftie/greenie Yarravillians would not have co-operated. We would have parked our cars in the street.

We could have sneaked out in the dark and filled in the holes with rubbish. And my older women book group might have staged a sit-in protest (with chairs) but no removal of our tops!

Do you blame us?

Rae Swan, Yarraville Underground thinking

In all the research trips taken by politicians, I wonder if any of them have thought to ask how every European city, large and small, has managed to put its electrical services underground. This allows uncluttered sky and street views with trees that retain their natural shape and provides a calm and attractive environment, all within the challenge of narrow, often cobblestone streets without footpaths, centuries-old buildings and limited access.

We did put the NBN underground, and now my heart sinks when I see proposals such as the new pylons in Yarraville.

Heather Barker, Albert Park Yikes, Yarraville

As if Yarraville has not had enough huge trucks running through their streets, now there’s massive electricity poles. Yarraville is a place of narrow streets, so good on the community for standing up.

However, this may be just the tip of the iceberg: what suburb could be next? I would like to see the company trying to install them in Brighton.

If the government sits on its hands lord knows what Melbourne will be like if these data centres need massive amounts of power. These huge poles could end up anywhere. The government needs to listen to the people. We are the ones who will pay the price.

Forward thinking is needed here otherwise government can expect a backlash.

Nola Cormick, Albert Park



Good after bad

During a recent visit to the Latrobe Valley One Nation announced its Victorian energy policy. Its Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, said he would not allow Loy Yang A power station to close in 2035 as planned. The reason this closure date has been chosen is obvious: the company that owns it knows it would be grossly uneconomic to maintain what, by then, will be a highly unreliable coal-fired generating plant that’s more than 50-years-old. To extend its life beyond 2035 the Victorian government would have to underwrite its ongoing uneconomic operation. In other words, Victorian taxpayers will have to pour good money after bad. How much and for how long is unknown because Pickering didn’t say.

Kevin Bailey, Croydon Not prepared

Do our politicians understand the science of climate change? There is a difference between understanding the science and grasping what 2.6°C of warming will actually mean for life on Earth (″⁣Pacific anger at Australia after climate target failure″⁣, 3/9). Our governments acknowledge that climate change is happening and that further warming will create serious risks. Yet the political discussion is often framed around emissions targets, renewable energy, economic costs and achieving net zero. These are important, but they can obscure the much larger issue. A world around 2.6°C warmer than before industrialisation would resemble conditions experienced millions of years ago. We have never had to maintain modern cities, agriculture, water supplies and infrastructure in a climate this warm.

This raises a fundamental question: are our politicians really planning for the climate we are heading towards? Reducing emissions remains essential, but it is only part of the challenge. We also need to prepare for how a hotter and more unpredictable climate will affect our communities, ecosystems, food production and water supplies. Politicians may understand the numbers, but understanding what those numbers mean for everyday life is another matter. That gap deserves much greater attention.

Paul Caine, Glen Huntly Worlds apart

Perhaps your correspondent (Letters, 3/9) inhabits a different world? “Sure, fix the roads. Then what? Stop building the SRL? Then what?” That would be enough to swing votes down this end of the woods. Killing off SRL East releases billions for desperately needed infrastructure in the western suburbs; and our hospitals, schools, libraries, nurses, teachers, national parks and environmental remediation – and not just potholes.

As for “Victoria, as the most progressive state in the nation”, why not simply tell those who are fed up to ignore widespread crime, violence and corruption? Looks like we’ll need the LNP assisted by One Nation to tackle the “heavy lifting”.

James Richardson, Langwarrin Everyone a winner

So my home is worth less than it was a year ago? Great! Just possibly, with a lot of hard saving, my Gen Z daughter might have a fighting chance of getting into the market one day. And if I want to upgrade my home, the proportionate reduction in the sale price will be really helpful. What’s not to like? Investors might lose out? No worries, they will hang onto their tax benefits thanks to grandfathering. Everyone’s a winner.

Chris Millgate-Smith, Sandringham Better planning needed

My sister recently decided to downsize so we went looking at apartments and townhouses. It was illuminating as to how bad design could be.

My favourite was the (empty) bathroom-laundry space where you could not open the washing machine door due to the adjacent toilet. But allowing more of the sort of profit-driven rapid development that the planning minister is proposing with rapid fire four dwellings on a block subdivision will mean more of this rubbish development.

Instead, we need a process between councils and the state to identify and develop sites with increased density, suitable for long-term living. Near where I live a 1-hectare block was sold a couple of years ago. It could have been developed into 16 to 20 well-designed apartments or town houses with a central area of shared open space, preserving some existing trees. But it was subdivided into eight ″⁣luxury″⁣ blocks. Currently, there are three treeless Mcmansions, a medical centre and an application for a large childcare centre despite one directly across the road. Located near shops and transport it is the sort of opportunity lost to provide well designed, climate friendly housing.

We need government that looks for better opportunities rather than quick fixes.

Clancy Briggs, Berwick



Bereft of ideas

The federal government is adding fuel to a global catastrophe while giving token support to the plight of our Pacific neighbours. Sadly neither the Coalition nor One Nation have policies that would see them do better.

Kevin Fahey, Red Hill Dream of humanity

It seems so morally conflicted that while everyone is desperate to save lives in Nepal, others are desperate to destroy lives in the Middle East and the Ukraine and elsewhere. Humanity first.

Marisa Spiller, Harrietville Changing banks

Re the Commonwealth Bank’s 13-year slugging of fees for an inactive card (″⁣CBA charged customer fees on an unactivated card for 13 years″⁣, 2/9), so much of corporate customer service is anonymous and heartless.

After 50 years as a loyal CBA customer who never once missed a credit card payment, I fell short by a single day last month. The bank’s response to half a century of fidelity? An immediate $80 penalty.

It was the straw that broke the camel’s back.

After five decades, I changed banks.

Jodie Brown, Northcote Erosion of quality

According to numerous articles I have read in The Age, people are losing base-level jobs due to AI, financial fraud cases are increasing due to AI, students and job applicants are cheating using AI, cases are thrown out of court due to legal staff using AI, young people are not learning how to reason, analyse and construct arguments or proposals due to relying on AI.

If the majority of people don’t want huge data centres because they cost jobs, they drain huge amounts of resources at the expense of the community, and the centres require mega power poles cutting through residential areas, could someone please justify why we must be subjected to all this?

Our quality of life is being eroded, not improved.

Julie Christensen, Blackburn Nth Chipping away at us

What a pity our common sense hasn’t kept up with our intelligence.

AI and much of what it is producing is taking away what it is to be human.

Robyn Williams, Sale



AND ANOTHER THING Power poles

Those Jemena power poles in Yarraville (″⁣Suburban fury stalls data centre power pole plan″⁣, 3/9) will look terrific with added Christmas decorations, props for all seasonal events and celebrations.

Margaret Skeen, Ocean Grove If the data centres are using their own or recycled power, why do they need giant power poles in suburban streets?

Barbara Lynch, South Yarra Congratulations to the residents in Yarraville who are protesting against the ugly power poles. Keep up the good fight.

Mary Fenelon, Doncaster East I didn’t realise “cloud” storage meant data centre power poles had to actually touch the cloud.

Paul Custance, Highett



Furthermore

Donald Trump and his war against Iran seems to be channelling Mark Twain giving up smoking. Making peace is the easiest thing in the world: Trump has done it dozens of times.

Kevin Prince, Trieste, Italy Imagine. One Nation demanding energy freedom for all – solar, batteries and plug-in vehicles. Instead, years of high power bills due to public funding of decrepit coal power plants (″⁣AGL warns Hanson coal power plan will lift power costs″⁣, 3/9).

Jenny Henty, Canterbury RIP holding global warming to 1.5degrees. Those who have allowed fossil fuel pollution to grow over the past 40 years despite the warnings bow your heads in shame (″⁣Pacific anger at Australia after climate target failure″⁣, 3/9).

Jenny Smithers, Ashburton Will Anthony Albanese explain to the Pacific Island Forum in Palau why his government has approved 36 new or expanded fossil fuel developments since coming to power?

Ian Bayly, Upwey Finally

Surely, a major cause of the potholes must be the unnecessarily large cars, vans and trucks pummelling their way down the streets these days.

Jacki Burgess, Port Melbourne

World.title: Thinking of trying for a baby? Beware the false promises of ‘trimester zero’
World.content:
LifestyleHealth & wellnessFertility Thinking of trying for a baby? Beware the false promises of ‘trimester zero’ Courtney Thompson September 3, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

For as far as we’ve come in technological advancements to help people conceive, fertility is still – largely – something we cannot control. Unless, that is, you believe what you might hear in one of the thousands of videos about trimester zero on social media. Describing the three-to-six-month period of preparation before a couple starts trying for a baby, trimester zero has emerged as a popular – and profitable – concept among wellness and parenting influencers, some who claim that by following certain rules or protocols, you can prevent future fertility issues. It’s an attractive concept. But is it true? Age is one of the biggest determining factors. Aresna Villanueva



What is trimester zero? Related Article Fertility Behind the rise of the ‘fertility test’ – and why doctors say it’s misleading women Coined by American sociologist Miranda R Waggoner in 2017 to describe the shift in emphasis on preconception care in public health approaches to women of childbearing age, she argued trimester zero creates undue pressure for women to be in a perpetual state of “pre-conception”. Since then, the idea has been co-opted by the wellness industry, which pedals expensive and extensive guides, supplements and toxin-free products with the message that in buying and using them, you can prevent future fertility issues. Often, the emphasis is on what women can do in this preconception period but, as Dr Jessica Dunleavy explains, men have just as big a part to play.



“Men’s preconception health has a huge impact on not only fertility, but the health of the pregnancy and the health of the offspring,” explains Dunleavy, a fellow in School of BioSciences at the University of Melbourne, noting that male factors account for an estimated 50 per cent of infertility issues. What does the evidence say? It’s true that if you’re preparing to try to conceive, starting three to six months out is a good idea. The main things that will impact your fertility are age, weight and genetics. Most supplements, guides and strict advice pedalled by influencers about trimester zero are not backed by science and will not make a difference in your efforts to conceive. But there are some things you can do to put yourself in the best position to try to fall pregnant.



In this time, you should stop drinking, smoking, vaping or doing drugs. Smoking has been proven to be detrimental to egg and sperm health. Alcohol consumption can be detrimental to sperm quality, lower testosterone production, and make it harder to achieve an erection. For women, there is no established safe level of alcohol consumption, so experts recommend stop drinking altogether when you start trying, says Dr Vijay Roach, an obstetrician, gynaecologist and former president of the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists. He notes that age is one of the biggest determining factors in a woman and man’s fertility and due to the rising average age of first parenthood, it’s more relevant than ever because the older you are, the more likely you are to have put on weight, develop high cholesterol or be at greater risk of diabetes in pregnancy or preeclampsia. “So getting older is not necessarily helpful for somebody who’s planning to be pregnant.” Likewise, sperm quality is closely correlated with age. “Males produce sperm for their whole life, but sperm quality does decline with age,” Dunleavy says.



Most experts say the best advice for any couple thinking of having a baby is to start trying naturally. If you’re under 30 and don’t fall pregnant after 12 months, go to your GP to investigate further. If you’re over 35, you should investigate if you haven’t conceived naturally after six months. Related Article Exclusive

Parenting Can mothers prevent passing on mental illness? This new study offers insight The best place to start is with a visit to their GP or specialist, says Dr Kath Whitton, gynaecologist and specialist with IVF Australia: “Get a comprehensive screening for your medical history, review medications and get infection screens for immunity to certain things like chickenpox and rubella.” Genetic carrier screening is also recommended. One option is a test for the woman to see if she is a carrier for cystic fibrosis, spinal muscular atrophy and fragile X syndrome, which is covered by Medicare.



Expanded genetic carrier screening for both partners is also available, checking whether the couple carry the same genetic mutations, therefore putting them at risk of having a child with a genetic disorder. The out-of-pocket cost for this can be between $700 and $1500. Put on your own oxygen mask The importance of the psychosocial health of wannabe parents can be an underestimated factor of preparation says Julie Borninkhof, clinical psychologist and chief executive of Perinatal Anxiety & Depression Australia (PANDA). “You can’t give from an empty basket. So if you’re worn out, if you’re overwhelmed, your ability to help seek is lessened,” Borninkhof says. Roach agrees that when you visit your GP or specialist, they should be screening for your psychosocial history: “That might include their family history or own experiences of anxiety and depression in the past. And always, always, always screen for domestic violence because following the birth of a child is one of the highest risk times for domestic violence.”



What to eat and how to train Changes to diet and exercise can have a positive effect on your overall health, but for women, they won’t improve the quality of your eggs, says Roach. “Having a more balanced diet in terms of our nutrient intake might improve your general health, but your fertility will only be improved via weight,” he says. In women, weight and body mass index (BMI) has been found to affect the hormonal balance that regulates the menstrual cycle. As such, studies have found that women with a BMI over 27 are three times more likely to struggle to conceive naturally. This is why women with type 2 diabetes or PMOS can struggle with fertility: both are often linked with obesity.



Commonly, the first line of treatment for these conditions is working with a personal trainer or dietician because in modifying their diet or exercise routine, they lose weight, which will balance their hormones, resulting in a more regular menstrual cycle and improved fertility. Related Article Fertility ‘Social egg-freezing’ is on the rise, but at what cost? The exact causes of male infertility are still unknown, but Dunleavy says in roughly 50 per cent of cases, they believe it’s genetic. So for those men, you can be the picture of health and still run into problems. Sperm are, however, more sensitive to environmental insults, making it especially important for men to be eating well and looking after themselves. Given sperm are made every three months, these lifestyle choices can have an impact on sperm quality. Dunleavy says prolonged excessive heat exposure is damaging for sperm, so best to avoid

“sitting your laptop on your lap and spending 10 hours in the spa”. She also recommends avoiding microwaving food in plastic as the chemicals can interfere with their endocrine system.



For both women and men, having a well-rounded diet that incorporates healthy vegetables, fruits, protein, fibre and healthy fats is beneficial. As such, the Mediterranean diet is most commonly recommended. Likewise, there aren’t any particular exercise routines that will impact your fertility, but general advice is to hit the recommended 150 minutes of vigorous exercise per week. What about supplements? Women should start taking a supplement with folic acid and iodine as soon as they’re thinking of trying to conceive, says Whitton. “Folic acid supplements should be started at least one month before conception, but we like to see it started about three months prior,” Whitton explains.



“Data suggests that it significantly reduces the risk of neural tube defects, which form from the very beginning of pregnancy. “Iodine is much the same; it’s about thyroid hormone production, which is really important because that drives foetal brain and nervous system development, and deficiencies in pregnancy can be linked to impaired cognitive development in children.” For men, Dunleavy says there are no broad guidelines as the data is limited and somewhat mixed. “Focusing on a well-balanced, healthy diet is best as opposed to relying on any supplements.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. Get it in your inbox every Monday.

World.title: Middlemore Hospital swamped in 'appalling' late-night surge of patients
World.content:
An emergency department (ED) doctor at Auckland's Middlemore Hospital says there were more than 100 people waiting to be seen late on Wednesday night.

They told RNZ it was an "appalling" situation for all involved.

They said Middlemore hit 103 patients waiting in queue at 11.15pm, with seven doctors rostered overnight.

They said these patients were in addition to those already under treatment and waiting for beds.

Last year's record was 109 patients, they said.

The nurses union says nurses described the past 24 hours as hectic, staff swamped with patients with medical issues stemming from the flu.

Health New Zealand group director of operations for Counties Manukau, Vanessa Thornton, said in a statement there were 457 presentations to Middlemore's ED in the 24-hour period from midnight on Wednesday, following consecutive days of high demand for care.

Earlier on one of the days in August, Middlemore's ED saw 494 presentations - the highest number of patients over a 24-hour period for this year.

Thornton said the demand reflected increased seasonal illness in the community.

"Additional staffing and operation support is being brought on at Middlemore, and we are reviewing elective services.

"Where appropriate, patients are being moved from Middlemore to Manukau Health Park to improve hospital flow, and we are looking to maximise the use of Hospital in the Home and work regionally with other hospitals to improve patient flow and free up capacity."

"Hospital in Home" allows eligible patients to receive hospital-level care in their own home rather than staying in hospital, a Health NZ communications staffer explained.

RNZ has approached HNZ for comment on whether patients from Middlemore ED have been transferred to other regional hospitals on Wednesday.

New Zealand Nurses Organisation (NZNO) president Anne Daniels, who's also an ED nurse at a tertiary hospital, questions how HNZ will find the resourcing to help with the situation at Middlemore Hospital.

"On the face of it they're actually doing something, I'm pleased that they got a plan in place, "but the fact is that all those strategies require resourcing and there aren't enough nurses, we know that for a fact - we know there's a total recruitment freeze, even though there's 1400 vacancies on Te Whatu Ora's job list for nurses," she said.

Daniels said hospital transfers for sick patients require nurses, and she wonders whether the people HNZ are assigning those jobs are competent to do the transfers.

She pointed to a report by NZNO that found New Zealand public hospitals were short of 587 nurses for every shift in 2024.

Daniels said while "Hospital in Home" is a good strategy, district nursing staffing is already overstretched.

"All of these things are a sign of desperation," she added.

Hospitals already weren't coping before the flu came, and now the influx of flu patients has made existing problems in the health system more visible, said Daniels.

She said EDs across the country were struggling.

Daniels said she took a neighbour into ED three times these past few weeks and was "flabbergasted" at what she saw.

World.title: Conservation bill clause puts economic growth ahead of conservation, critics say
World.content:
The government has kept a controversial clause in its Conservation Amendment Bill, which critics say undermines the purpose of conservation law.

The draft bill, released by the Environment Select Committee, retains clause 6(ea) which says the Department of Conservation (DOC) should recognise and enable "economic opportunities" on conservation land to "the greatest extent practicable".

Greenpeace spokesperson Gen Toop said the government was attacking the fundamental principle of conservation land.

"What we are talking about here is public conservation land - that is land that is supposed to be protected and preserved for nature to thrive and for the public and for future generations to enjoy.

"It is not land that has been set aside for economic exploitation, but that is what this government is trying to change the law so it will be able to happen on that land."

Conservation Minister Tama Potaka backed down from other proposed changes earlier this year which would have made 2.8 million hectares of conservation land eligible for sale.

The revised bill has removed those changes.

But Toop said the bill was still "rotten to its core".

"We expect that if they are able to pass this bill we will see more mines - more open cast mines - on public conservation land.

"It's our opinion that conservation land should be a place where the native wildlife of New Zealand can thrive, and it should be a place we protect, for future generations can enjoy."

She said a proposal to set up visitor amenity areas on conservation land, which included toilets, visitor centres, accommodation, car parks, restaurants and cafes, was also controversial.

Toop said there were very few safeguards from development in these areas - and one day could see conservation land locked away for private luxury resorts.

"We do not want to see ancient forests felled for car parks."

Toop said she expected thousands of people to march against the bill later this month.

Green Party MP Ricardo Menéndez March was also against the clause.

"Allowing economic development at any cost without the consideration or protection of the environment will simply see environmental degradation and profits put over people and the planet."

Conservation Minister Tama Potaka said submissions were ongoing and he expected further amendments to the bill before the final report due in November.

He said the redrafted version of the bill was a procedural step to remove the land exchange and disposal provisions from it.

World.title: All Blacks bring in fresh legs for third test against the Springboks
World.content:
All Blacks coach Dave Rennie has made three changes to his starting XV for Sunday morning's third test against the Springboks in Johannesburg.

Hooker Codie Taylor, who started in the first and second tests, has been replaced in the run-on side by Asafo Aumua, who gets his first start in the test series after some impressive performances coming off the bench.

Taylor has been left out of the matchday 23, with Samisoni Taukei'aho coming into the reserves.

George Bower and Tyrel Lomax are retained as the starting props.

Sam Darry, who hasn't featured in either of the first two tests, starts at lock alongside Tupou Vaa'i, pushing Fabian Holland to the bench.

Peter Lakai, who was also impressive coming off the bench in Cape Town, will start at blindside flanker, with Simon Parker, who started at No. 6 last weekend, omitted from the matchday 23.

Peter Lakai will start at blindside in the third test against the Springboks. Photosport

Luke Jacobson remains at openside with captain Ardie Savea at No. 8.

Wallace Sititi will make his first test appearance in the series, coming into the 23 as loose forward impact.

The starting backline remains the same as last weekend with Cam Roigard and Ruben Love in the halves, Jordie Barrett and Quinn Tupaea in the midfield and Damian McKenzie, Will Jordan and Leroy Carter in the back three.

Prop Ethan de Groot and lock Josh Lord, who missed the second test with concussion, have cleared concussion protocols, but Rennie decided it would be best to give them another week to recover.

With the series tied 1-1 both sides are desperate to win the last test on South African soil before the fourth and final match in Baltimore in the US.

Sunday morning's (NZT) match is at the Soccer City stadium in Soweto, Johannesburg, which holds about 94,000 fans.
